items.mnemonic_text: 'What, ah, she?' — no, watashi means I.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a tanuki knocks over the shiny new security mirror by the till and freezes, nose to nose with itself. It taps the glass, tilts its head, and decides, flatly, that the animal staring back must be the most important customer in the store: itself. From then on it restocks the onigiri shelf for nobody else, certain of exactly who it means when it talks about I.
items.reading_mnemonic: The tanuki taps the glass and gasps at what it sees — <reading>what a shiny</reading> creature — then realizes it's only its own reflection, saying <reading>わたし</reading>, I, over and over, delighted that the shiniest thing in the konbini turned out to be itself.

items.mnemonic_text: watashi plus tachi: I and my group, we.
items.meaning_mnemonic: On the mossy steps of Grandma Kane's shrine, one cat rings the enormous bell and every other cat in the place mobs the sound, wedging in shoulder to shoulder until they're one solid, purring mass on the step. Ask any single cat its name and the whole pile answers at once, because as far as they're concerned there's no such thing as one cat here anymore, only the pile. That fused, shoulder-to-shoulder answer is the meaning you want: we.
items.reading_mnemonic: Try to pet just one cat in the pile and the whole mass yowls back what sounds like <reading>what a she, touchy</reading> bunch — really the cats shouting <reading>わたしたち</reading>, we, in one voice, refusing to be split apart even for the bell.

items.mnemonic_text: A boy says boku when he means I.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a boy waist-deep in the current catches nothing all afternoon, and when a fish finally leaps straight into his rival's net instead of his own, he plants his rod in the mud and announces to the whole bank that he, personally, will be the one telling this story later — not his friend, not the fish, him. That flat, proud claim to being the one talking is the meaning you want: I, said the rough, boyish way a kid says it.
items.reading_mnemonic: He slaps his soggy fishing log down on a rock and reads the cover aloud in a gruff voice, <reading>book</reading>, <reading>book</reading>, until it slurs into <reading>ぼく</reading> — the plain, boyish way to say I that he now uses for himself as often as for the log.
items.description: Used mainly by men and boys, in casual to neutral speech; it reads as too soft or boyish for very formal contexts and is rarely used by adult women.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till breaks and starts beeping the same word at whoever steps up to pay — anata, anata — refusing to learn a single name. Customers give up introducing themselves and just answer to it, until the word stops being rude and becomes the only way anyone in that line ever gets addressed: you.
items.reading_mnemonic: あなた is written exactly the way it sounds — plain kana, no kanji hiding a different reading — so the word you say is simply 「<reading>あなた</reading>」.
items.description: In real conversation あなた is used sparingly — Japanese usually addresses people by name or title, and aiming あなた at a stranger or superior can sound distant or even confrontational; it is most naturally heard from a wife speaking to her husband.

items.mnemonic_text: A close 'kimi' for you, my friend.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the coach's whistle breaks, so instead of names he just barks the same word at whichever kid is nearest the ball — kimi, kimi — pointing, never naming. By the end of practice the whole team answers to it, the casual, jabbing word you'd only ever aim at a friend or someone younger than you.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the sports field at Sei's school, a scruffy stray dog answers only to the coach's shout of <reading>きみ</reading> — it sounds just like calling out <reading>key, me!</reading> while he jangles his whistle-keys — and the dog comes running to whichever kid the coach is jabbing a finger at.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a heron keeps prying the side mirror off a toy car and dropping it at the feet of whichever man happens to be standing closest, like a tiny crown. The locals start calling that unlucky guy by the same word every single time — and since he's always some woman's boyfriend waiting there for her, the word settles on him: he, boyfriend.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a heron drops a plastic toy <reading>car</reading> at your feet, and someone mutters <reading>かれ</reading>, eh, nodding toward whichever man it landed nearest — and the name sticks to him alone, every single time the bird does it.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi points across the konbini at the kneeling <kanji>woman</kanji> restocking the onigiri shelf, arm sweeping the row into place. He doesn't explain, just tilts his head and grins: that's the one he's been talking about all week. You don't need more than that look to know she's his girlfriend, and now you know who she is too.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, she keeps introducing the same woman standing by the bell alongside a man named Joe: Kane, and Joe. Say it fast — <reading>Kane-Joe</reading> — and you land on <reading>かのじょ</reading>, the word for her, the girlfriend everyone at the shrine already knows by name.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini you jab a finger at the onigiri closest to you, ignoring the whole shelf behind it. The cashier doesn't ask which one — pointing already decided it. That's the one you meant, this one, and nothing else on the shelf matters anymore.
items.reading_mnemonic: これ is kana all the way through, no kanji hiding underneath — just read <reading>これ</reading> exactly the way it's written.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini a customer holds an onigiri up under your nose, and your pointing finger is so sore from a full shift at the beeping till that you can barely straighten it. You waggle the sore finger at the rice ball sitting there in his hands and grunt. Whatever is over by him, close enough for him to touch — that one.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it is said, <reading>それ</reading>, so there is no reading to decode.
items.description: Points at something near the person you are talking to, rather than near you — the middle rung of the near, middle, far set. It stands alone as a pronoun, so it never sits directly in front of a noun; the form that does that is a separate word.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail you and a stranger both stop and squint at the vending machine glowing at the very summit, hopelessly far from either of you. All you can manage is a long flat ahh, and the stranger adds a defeated eh. Nobody is reaching it today. Not near you, not near them, just a speck up the slope — that over there.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kana only, said exactly as it is written: <reading>あれ</reading>, with nothing to decode.
items.description: Used for something far from both you and the person you are talking to, not merely far from you. It also does duty for a thing you both already know about but is not present — the that in that trip we took — which is why it turns up so often in conversation with no object in sight.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Sei's school hallway has twelve identical doors, and behind exactly one of them a ball is bouncing. You work down the row knocking on every door, and each knock comes back the same hollow thud, so you start rattling handles instead. Twelve doors, one ball, and only one question left in your head — which one.
items.reading_mnemonic: Written in kana just as it sounds, <reading>どれ</reading>, so there is nothing to work out.
items.description: Asks you to pick from three or more things in view. When the choice is between exactly two, Japanese uses a different question word instead. Like its near and far partners, it stands alone as a pronoun and is not placed directly before a noun.

items.mnemonic_text: kore's cousin that hugs a noun: this ___.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You are in Koichi's konbini holding a waffle cone, and the beeping till will not stop until you name what you are buying. You do not know the word for cone, so you jab it at Koichi and repeat cone-oh, cone-oh until he gives up. He rings up whatever you are jabbing at: this cone, this onigiri, this rice ball — always the one right here in your hand.
items.reading_mnemonic: There is nothing to decode here: the word is written in kana exactly as it is said, <reading>この</reading>.
items.description: Always attaches directly to a noun and never stands on its own. English happily says I want this with nothing after it; this word cannot do that, and a bare this needs a different standalone word. It marks the thing as near you, the speaker, rather than near the person you are talking to.

items.mnemonic_text: sore's cousin that hugs a noun: that ___.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Your friend is squatting on the riverbank with three soaked shoes lined up beside them, and you are holding a sonar gun that refuses to lock onto anything near you. It only pings at objects sitting next to somebody else, whining so-no, so-no as it swings toward them. Whatever it picks out is that shoe, that bucket, that dripping thing over by your friend.
items.reading_mnemonic: No decoding needed: this word is spelled in kana precisely as it is pronounced, <reading>その</reading>.
items.description: Attaches directly to a noun and never stands alone. It points at something in the listener's zone rather than yours, so a thing in their hand or on their side of the table takes this word even where English would say this. It also picks up something the other person has just mentioned, with nothing visible to point at.

items.mnemonic_text: are's cousin that hugs a noun: that ___.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail a goat sits down across the path and will not budge until you say what you are climbing toward. You point at the vending machine improbably parked at the summit, a speck against the sky, and groan ah, no, not that far. The goat only accepts things too distant to touch: that vending machine over there, that peak over there.
items.reading_mnemonic: Nothing hidden in this one: it is written in kana exactly the way it is spoken, <reading>あの</reading>.
items.description: Attaches directly to a noun and never stands alone. It points at something far from both you and the listener, or at something you both already know about even when it is nowhere in sight. Stretched out on its own, with the first vowel held, it is also the ordinary hesitation noise, roughly English um, and carries no pointing sense at all.

items.mnemonic_text: dore's cousin that hugs a noun: which ___.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the onigiri shelf holds forty identical rice balls, and the man ahead of you has frozen solid, finger hovering back and forth while the till beeps behind him. Which one, which one, which one — he can never land on an answer, and now the whole line is stuck asking the same thing he is: which.
items.reading_mnemonic: どの is written in kana exactly as it's read, with no kanji to decode — just sound out <reading>どの</reading> as it appears on the page.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane rings the shrine's one enormous bell every morning, but the rope has vanished among the mossy steps and circling cats. She stamps one paving stone and declares the rope must be tied down right there, jabbing the ground: here, here, here — and that exact stamped spot is where it's always been.
items.reading_mnemonic: ここ is pure kana, read exactly as it looks, so there's no hidden kanji to unpack — <reading>ここ</reading> is simply pronounced as written.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, someone drops a sandal mid-crossing and it snags on a rock partway across the water. You point at the exact spot from the near bank, arm out straight, calling out to the person wading in: there, there, no, THERE — the sandal never moves, but your pointing finger fixes the place for good.
items.reading_mnemonic: そこ is written entirely in kana the way it sounds, with no kanji standing behind it — you read <reading>そこ</reading> exactly as it's spelled.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a stray sock slips off the washing line and drifts downstream before anyone notices. By the time someone looks up, it's bobbing far off, snagged on a rock past the bend — not here, not nearby, just over there. That distant, can't-quite-reach spot is exactly what this word points at: over there.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it's read — <reading>あそこ</reading>, nothing more to decode.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Partway up the mountain trail, a hiker's bag splits open and rice balls tumble everywhere. She scrambles after them, asking every passerby the same question over and over, all the way to the vending machine at the top: where did they go, where did that one land, where is the last one. The whole climb becomes one word, repeated: where.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it's read — <reading>どこ</reading>, no hidden reading underneath.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, on the sports field, the coach spots a shy transfer student hovering by the gate and waves the whole team over with one arm: this way, everyone — then, turning to the team, this is our new player. One gesture does both jobs, aiming a direction and introducing a person, which is exactly what this word covers: this way, this person.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it's read — <reading>こちら</reading>, nothing to derive.
items.description: This is the polite register: it is what you use to gesture someone toward a direction in front of others, or to introduce a person formally (a host presenting a guest, a clerk directing a customer), not casual chatter between friends about where something is.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You're already at Koichi's till, practically leaning on the register, when you ask where the onigiri is. Koichi doesn't even look up — he just tilts his chin two feet toward the shelf you're basically touching and grunts the sound out, because when the thing you want is that close, all you need to say is that way.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know そ, ち, and ら from other kana words; <reading>そちら</reading> just strings them together into the sound <reading>"so-chee-rah"</reading>, read exactly as it's spelled, no twist to catch you out.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a tourist bows too deep and asks, ever so formally, where the enormous bell hangs. Grandma Kane doesn't just point — she straightens up, sweeps her whole arm in a slow, ceremonial arc past the mossy steps and every lounging cat, all the way to the far tower, because when the distance is real and the company deserves manners, you don't jab a finger — you gesture, grandly, over there.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know あ, ち, and ら from other kana words; <reading>あちら</reading> just strings them together into the sound <reading>"ah-chee-rah"</reading>, read exactly as it's spelled, nothing hidden underneath.
items.description: This is the polite, distance-marking form of "over there" — the one you use with strangers, customers, or anyone above you in status, not the clipped, casual version you'd use with close friends. Point far away formally, not with a jabbed finger.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You've dragged yourself up the mountain trail to the one improbable vending machine at the top, expecting relief, and instead find the path splits into two identical forks beyond it. The machine hums, unhelpful as ever, while you stand there turning your head between both paths, asking the trail itself, out loud, which way.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know ど, ち, and ら from other kana words; <reading>どちら</reading> just strings them together into the sound <reading>"doh-chee-rah"</reading>, read exactly as it's spelled, no surprises left to decode.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi is standing behind his own register, holding up the onigiri that is already in his hand, insisting to the customer that no substitute will do — only this kind of rice ball, the exact one gripped between his fingers, right here and nowhere else.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is written the way it sounds, straight kana, so <reading>こんな</reading> is read exactly as it looks — no hidden reading to hunt for.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat knocks the enormous bell clean off its stand, and when she's told it was an accident she just stares at the wreckage — that kind of excuse, the kind aimed right back at whoever just spoke, never quite convincing her.
items.reading_mnemonic: Like its cousins, this word is pure kana, so <reading>そんな</reading> is pronounced exactly as spelled, with nothing underneath to decode.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Partway up the mountain trail, Sei points at the vending machine improbably perched at the summit, far beyond arm's reach, and mutters that only that kind of machine — the distant one neither of them chose — would end up all the way up there.
items.reading_mnemonic: This is another kana-only word, so <reading>あんな</reading> is simply read as written, with no separate derivation needed.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a clerk named Donna refuses to just ring anything up. She grabs every item — onigiri, drinks, gum — and interrogates the shopper: what kind of rice is inside, what kind of flavor, what kind of wrapper. The beeping till never moves on until she gets an answer to her only question: what kind of.
items.reading_mnemonic: どんな is written exactly as it sounds — kana only, nothing to dig for — just read <reading>どんな</reading> straight through as it's written.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the enormous bell rings itself in the dead of night. The cats scatter, the mossy steps creak, and no one is standing anywhere near the rope. Grandma Kane storms out onto the steps demanding an answer to the only question that matters: who.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every night the bell rings and nobody's there, so Grandma Kane leans out over the mossy steps and bellows into the dark: who <reading>dares</reading> touch my bell? The cats scatter at the challenge in her voice, and that same dare is exactly the sound of <reading>だれ</reading> — the question of who it could possibly be.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, past the lone vending machine, a hiker meets a stranger wrapped head to toe against the wind. Too winded to be casual, they bow deeply and ask with careful formality: might I ask, to whom do I have the honor of speaking? The mountain answers only with silence, and the polite question just hangs there: who, respectfully asked.
items.reading_mnemonic: どなた is written exactly as it sounds, kana only — read straight through as <reading>どなた</reading>, no hidden reading to derive.
items.description: This is the polite version of the plain word for who, used when asking after a stranger, a guest, or anyone you would address formally, the way English shifts from a blunt who's that to who, may I ask. Save the plain form for friends and family instead.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A frazzled nanny in the echoing hallways of Sei's school is handed things by a toddler all morning: a wet sock, half a stapler, a beetle that is still alive. She has stopped guessing what any of it is. She just holds each object out at arm's length and asks the one flat question that covers all of it — what.
items.reading_mnemonic: The same <reading>nanny</reading> takes a night shift at Koichi's konbini, and every time the beeping till coughs up an item she does not recognise she holds it over the onigiri shelf and says <reading>なに</reading> at the ceiling. By closing she has said it forty times and solved nothing.
items.description: On its own — as a bare question, or with most particles — the word takes this reading. When a counter, the plain copula, or a word beginning with a t, d, or n sound follows, it switches to the shorter reading you learn separately.

items.mnemonic_text: nani shortened to nan before counters.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Cats keep arriving on the mossy steps of Grandma Kane's shrine, and you gave up asking what a cat is hours ago. Every question you have left comes with a number stuck to it: how many cats, what floor they have reached, what time they stop. This is the shape the question takes when a counter follows — what, before counters.
items.reading_mnemonic: A tiny <reading>nun</reading> has claimed the vending machine at the top of the mountain trail and runs it like a ticket window. She will not press a button until you say <reading>なん</reading> and then the counter for what you want, and she makes you start again if you mumble the number.
items.description: This is the same word as the standalone question, wearing the shape it takes when a counter, the plain copula, or a word beginning with a t, d, or n sound follows it. You almost never meet it alone; it arrives glued to whatever is being counted.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A heron standing in the shallows at the riverbank wears a wristwatch and answers questions for free. You ask about the water going down: it's two. You ask about the ferry: it's two. You ask about getting your own watch back off its leg: it's two. Ask a heron anything and it hands you a time, so the question you are really asking is when.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it is said, so <reading>いつ</reading> is both the spelling and the reading — nothing to decode.
items.description: English lets you say when for both the question and the joining word, as in the sentence about what happens when it rains. This word only does the question. The joining sense uses different grammar entirely.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a fisherman reels in his line for the ninth time and finds nothing but a waterlogged boot, same as the last eight. He doesn't swear, doesn't sigh — he just plants his feet in the mud, glares at the current, and asks the only question left standing: why.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it sounds: <reading>なぜ</reading>.
items.description: なぜ reads as blunter and more formal than a casual why — common in writing, official questions, and pointed interrogation. Dropped into an ordinary chat with a friend, on its own it can land as accusatory rather than merely curious.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till beeps and charges double for the same onigiri, for the third night running. Koichi stares at the receipt under the fluorescent lights, not with a customer's cool complaint but a genuine, immediate splutter — why, how come, what is going on here.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it sounds: <reading>どうして</reading>.
items.description: どうして carries more feeling than a neutral question — it often doubles as an exclamation of surprise or frustration, how did this even happen, rather than a calm request for a reason, and it's the version heard far more in casual conversation than in writing.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, one impossible vending machine hums between the trees, accepting a coin no one on the trail carries. A hiker who just spent an hour climbing pokes button after button, turns to a stranger nearby, and asks the only sensible question left: how does this thing even work.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it sounds: <reading>どう</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane catches a cat dragging a rice offering off the shrine's mossy steps. Instead of shouting, she bows a fraction and asks, syrupy with formality, how the day has been treating it. The cat freezes mid-theft, offering still in its mouth, trapped by the world's politest how. Courtesy, not curiosity, is the whole word.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it sounds: 「<reading>いかが</reading>」.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A kid parked at Koichi's till points at the leaning tower of onigiri and demands how many are stacked there. Koichi starts counting, and halfway through, the kid swivels and asks the identical question about his age. The tower wobbles, forgotten, as Koichi answers both with the same flat number — how many and how old are one demand wearing two coats to this kid.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it sounds: 「<reading>いくつ</reading>」.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A hiker drags himself up the mountain trail to the vending machine improbably waiting at the top, expecting water. The display keeps climbing past every price he's paid for a drink, digit by digit, as he jabs the button asking how much this could possibly cost. It never stops long enough to answer — the only punchline the machine needs.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it sounds: 「<reading>いくら</reading>」.
items.description: いくら written this way is also the everyday word for salmon roe, the bright orange fish eggs served over rice — a completely different word that happens to share the same sound and spelling. Context sorts them out fast: paired with a price or a question, it means how much; sitting on a plate, it means the food.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the <kanji>time</kanji>-sun still crawls its slow arc overhead. A dazed tourist wanders in, squinting up, unable to read a single hour off it, and grabs a passing cat to blurt the same question over and over: what <kanji>time</kanji> is it? Her whole visit is just that one question: what time.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the shrine, a jetlagged traveler keeps calling to her grandmother, 'Nan, gee, what time is it?' — sliding into <reading>Nan-gee</reading> each time. The cats now answer back with that same sound, <reading>なんじ</reading>, since that's all anyone there asks: what time.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the team spends the entire match slipping on the wet grass, missing every shot, while the goalkeeper falls asleep against the post. The final whistle blows, the scoreboard locks in one flat, humiliating number, and the whole bench stares at it in silence. That number is zero.
items.reading_mnemonic: ゼロ is spelled exactly the way it sounds — read the katakana <reading>ゼロ</reading> straight through, no hidden reading to dig for.
items.description: ゼロ is the everyday spoken form, heard in scores, phone numbers, and casual temperature talk; formal or written contexts often reach for a different, more formal word instead.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the vending machine on the mountain trail, a ranger posts an official notice board each morning with the exact temperature. One frost-bitten dawn, the mercury refuses to rise past the middle line at all, and the ranger stamps the report with one stiff, formal number before trudging back down. That number is zero.
items.reading_mnemonic: The ranger reading the thermometer is named Ray, and he announces temperatures stiffly, formally, no contractions ever. He reads the number in one clipped word, <reading>れい</reading> — <reading>Ray</reading> only sounds this formal when the mercury freezes at zero.
items.description: 零 is the formal, written register for zero — the word you'd see on an official temperature report or hear in a stiff announcement, not the one you'd use casually reading out a phone number or a game score.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Judging her own talent show yet again, the smug goat holds up a single hoof and announces the score before anyone can ask: <kanji>one</kanji> out of one. There was only ever one entrant, one stage, one strip of dirt to stand on, so the number was settled before the show even began. She says it like a verdict, not a count: one.
items.reading_mnemonic: One line, one reading: 一 alone still reads <reading>いち</reading>, the same reading you already learned for it standing by itself.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The waiter arrives to ask how many are dining and finds his answer already snapped in half on the table: two chopsticks, a short one laid over a long one, matching exactly like the pair of raccoons who broke them that way. He doesn't need to count paws underneath — the <kanji>two</kanji> sticks already told him. Table for two.
items.reading_mnemonic: 二 alone already reads <reading>に</reading>, the same reading it carried in the chopstick story — nothing new to learn here.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A teacher taps a chalk pointer against three stacked lines on the board, one, two, three, and by the third tap the class already knows what word is coming before she says it. There is no trick to uncover here: <kanji>three</kanji> lines stacked in a character just spells the word three, plainly, the way it has all along.
items.reading_mnemonic: 三 alone already reads <reading>さん</reading>, the same reading you counted out tapping the three lines.

items.mnemonic_text: Four kicking legs in a box: yon.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Behind the beeping till at Koichi's konbini sits that same sealed box, the mouth still trapped inside counting onigiri through the glass. Tonight it's a slow delivery — one, two, three — and on the next rice ball the mouth presses flat against the glass and stops. That flattened stare is the number stamped on this word: <kanji>four</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Nothing to derive here — 四 already taught you the <reading>よん</reading> reading, the same stretch you reach for right before a big <reading>yawn</reading>.

items.mnemonic_text: The alternate, ominous reading of four: shi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the same sealed box waits among the mossy steps, its trapped mouth still murmuring numbers into the corner. A cat swats it off the step and the lid cracks — the mouth peeks out just far enough to hiss a hushed <kanji>four</kanji> before a monk claps the lid shut, refusing to let it say the number again.
items.reading_mnemonic: That hushed <reading>し</reading> is the same reading 四 already taught you — the clipped <reading>shh</reading> the monk uses to cut the mouth off mid-count.
items.description: This reading of 四 sounds identical to a much darker word, so hospitals, hotels, and gift-givers avoid it — floor numbers, room numbers, and counted items switch to the other reading, よん, instead. Learn to recognize both, but default to よん when you're the one speaking.

items.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, that same hooked hand reaches out from beside the vending machine, snagging snacks lined along the ledge. It's already got four stacked in your arms when the crooked hook swipes once more and lands a fifth off the top shelf. One hook, five snacks: that's the word for <kanji>five</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: That practiced swipe already speaks the <reading>ご</reading> reading you learned for 五 — the clipped <reading>go</reading> you mutter to yourself right before you reach.

items.mnemonic_text: A hat over two legs: roku.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, eight cats are sprawled across the mossy steps at dawn. She sets the heavy iron offering lid down with a clang right on the top step, and two cats bolt at the sound, tails high. What's left staring up at the enormous bell is <kanji>six</kanji> cats, thoroughly unimpressed by the racket. The lid on top of eight, as always, leaves <kanji>six</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 六's reading here is just the number's own reading you already learned: <reading>ろく</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: By the door of Koichi's konbini, the coat hook is really just one bent nail sticking out of the wall. A delivery driver piles dripping rain jackets onto it between beeps of the till, one after another, until the nail bends almost flat under the weight. You count the jackets before it snaps: <kanji>seven</kanji>, all hanging off one crooked hook.
items.reading_mnemonic: 七's reading here is the one you already know from the kanji itself: <reading>なな</reading>.

items.mnemonic_text: The alternate reading of seven: shichi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: In Sei's school hallway, the same bent-nail hook holds gym jerseys instead of coats. There's only one hook by the lockers, so seven players fresh off the field cram their jerseys onto it at once, the nail sagging nearly sideways under the pile. The coach counts before it gives way: <kanji>seven</kanji> jerseys, all balanced on one crooked hook.
items.reading_mnemonic: 七's reading here keeps the reading you already learned for formal counting: <reading>しち</reading>.
items.description: しち is the older, more formal reading of 七 — used in compounds, in reading dates and times aloud, and in fixed set phrases. なな is generally preferred when counting items alone or aloud, since しち can be mistaken for the word for one in quick speech.

items.mnemonic_text: Strokes opening like the number eight: hachi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Those two strokes are still splitting wider at the bottom, the same spread that already meant <kanji>eight</kanji> when you met the kanji alone. Let that split happen four times over, fanned out beneath one twitching body, legs still moving until there are eight of them — a spider, standing on exactly the number this word names.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word borrows 八's own reading untouched, so it's read exactly <reading>はち</reading>, the same sound you already learned for the kanji itself.

items.mnemonic_text: A hook at the top of the count: kyuu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The hook is still propped at the last switchback of the mountain trail, right where you left it leaning into <kanji>nine</kanji>. This time it's snagged a sock, blown off a line at the riverbank and dragged all the way up, caught fast on the hook at the top — bend nine, the last one, the whole climb done.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word just keeps 九's own reading, so it's read exactly <reading>きゅう</reading>, the same sound you already learned for the kanji by itself.

items.mnemonic_text: The short reading of nine: ku.
items.meaning_mnemonic: That same hook is on closing duty tonight, yanking down the shutter at Koichi's konbini one slat at a time. It catches, drags, catches again — nine short tugs before the shutter seals shut, and the last tug is the one that lands on <kanji>nine</kanji>, alt reading and all, right as the beeping till goes quiet.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a lone dove has nested in among the cats, and none of them touch it. When the bell rings, it doesn't screech — it lets out one flat <reading>coo</reading>, over and over, and that flat sound is exactly how this word is read: <reading>く</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the till beeps once for every raised finger, and the cashier keeps raising both hands until every finger is up, tracing the same <kanji>ten</kanji> cross in the air. The till stops beeping exactly when both hands are full — ten, and not one beep more.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is just the kanji 十 on its own, so it keeps exactly the reading you already know: <reading>じゅう</reading>.

items.mnemonic_text: White sheets counted a hundred times: hyaku.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane lights one stick of incense at the shrine, and the smoke catches the white glow off the mossy steps until it multiplies before her eyes, exactly like that lone stroke stacking over the whiteness. By the time she looks up, the courtyard cats have multiplied to match — a whole <kanji>hundred</kanji> of them prowling the steps.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is just the kanji 百 by itself, so it keeps exactly the reading you already know: <reading>ひゃく</reading>.

items.mnemonic_text: Ten multiplied by a slash: sen.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the lone vending machine's price display multiplies without warning: one bold slash scratches straight across the readout, the same slash that once capped that plus-sign cross into something bigger, and the number keeps climbing past every digit until it locks on one round <kanji>thousand</kanji> and finally stops beeping.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is just the kanji 千 on its own, so it keeps exactly the reading you already know: <reading>せん</reading>.

items.mnemonic_text: A single mark for ten thousand: man.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Someone climbs a ladder to recount the banner's zeros herself, licking a finger to peel back each heavy fold of cloth. Her arms give out before the counting does, so she chalks a final total on the last scrap of space and declares the stall sold out at <kanji>ten thousand</kanji> onigiri — not one more, not one less.
items.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just 万 read <reading>まん</reading>, exactly like the banner kanji you already know.
items.description: Japanese counts large numbers in blocks of ten thousand rather than thousands, so 万 anchors the whole system used for big figures. English commas group by thousands, so converting between the two takes practice — a million lands on a multiple of ten thousand here, not on a clean round number.

items.mnemonic_text: One counted the native way: hitotsu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Backstage after her talent show, the goat is handed a raffle box to count the night's takings. She digs through it hoping for more, but there is exactly <kanji>one</kanji> ticket rattling around inside, no stub, no runner-up prize. She holds it to the light anyway, satisfied that at least one thing tonight was worth keeping.
items.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just 一（ひと）plus the counter つ, giving you <reading>ひとつ</reading> exactly as you'd expect.
items.description: This is one of the native Japanese numbers used for counting generic objects, distinct from the Chinese-derived counting series paired with counter words for people, flat objects, and so on. It stands on its own without a separate counter attached, up through ten items.

items.mnemonic_text: Two counted the native way: futatsu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The second raccoon inspects the snapped chopsticks on the table, short stick over long stick, and realizes they aren't cutlery anymore — just identical wooden splinters. It pockets both, satisfied that whatever it's counting tonight, the tally stops right there at <kanji>two</kanji> things, no broth-soaked evidence left to explain.
items.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just 二（ふた）plus the counter つ, giving you <reading>ふたつ</reading> exactly as you'd expect.
items.description: Like its sibling word for one item, this is a native Japanese number used for counting generic objects on its own, without a separate counter word attached — distinct from the Chinese-derived counting series paired with counters for people, flat objects, and so on.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You're at the riverbank stacking flat stones into a cairn, the way the character for <kanji>three</kanji> stacks its own three flat lines. items.reading_mnemonic: 三 already carries the reading <reading>みっ</reading>, and つ stays つ, so together they give you exactly <reading>みっつ</reading> — three things, built straight from readings you already know.

items.reading_mnemonic: 五 already carries the reading <reading>いつ</reading>, and つ stays つ, giving you exactly <reading>いつつ</reading> — five things, straight from the readings you already know.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The hook by the konbini door already sags under a full row of <kanji>seven</kanji> coats, bent halfway into the wall from the weight. A customer tries to squeeze one more sleeve onto it and the whole thing groans, but the hook holds firm — it was built to carry exactly seven things and not one more.

items.reading_mnemonic: 八 reads やっ here and combines with the counter つ, giving you 「<reading>やっつ</reading>」.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Hana reaches switchback <kanji>nine</kanji> on the mountain trail, exactly where hikers lean their hooked canes against the rock to catch their breath. Someone already got there first — not one cane but a whole row of them, hooked over the same ledge like abandoned question marks. She counts twice to be sure: nine things, propped together at the ninth bend.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word simply takes 九's kun'yomi reading ここの and adds つ, the counter for physical things, giving 「<reading>ここのつ</reading>」.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, someone has arranged the onigiri into a stack of perfect crosses — the <kanji>ten</kanji> mark hikers make with two raised hands when they reach a full count. There are ten of them lined up by the register, each shaped like that same cross, and the till beeps once for every single one as the clerk recounts them. Ten things, stacked in crosses at the counter.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is just 十's kun'yomi reading standing alone as the number word for ten things: 「<reading>とお</reading>」.

items.mnemonic_text: The present moment, right now: ima.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat ducks under the eaves the instant the rain starts — exactly the <kanji>now</kanji> image, a person taking cover under a wide roof, caring about nothing before or after. It won't budge from that dry spot even when the enormous bell rings, because for that cat there is no later, only this exact drip-free moment: now.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Ducking under that same wide roof, the <kanji>now</kanji> person refuses to think about yesterday or tomorrow — this instant is all there is. Beside them, through the barred window, the <kanji>day</kanji>'s sun blazes straight in, swallowing the doorway in light. That flood of light, happening right now, on this day: today.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till only sounds its <reading>cue</reading> once every rotation, right as sunrise floods the doorway. Grandma Kane hears it, checks the light, and mutters 「<reading>きょう</reading>」 — the one signal that tells her which day she's actually standing in.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture that same barred window from the <kanji>day</kanji> story, sun and all — except now it's already downriver. The current has carried the whole sunlit frame past the bank, out past where you could ever wade in after it. Whatever daylight you missed while it drifted by is gone for good: yesterday.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every evening, Grandma Kane's shrine cats knock her <reading>keno</reading> ticket off the mossy steps, and by the time she finds it, the numbers already belong to a closed draw. She reads them anyway and sighs 「<reading>きのう</reading>」 — already over, every time.

You can feel it waiting just behind the horizon, ready to flood in the moment this window opens again. The day still queued up behind that glass is tomorrow.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the vending machine stocks one item: a single <reading>ashtray</reading> that never fills, no matter how much ash hikers tap into it. It's saving that ash for a day that hasn't come yet — 「<reading>あした</reading>」, tomorrow, one climb away.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The trailing runner is so far <kanji>behind</kanji> the pack he misses today's finish line entirely. He staggers past the sun's <kanji>day</kanji> window just as it flips shut — then flips shut again before he arrives. Two whole days close inside that window before he shows up, so nobody calls it tomorrow. It's the day after tomorrow.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the mountain trail's vending machine, a hiker drops a salty tray of dried squid clean over the edge. It bounces ledge to ledge so long that two sunrises pass before it clatters to a stop below, and by then everyone agrees the <reading>a salty tray</reading> landed on <reading>あさって</reading> — the day after tomorrow.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The smug goat is certain her one-contestant talent show already happened — she just can't recall which sun-window <kanji>day</kanji> it played in. She backs through yesterday's window, then one more window behind that, since in her world there is only ever <kanji>one</kanji> winner. Two windows back is where she finds it: the day before yesterday.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a scruffy otter drags the same battered toy from the water, swearing it's the first time. The other otters know better — they watched that toy sink two mornings back, on <reading>おととい</reading>, and nobody tells the <reading>otter</reading> <reading>toy</reading> story twice.

items.mnemonic_text: The 'ah' when the sun rises: asa.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi bolts a plastic rooster above the konbini door that shrieks the instant the shutters roll up — never at lunch, never at night, only in that grey hour when the sky is still dim and the onigiri shelves are half-stocked. That first shriek of the day is morning, whether Koichi likes it or not.
items.reading_mnemonic: Each dawn the rooster mounted above Koichi's door screeches <reading>あさ</reading> into his ear, and it comes out sounding exactly like <reading>ah, sir</reading> — a rude little wake-up call Koichi has never forgiven. That screech, not the sunrise, is what actually starts his morning.

items.mnemonic_text: The bright middle of the day: hiru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail the vending machine unlocks its second slot only once the sun sits directly overhead — no earlier, no later. Hikers who arrive starving learn to wait for that one narrow window, because whatever the machine drops then is the only lunch they get: noon, dead center of the day.
items.reading_mnemonic: A hiker collapses at the mountain-trail vending machine at midday, and it dispenses a bandage instead of a drink, printed with the words <reading>heal you</reading> — which is exactly how <reading>ひる</reading> sounds when the machine's speaker crackles it out at noon, every single day.

items.mnemonic_text: The direction the day fades: yuugata.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine the enormous bell only rings once the light turns orange and the mossy steps fill with cats — never at noon, never after full dark, only in that hinge between day and night. That one ring marks evening arriving, gonged out over a hundred cats who all seem to expect it.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every dusk the shrine cats surround Grandma Kane and yowl what sounds exactly like <reading>you got a</reading> curfew, and it's true: the bell tolls <reading>ゆうがた</reading> the moment the sky goes orange, and every cat scatters home for the night.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the automatic doors sigh shut for the day just as the fluorescent sign outside buzzes off, leaving one register light glowing over the empty onigiri shelf. That last dim bulb holding on while everything else goes dark is the whole picture: evening has arrived, and night is settling in right behind it.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the caretaker everyone calls <reading>Ban</reading> shows up right as the sky bruises purple, unlocking the gate for the evening service while the cats crowd the mossy steps behind him. His arrival marks the hour itself — <reading>ばん</reading>, evening settling over the shrine.

items.mnemonic_text: When you 'yo, roll' into bed: yoru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Every cat in the neighborhood gathers on Grandma Kane's mossy shrine steps only once the enormous bell has gone silent and the sky has turned fully black, packed shoulder to shoulder in a way they'd never risk in daylight. That one pitch-dark hour when they finally show themselves is the only word for it: night.
items.reading_mnemonic: The oldest cat on those steps is known only as <reading>Yore</reading> — legend has it she's kept watch since days of <reading>yore</reading>, though nobody living has ever actually seen her arrive. She only appears once <reading>よる</reading> falls, prowling the shrine in total dark before vanishing again by sunrise.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the sundial's shadow first thing in the morning, still sprawled out long across the ground, well <kanji>before</kanji> it ever shrinks down to nothing at <kanji>noon</kanji>. That's the storefront's awning logic all over again — the part that greets you first, out ahead of the rest of the day. This whole early stretch, before noon ever swallows the shadow whole, is a.m., the morning half of the day.
items.reading_mnemonic: It's just the readings you already know, stacked together: 午 as ご plus 前 as ぜん gives you <reading>ごぜん</reading>, morning laid out in front of noon.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The instant the sundial's shadow vanishes into the <kanji>noon</kanji> line, the trailing runner finally lurches into motion — he's always <kanji>after</kanji> everyone else, and now he's after noon itself. Every stride he drags out from there on, still trailing that line behind him, happens in the afternoon.
items.reading_mnemonic: 午 already reads ご and 後 already reads ご, so 午後 just stacks those two sounds straight into <reading>ごご</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The wind-up alarm clock that means <kanji>every</kanji> is bolted straight onto the window-with-a-bar that means <kanji>day</kanji>. It doesn't wait for the sun to climb — the second it rings, it drags the window open by force, hour after identical hour, and daylight has no choice but to show up. That's every day.
items.reading_mnemonic: 毎 gives you まい and 日 gives you にち, so stack them exactly as taught and you get <reading>まいにち</reading> — no surprises here.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The wind-up alarm clock that means <kanji>every</kanji> doesn't sit on a nightstand — it sits on the windowsill, cranked so tight that the instant morning light touches it, it detonates. Every morning: same crank, same detonation, same jolt out of bed. You can set your dawn by it.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every morning, Sei's school gate creaks open for a boy called Asa — never late, never early, wound up like clockwork. Call the roll and mutter that <reading>my Asa</reading>'s here again, and you've said <reading>まいあさ</reading>. Same boy, same gate, every single morning.

items.meaning_mnemonic: That wind-up alarm clock that means <kanji>every</kanji> got smuggled onto the riverbank and buried in the mud with its key still poking out. At the same instant each night, the current winds it tight and it clangs itself off in the dark, startling every fish for a mile. Same hour, same racket, every night.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every night at Grandma Kane's shrine, the enormous bell tolls once for a caretaker named Ban, who never misses a shift. The cats grumble that <reading>my Ban</reading>'s back on the mossy steps — and that's exactly <reading>まいばん</reading>: same bell, same watchman, every night.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The wind-up alarm clock drags itself onto the calendar page, walking the winding path one square at a time and ringing at every stop. Once it clanks around the whole seven-day loop and lands back at the start, it winds itself straight back up to walk the same route again, without fail. That's a clock stuck doing <kanji>every</kanji> single <kanji>week</kanji> on repeat.
items.reading_mnemonic: 毎 keeps its taught まい and 週 keeps its taught しゅう, combining exactly as expected into <reading>まいしゅう</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The wind-up alarm clock sits on its shelf watching the crescent moon through the window, refusing to ring until it fattens, fades, then swings back to that same thin sliver. Only once that full swing is done does the clock finally clank off — then winds itself right back up to keep watching, without fail. That's the clock marking off <kanji>every</kanji> single <kanji>month</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 毎 keeps its taught まい and 月 keeps its taught つき, combining exactly as expected into <reading>まいつき</reading>.

That's the clock marking <kanji>every</kanji> single <kanji>year</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 毎 keeps its taught まい and 年 keeps its taught ねん, combining exactly as expected into <reading>まいねん</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>now</kanji> person, still huddled under their roof ignoring past and future, turns out to be standing right on the calendar page — the winding path of the <kanji>week</kanji> loops directly under their feet. items.meaning_mnemonic: The tree at the crossroads is still waving <kanji>come</kanji> at anyone nearby, but now it's leaning off the far edge of the calendar page, calling toward the square just past the current loop of the <kanji>week</kanji> — beckoning travelers to a loop that hasn't even started. items.mnemonic_text: The week ahead of now, past: senshuu.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The person under that wide roof stops watching the rain and looks up through a gap in the tiles at the crescent hanging there. items.meaning_mnemonic: The tree at the crossroads still waves in every traveler for shade, but tonight it's packed solid. items.meaning_mnemonic: You invite the scarecrow to take cover under the roof right <kanji>now</kanji>. It's used to standing out in the weather for a full <kanji>year</kanji> at a time, but you decide it deserves to stay inside for this year.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You are buying an onigiri at the fluorescent-bright convenience store. items.meaning_mnemonic: You are sitting on the riverbank with a massive pie. You use a heavy knife to chop off a <kanji>minute</kanji> wedge to throw to the ducks. The ducks completely ignore the pastry and aggressively bite your ankles for an entire minute.
items.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this word is exactly what you learned for the kanji: <reading>ふん</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You stare at the clock as the minute hand hits the bottom, turning the face into a giant exclamation point split right down the middle. That exact moment when the hour is chopped in <kanji>half</kanji> means it is half (past).
items.reading_mnemonic: Since you already know the reading for this kanji, you know the reading for this word is <reading>はん</reading>.
items.description: You will see this attached directly to hour counters to say half past the hour.

items.mnemonic_text: The end of the week: shuumatsu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You trace the winding path for the <kanji>week</kanji> until you run out of calendar page completely and your finger slips off the paper. Dropping off the edge of that grid lands you right in the weekend.
items.reading_mnemonic: You spend your entire weekend at the riverbank scrubbing the mud out of your car's <reading>shoe mats</reading> (<reading>しゅうまつ</reading>). You wash them for two days straight, completely ruining your actual weekend.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You peer through a window at the <kanji>sun</kanji>, only to realize it is just a painting inside a massive <kanji>weekday</kanji> calendar square. Before you can process the trick, a real <kanji>sun</kanji> rises behind it and sets the whole paper structure on fire to celebrate Sunday.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know the readings for the kanji in this word, so you just put them together to get <reading>にちようび</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The squawking birds on your <kanji>weekday</kanji> calendar square are completely asleep under a thin crescent <kanji>moon</kanji>. They stubbornly refuse to wake up and look at the window showing the morning <kanji>sun</kanji>, because everyone is too exhausted on Monday.
items.reading_mnemonic: Since you learned the readings for these kanji already, combining them gives you <reading>げつようび</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You flip your calendar to check the <kanji>weekday</kanji>, but the square for today's <kanji>day</kanji> is completely charred. Looking closely, a tiny sparking figure made of <kanji>fire</kanji> is running around inside the window frame, burning up the paper. You sigh. The calendar always bursts into flames on Tuesday.
items.reading_mnemonic: Since you already know the reading for each kanji, you can simply put them together to form <reading>かようび</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every <kanji>weekday</kanji>, you stand by the riverbank to watch the <kanji>sun</kanji> come up, but today a massive geyser of freezing <kanji>water</kanji> blasts out of the river and knocks you flat into the mud. You scrape yourself off, remembering that this mid-week flood always happens on Wednesday.
items.reading_mnemonic: There are no new sounds to learn here, just combine the kanji readings you already know into <reading>すいようび</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You arrive at Sei's school for a normal <kanji>weekday</kanji> of classes, but looking out the window, a massive <kanji>tree</kanji> has smashed right through the sports field to block out the <kanji>sun</kanji>. The principal announces over the intercom that classes are cancelled, which is typical for Thursday.
items.reading_mnemonic: You can sound this word out by stringing together the readings you learned for its component kanji to get <reading>もくようび</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You go into Koichi's konbini to buy a single onigiri to start your <kanji>day</kanji>. When the till beeps, Koichi doesn't ask for regular yen; he demands a literal pile of <kanji>gold</kanji>. You complain that this is the only <kanji>weekday</kanji> he does this, and hand over your treasure because it is Friday.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is completely regular, so just read the kanji exactly as you learned them to get <reading>きんようび</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: On the calendar, Saturday's square holds a wooden cross planted into the page, dirt piling around its base — <kanji>earth</kanji> dug into the paper. Beside it crowds a tangle of feathers marking the square as a <kanji>weekday</kanji>, while a windowed frame shows the sun climbing to start the <kanji>day</kanji>: earth, weekday, and day stacked on one square make Saturday.
items.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just the pieces you already know lined up in order: 土（ど）＋曜（よう）＋日（び）＝<reading>どようび</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The smug goat's one-contestant talent show — one stage, one prize, one judge, all her — only ever opens the instant the sun first climbs through the windowed frame of a brand new <kanji>day</kanji>. She refuses to be anything but <kanji>one</kanji>, so she insists on staging it the very moment each month's sun rises for the first time, never later. That stubborn need to go first, first day, every single month: the 1st.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane opens the shrine on the very first morning of the month and finds her legs unbearably <reading>too itchy</reading> — poison ivy from clearing the mossy steps. She scratches through the whole ceremony, grumbling that the reading for this day, <reading>ついたち</reading>, always shows up with an itch she can't shake.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The raccoon's broth has already gone cold once, but true to form, a second raccoon slips in and snaps its own chopstick to match the <kanji>two</kanji> lines exactly — and it only ever happens after the sun has climbed back through the window to open a fresh <kanji>day</kanji>. By the time the matching ritual is finished, that first day is gone and a second one has quietly started: two days, four paws, still nobody eating.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini clerk trips over the same forgotten mop bucket two mornings running and lands flat on his back, socks soaked both times, groaning that his feet have gone <reading>footsore</reading>. Everyone at the register agrees this is just how <reading>ふつか</reading> goes — the second day is always the one that actually gets you.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Stack the <kanji>three</kanji> flat lines on top of each other and each one turns out to be its own tiny windowed frame with a sun climbing up through it — a triple-decker calendar. One <kanji>day</kanji> passes on the bottom line, then the middle one lights up, then the top, and the sun never bothers waiting around for a fourth: three days, no more, no less.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei collapses after the third whistle blast on the sports field, and the nurse says she's gone <reading>meeker</reading> by the hour — flu, straight home for <reading>みっか</reading>, three full days in bed before anyone lets her back on the field.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Trapped inside the enclosure, the mouth keeps counting under its breath, and on the try that decides everything it finally lands on <kanji>four</kanji>. The instant it shouts the number, the window's bar snaps back and the <kanji>sun</kanji> pours through into a brand new <kanji>day</kanji>. Four counted breaths, one sunrise — that's the 4th, four days gone.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the onigiri shelf is stocked with egg yolks instead of rice this morning. He counts them rolling off one by one — one, two, three — and on the <reading>yolk</reading> that nearly hits the floor he calls out <reading>よっか</reading>, the fourth yolk saved just before day four's shift ends.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The hooked hand sweeps the shelf one more time, snagging snacks until the last crooked pull lands a perfect <kanji>five</kanji>, its fifth catch of the morning. By the time it stacks them by the window, the bar overhead has swung wide and the <kanji>sun</kanji> is climbing into a fresh <kanji>day</kanji> — five snacks, five days counted off on the shelf.
items.reading_mnemonic: Partway up the mountain trail, the hiker stops at the lone vending machine and <reading>eats a</reading> whole bag of chips — her fifth stop like this today. She sighs and calls it <reading>いつか</reading>, day five of pretending she'll pace herself.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The eight stands tall until someone claps a lid on top, capping it down to <kanji>six</kanji>. That very lid turns out to be the window's bar swinging shut over the <kanji>sun</kanji>, sealing off one whole <kanji>day</kanji> at a time — six lids, six sunsets, and that's the 6th, six days gone.
items.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank a cow wades in to wash off and lets out six long moos in a row, counting each one on its hooves. On the sixth <reading>moo</reading> it wobbles and calls out <reading>むいか</reading> before toppling into the current — six days, six moos, one soaked cow.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The bent nail hook holds seven coats until one more lands and it creaks under the weight, confirming <kanji>seven</kanji>. Framed just behind it, the window's bar lets the <kanji>sun</kanji> through for one more <kanji>day</kanji> to close out — seven coats, seven days, the 7th of the month.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine the enormous bell tolls seven times, and on the last strike she looks up bewildered and mutters '<reading>Nan, oh, kah</reading>?' — her way of asking if it's really day seven already. The cats don't answer, and <reading>なのか</reading> is what she calls the day from then on.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every <kanji>day</kanji> the sun climbs through its window and lights the same crack in the riverbank ice — a crack shaped exactly like the splitting legs of <kanji>eight</kanji>. Each sunrise splits it wider: one, two, three, all the way to the eighth. By the eighth sunrise the ice has split clean into two drifting halves, eight days of widening, and it's officially the eighth.
items.reading_mnemonic: A yoga instructor greets every sunrise with a pose that curls her spine into two loops, exactly like the number eight. She names this ritual her <reading>yoga</reading> day, and said quickly in Japanese it comes out as <reading>ようか</reading> — the 8th, eight days of practice in.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every <kanji>day</kanji> a fresh sun climbs through its window and lights one more switchback on the mountain trail, but you don't stop until the final bend, the one curled like a cane — the shape of <kanji>nine</kanji>. Eight sunrises come and go while you climb. On the ninth sunrise you finally round that hooked bend and lean your whole weight on the cane at last: nine days of switchbacks to reach the ninth.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, past the hooked bend of nine, a vendor next to the lone vending machine sells nothing but <reading>coconut</reading>s, shouting the word at every exhausted hiker. It sounds close enough to <reading>ここのか</reading> that hikers now just call this spot the ninth — nine days of trail to reach a man and his coconuts.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every <kanji>day</kanji> the sun climbs through its window and finds you at the shrine steps, raising both hands a little higher than yesterday, palms open like the <kanji>ten</kanji>-shaped cross you make once all your fingers are up. Nine sunrises of half-raised hands pass before the tenth, when both hands finally form that perfect cross overhead — ten days of raising, and it's the tenth.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat keeps shoving the same toy car down all ten mossy steps, and it lands on your <reading>toe</reading> every single time. <reading>とおか</reading>, right on the toe, ten steps down — ten days of bruises later, you finally admit that's the sound of the tenth.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The two raccoons are still hunched over their cold noodle broth, each guarding its snapped chopstick — the same two you met before. Every <kanji>day</kanji> new sun through the window finds them arranging the four chopstick halves into one perfect cross, the shape of <kanji>ten</kanji>, then doubling that cross because there are <kanji>two</kanji> raccoons at the table. After twenty of these sunrises nobody has eaten a single noodle: the twentieth day.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer grabs coffee straight off the warmer and spills it across the hood of his parked <reading>hot car</reading> right by the beeping till. Twenty days running he does this at checkout, and the staff now just call it <reading>はつか</reading> — the 20th, twenty days of the same scalded hood.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Zookeeper Zoe stopped filing her animals by species years ago. Now every enclosure is sorted by family: otters piled in one tank, meerkats packed into one den, and the daily headcount sheet has only one column, because at her zoo the only unit that ever matters is the whole family showing up together.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every evening Zoe cups her hands at the gate and calls out, a shout that lands in your ear as <reading>call-a-zoo, koo</reading>, the same two beats as <reading>かぞく</reading>. Every parent and cub trots out together the second they hear it, because that call means the whole family, not one animal.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini you're bragging to the clerk about how your father rewired the flickering sign himself. But every time the word for father leaves your mouth it comes out clipped and small, a fast double note like a chick cheeping under the counter, because that's the plain, low-key way you refer to your own father, never anyone else's.
items.reading_mnemonic: A chick has gotten loose behind Koichi's register and won't stop cheeping two identical notes at the customers. The sound lands exactly like <reading>ちち</reading>, the same clipped double <reading>chee-chee</reading> twice in a row, and it's the one word stuck to that particular chirp from now on.
items.description: 父 (chichi) is the plain, humble word for your own father, used only when talking about him to people outside the family — never for someone else's father, and not usually what you'd call him to his face. お父さん (otousan) is the polite counterpart: what you call your own dad directly, or how you refer to someone else's father.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, red-faced and sweating under the noon sun, a father hauls a stalled cart the last hundred meters by rope while his kid cheers from beside the lone vending machine. That's the picture pinned to father, polite: the dad you'd point out respectfully to a stranger, not the tired grumble you'd use at home.
items.reading_mnemonic: As he heaves the cart past the vending machine, the kid shouts the word for him, and it lands in your ear as <reading>oh, tow, sun</reading> — dad towing, sun blazing overhead — the same beats as <reading>おとうさん</reading>. That's the polite word for pointing him out to a stranger on the trail, not the plain one for talking about your own.
items.description: お父さん (otousan) is the polite, respectful word for father — what you call your own dad directly, or how you refer to someone else's father in conversation. It contrasts with the plain 父 (chichi), which you use only when talking about your own father to people outside the family.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, among the mossy steps and the cats sprawled everywhere, your mother doubles over laughing at some joke only she finds funny, the sound bouncing flat off the one enormous bell. That plain, unpolished laugh is exactly the humble word you use for your own mother, never for anyone else's.
items.reading_mnemonic: Her laugh rings off the shrine bell as two dry, identical beats, <reading>ha-ha</reading>, the same flat sound as <reading>はは</reading>, over and over until the cats scatter. It's a plain, low sound on purpose, nothing decorative, matching the plain word it belongs to.
items.description: 母 (haha) is the plain, humble word for your own mother, used when speaking about her to people outside the family — never for someone else's mother, and not typically what you call her to her face. It contrasts with お母さん (okaasan), the polite form used to address your own mother directly or refer to someone else's.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, a boy collapses by the lone vending machine, certain he can't take one more step. Then his mother crests the rise behind him, unbothered, carrying his backpack, her water bottle, and a spare pair of socks, somehow not out of breath. That endless, unglamorous readiness is what mother (polite) means.
items.reading_mnemonic: Driving the mountain trail's last hairpin toward the vending machine at the top, she doesn't slow down. The kids in the back seat brace and yell <reading>oh, car, san</reading> — which is exactly how <reading>おかあさん</reading> sounds, screamed by children who have done this drive with her before.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the last good onigiri is one shelf away. Your older brother doesn't ask — he plants a hand on your shoulder, uses you as a step stool, and takes it while you're still off balance. That casual, lifelong right to shove you aside without apologizing is what (my) older brother names.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, he shoves past you and you catch the shelf edge with your knee. <reading>Ah, knee</reading>, you groan, doubled over by the onigiri — which is exactly how <reading>あに</reading> sounds, and exactly who just walked off without noticing.
items.description: A plain, informal word for your own older brother when talking about him to someone else — never used to address him directly, and not the word used to speak politely about someone else's older brother (that is oniisan).

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a young man rings the enormous bell for an elderly stranger who can't reach the rope, then carries her offering up the mossy steps himself while the shrine cats trail behind them. Nobody there is related to him, but everyone calls him older brother (polite) anyway, because that is simply what the word is for.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the cats climb his leg the moment he sits on the mossy steps, and he winces <reading>oh, knee, sahn</reading> as claws land — which is exactly how <reading>おにいさん</reading> sounds, and exactly why the cats never leave him alone.
items.description: The polite, respectful form used to talk about or address someone else's older brother, or a young man in general as a courteous form of address — contrast with the plain word used only for your own older brother.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, your older sister has already claimed the flattest washing stone before you're even awake, scrubbing yesterday's clothes while lecturing you for not helping. She never once asks if you mind. That unasked-for seniority, exercised at six in the morning by the water, is what (my) older sister names.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a horse comes down to drink beside her washing stone and lets out a flat <reading>ah, neigh</reading> right in her ear — which is exactly how <reading>あね</reading> sounds, and exactly why she never washes clothes there again.
items.description: A plain, informal word for your own older sister when talking about her to someone else — not used to address her directly or to speak politely about someone else's older sister.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the captain of the school relay team, the one every younger kid looks up to and never dares call by her first name. She lines up the little ones, ties their shoelaces, and lets them win. That respectful, polite way you address someone's honored older sister is exactly this word.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school sports day, the team captain warms up by impersonating a horse, letting out an exaggerated <reading>neigh</reading> before every sprint. The younger kids salute her respectfully as <reading>おねえさん</reading>, the neighing captain, and nobody questions it.
items.description: This word is the respectful way to refer to or address someone else's older sister, or an unrelated older woman as a term of respect — it is not the plain, private term you'd use among your own family growing up with a younger sibling.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the pesky little brother who trails you everywhere, small enough that shopkeepers assume he's still in diapers, always demanding you carry him piggyback until your arms give out. That exact whiny, tag-along presence is what points straight at a younger brother.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the small brother stomps on the same customer's foot twice reaching for onigiri, and the customer yelps <reading>oh, toe, toe</reading> each time. The beeping till clerk sighs and says it again, plain: <reading>おとうと</reading>, always causing trouble.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the small girl who insists on carrying her own backpack up the mountain trail, refuses help, then sits down halfway and cries until someone caves and carries both the backpack and her. That stubborn, still-needs-looking-after littlest-girl energy is exactly a younger sister.
items.reading_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, the small girl stubs her toe on a root and yelps three sharp sounds — <reading>ee, moh, toe</reading> — before anyone can catch her. The hiker behind logs it plainly as <reading>いもうと</reading>, the toe-stubbing little sister, and keeps climbing.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the old man who rings Grandma Kane's one enormous shrine bell every single morning, out of habit rather than faith, then complains for an hour that his arm hurts. That specific, grumbling, ritual-bound old man is exactly your grandfather.
items.reading_mnemonic: After ringing the enormous bell, the old man collapses onto the shrine steps and announces he's <reading>so full</reading> — of aches, not food. The cats ignore him as he mutters it again, <reading>そふ</reading>, and refuses to get up.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the old bell-ringer finally hands the rope to someone new: a stooped man with a walking stick who has swept the mossy steps every morning for forty years. The cats accept him instantly. The children bow and call him grandfather, and from that day the enormous bell is his alone to ring.
items.reading_mnemonic: おじいさん is written exactly as it sounds, so there's no reading to decode — just the kana <reading>おじいさん</reading> read straight through.
items.description: おじいさん politely addresses or refers to any elderly man, related or not — closer to how English speakers might greet a stranger as "grandpa" than a strict family term.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till goes quiet as an elderly woman counts her coins one by one. Koichi leans over to the new hire and says simply: that's my grandmother, in for her onigiri. No polite title, no fuss — just family, plain and direct, the way you describe your own grandmother to someone else.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, an old woman mutters sew, bow, sew, bow while stitching ribbons onto scarves. A child mishears the rhythm as <reading>そぼ</reading>, the word for grandmother, and now everyone at the water's edge calls her the <reading>sew-bow</reading> lady who happens to be somebody's grandmother too.
items.description: 祖母 is how you refer to your own grandmother when speaking to someone outside the family — plain and humble, with no polite title attached. It isn't what you'd call her directly, or use for someone else's grandmother, both of which take an address term instead.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank where the washing happens, an old woman scrubs scarves for the whole village and refuses anyone's help. Children stop to greet her properly before crossing, and she waves them on with damp hands. To everyone nearby, respectfully, she's simply grandmother — polite, warm, and impossible to argue with.
items.reading_mnemonic: おばあさん is written exactly as it sounds, so there's no reading to decode — just the kana <reading>おばあさん</reading> read straight through.
items.description: おばあさん politely addresses or refers to any elderly woman, related or not — closer to how English speakers might greet a stranger as "ma'am" than a strict family term.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, past the point where most people turn back, a man in hiking boots is refilling the lone vending machine himself — turns out it's your uncle, who apparently owns the machine and hikes up every week just to restock it. Nobody in the family questions this anymore. That's just what your uncle does.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the vending machine on the mountain trail, a hiker rounds the last switchback and yelps, oh, gee, at the stranger already there. It's not a stranger — it's your uncle, and that startled gasp is exactly <reading>おじ</reading>: <reading>oh, gee</reading>, uncle, fancy meeting you up here.
items.description: 叔父 marks a younger uncle — your parent's younger brother, or one married in — as distinct from the term for an older uncle, though both get shortened to the same casual address form in speech.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, an aunt turns up every New Year wrapped in an absurd sheep-print scarf. The temple cats scatter, certain a sheep has invaded their mossy steps. Flustered, she throws up both hands and calls out across the courtyard — that startled, scarf-wrapped arrival is exactly who aunt means.
items.reading_mnemonic: As the cats bolt, she cries <reading>Oh, baa!</reading> — sheep noise, not sheep, just her own flustered yelp. That startled cry, <reading>おば</reading>, is the exact sound of an aunt arriving at Grandma Kane's shrine every single year, scarf and all.
items.description: The vowel here is short — don't stretch it into the longer sound used for the word for grandmother. They look and sound almost identical on the page but name different relatives, so lean on the mnemonic's short, startled yelp to keep the vowel length honest.

items.meaning_mnemonic: That swaddled <kanji>child</kanji>, arms still flung wide from its own story, wriggles loose right in Koichi's konbini and topples half the onigiri shelf reaching for it. The till beeps in protest as a clerk calls out for whoever's kid this troublemaker belongs to — arms flailing, wrapping gone, still unmistakably a child.
