items.reading_mnemonic: Standing in the wreckage, the toddler points at the shelf and demands, <reading>Cocoa dough, mo!</reading> — garbled, insistent, again and again. That exact chant, <reading>こども</reading>, is what Koichi hears every time a small customer causes chaos in his konbini.

items.meaning_mnemonic: That same swaddled <kanji>child</kanji>, arms flung wide, has somehow hauled itself up the whole mountain trail and is now feeding coins into the vending machine at the summit like it owns the place. A hiker asks the panting father trailing behind whose kid that is. He beams, chest out — that's his son.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the summit, the father spots a moose eyeing his boy's snack and bellows <reading>Moose, Coe!</reading> — the name of the trail's resident moose, shouted fast and clipped. That exact bark, <reading>むすこ</reading>, is what every hiker on this mountain learns to recognize as a warning about his son.

items.meaning_mnemonic: On the sports field at Sei's school, a girl in oversized cleats trips over the finish-line ribbon and drags the whole banner down with her. A woman in the stands leaps up, mortified and delighted at once, shouting across the entire field for her — this ribbon-tangled little disaster is her daughter.
items.reading_mnemonic: Still tangled in ribbon, she turns to the snack table and asks sweetly, <reading>Mousse, may?</reading> — polite as anything in the middle of a disaster. That well-mannered request, <reading>むすめ</reading>, is the reading you're listening for.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>person</kanji> striding forward suddenly stops and throws their arms out wide, legs spread as far as they'll go — the stance for showing off something <kanji>big</kanji>. Nobody teaches a kid to stand like that; you grow into needing the room. Standing tall enough to need the whole stance is what makes you an adult.
items.reading_mnemonic: Dai the giant baby stops wailing the second someone hands him <reading>a tuna</reading> — the calm is instant, like a switch. Jin ducks through the doorway just in time to see it: <reading>おとな</reading>, grown up right in front of him.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture two toddlers wedged together at Koichi's konbini, each gripping the same onigiri and refusing to let go, both wailing that the other one started it. Neither wins, neither releases, and the clerk just watches the identical tantrum play out twice over — that matched, tangled squabble is what siblings means.
items.reading_mnemonic: The twins grab a pool cue and dunk it straight into spilled dye, striping the whole konbini floor like tie-dye. Koichi yells <reading>cue dye</reading> at the mess — and that yell is exactly how <reading>きょうだい</reading> sounds: siblings, always making double the trouble.

items.mnemonic_text: The master of the house: goshujin.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>person</kanji> who strides in the door each night doesn't get his coat off before he's handed a list — go find the shoes, go find the remote, go find out why dinner's late. Everyone in the house treats him like hired help with a wedding ring: that's the respectful title for someone's husband.
items.reading_mnemonic: Jin the friendly giant barely ducks through the doorway before his wife barks: <reading>go, shoe, Jin</reading> — fetch her shoes off the shrine steps. That errand-running giant is exactly what <reading>ごしゅじん</reading> means: someone's husband, always sent to go find things.
items.description: This is the respectful term for someone else's husband, used when talking to or about the listener's family — not the word you'd use for your own husband. It leans on 主人 (master), so some speakers now avoid it for the gendered assumption baked in.

items.mnemonic_text: The one in the back rooms: okusan.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At the very top of the mountain trail, a woman leans against the lone vending machine, patient in the shade of an oak, clearly waiting for somebody. Every exhausted hiker who finally staggers up assumes she must belong to whoever shows up gasping right after — and that assumption, someone waiting up there for her other half, is exactly (someone's) wife.
items.reading_mnemonic: She waves at the oak baking in the noon sun and calls down the trail, <reading>oak sun</reading> — the greeting that carries all the way to the switchbacks. That call is just how <reading>おくさん</reading> sounds: someone's wife, waiting patiently at the top for him to catch up.
items.description: 奥さん is the respectful way to refer to or address someone else's wife — never your own. It also gets used casually to address a married woman in general, but it is not what a man calls his own wife.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a man climbs the mossy steps every evening expecting to be first, and every evening his own wife is already there ahead of him, feeding the shrine cats without a word of announcement. He never has to ask where she is — she is simply, quietly, always a step ahead of him. That settled certainty is (my) wife.
items.reading_mnemonic: He calls up the steps, <reading>Sue, ma!</reading>, thinking he's found Grandma Kane — but it's his own wife who turns around, cat in her arms. That startled beat is the sound of <reading>つま</reading>: realizing, again, that his wife got there first.
items.description: 妻 is the plain, slightly formal way a man refers to his own wife when talking to other people — it is not a word used for someone else's wife, and not one he'd use calling out to her directly.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a woman is washing laundry when her husband wades in fully dressed, chasing a sock that floated loose, soaking his only good shirt in the process. She doesn't even look up — of course that's who waded in after one sock, nobody else would bother. That reliable, faintly ridiculous devotion is (my) husband.
items.reading_mnemonic: He climbs out of the river dripping head to toe, sock triumphantly in hand, and she just sighs, <reading>Otto</reading>, not again — the exact sound of <reading>おっと</reading>, her name for the husband who always wades in after the laundry.
items.description: 夫 is the plain way a wife refers to her own husband when speaking to other people — not a word she'd use to call out to him directly, and not used for someone else's husband.

items.meaning_mnemonic: In Sei's school hallway, someone rounds the corner: just two legs mid-stride, a body carried along above them, heading forward without dragging anything else behind. Strip away every job title, every role, every name — what's left striding down that hallway is simply a <kanji>person</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 人 keeps the exact reading you already learned for this kanji: <reading>ひと</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a stranger reaches for the last onigiri the exact moment you do. Neither of you lets go. You end up splitting it on the curb outside, silent and suspicious of each other, until one bite in you're both laughing about it — and just like that, you've made a friend.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a boy named <reading>Tomo</reading> won't cross the water without his small <reading>dachshund</reading> tucked under one arm. The two go everywhere together, so the locals just call the pair 「<reading>ともだち</reading>」 — one word for two creatures who refuse to be apart.

items.mnemonic_text: The one born before you in knowledge: sensei.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The legs that always stride out <kanji>ahead</kanji> of everyone reach the classroom first, plant themselves at the front, and refuse to sit down. Beneath their feet is the same patch of ground where a seed cracks open into <kanji>life</kanji> — because this is the one person whose ideas take root in you and grow. That's a teacher.
items.reading_mnemonic: 先 gives せん and 生 supplies the same せい you know from <reading>Sei</reading>, the star student — stack them together and you get exactly 「<reading>せんせい</reading>」.

items.mnemonic_text: One in the life of study: gakusei.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The child camped beneath that roof of scribbled notes refuses to go home, and overnight the desk starts to feel like part of them — that's daily <kanji>study</kanji>. But they're not finished growing: the same soil that turns a seed into <kanji>life</kanji> is still working underneath them, a person still half-sprouted, still becoming. That's a student.
items.reading_mnemonic: 学 gives がく and 生 supplies the same せい you already know from <reading>Sei</reading>, the star student, combining exactly into 「<reading>がくせい</reading>」.

items.meaning_mnemonic: That same patch of earth where a seed splits open into <kanji>life</kanji> now stretches out as a schoolyard, planted with row after row of identical green shoots, all still too short to see over the fence. They're not finished yet — still rooted, still waiting their turn to grow — and that half-grown state is exactly what a pupil is.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the school, a mob of first-years shuffles so close behind <reading>Sei</reading> that they keep landing on her <reading>toe</reading> — "say... toe!" she yelps each time. The name sticks: these tagalong underclassmen following the star student's every step become known as 「<reading>せいと</reading>」.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A goldfish that stopped blinking gets carried into the clinic, though goldfish famously have no eyelids. The receptionist doesn't even look up — stranger visits happen weekly. When your name is finally called, the person in the white coat with a stethoscope swinging off one ear is exactly who you came for: the doctor.
items.reading_mnemonic: The woman in the white coat introduces herself as <reading>Isha</reading>, which sounds more like she should be selling produce at a stall. But she's the sharpest <reading>いしゃ</reading> in the building, diagnosing your cough before you've finished coughing it.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every floor the elevator stops at, the same tired figure in a grey suit steps on, straightens a badge, staples one form, and steps off two floors later to do it all again. Nobody remembers his name, only his badge and his sigh. That endless loop of suit, badge, and paperwork is exactly what the word means: company employee.
items.reading_mnemonic: His badge, half-covered by his tie, reads <reading>Kai Shain</reading> in blocky letters — no one at the company can pronounce it right, but everyone recognizes that a <reading>かいしゃいん</reading> like him has been riding this elevator since it was installed.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every morning the galloping <kanji>station</kanji> horse thunders onto the platform, and it isn't the conductor who deals with it — it's the whistle-blowing worker in uniform who chases it back off the tracks before the first train arrives. Radio crackling, cap crooked, unbothered by any of this: that worn-out but unshaken figure is your station staff.
items.reading_mnemonic: Over the radio the worker's reply crackles back garbled, just an <reading>echo in</reading> the tunnel — but that crackly <reading>えきいん</reading> is on every platform of this line, herding lost passengers back before the doors slide shut.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Someone's been dumping fish traps along the riverbank at night, and every trap turns up empty by morning except the one time a figure in a sharp uniform wades in at dawn, hauls the traps out by hand, and confiscates the lot without a word. That quiet, uniformed figure standing ankle-deep in river mud is exactly what the word means: police officer.
items.reading_mnemonic: The uniformed figure flashes a badge and introduces herself only as <reading>Kay Kahn</reading> — and the raccoon mid-heist at the fish trap doesn't even try to run, because everyone on this riverbank knows a <reading>けいかん</reading> named Kay Kahn always gets her culprit.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Follow the <kanji>person</kanji> already mid-stride past the slanted gate, headed <kanji>outside</kanji> — but this time they don't stop at the fence. They keep walking until the walls that wrap an entire <kanji>country</kanji> shrink into a smudge on the mountain trail behind them. Striding clean outside your own country's walls is what makes you a foreigner.
items.reading_mnemonic: Each kanji keeps its taught reading in a row — 外（がい）＋国（こく）＋人（じん） — giving you <reading>がいこくじん</reading> straight down the line.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the kneeling <kanji>woman</kanji> finally rises from her bow and falls into step beside the two legs she already knows as a <kanji>person</kanji>, the pair of them striding together past the cats toward the enormous bell. Kneeling figure plus striding legs, moving as one down the mossy steps — that's a grown woman.
items.reading_mnemonic: 女 reads おんな and 人 reads ひと, so the two known readings simply chain together into <reading>おんなのひと</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Out in the paddy, the <kanji>man</kanji> finally straightens up from the plow, gives his arm one last flex, and starts walking toward Koichi's konbini for something cold — those two legs carrying him off the field are exactly the <kanji>person</kanji> he becomes the second he stops working. Power in the field, then legs on the road: that's a grown man.
items.reading_mnemonic: 男 reads おとこ and 人 reads ひと, so the two known readings simply chain together into <reading>おとこのひと</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a tiny figure copies the kneeling <kanji>woman</kanji> pose out on the sports field, except her sweeping arm has curled inward to cradle a swaddled <kanji>child</kanji>, little arms flung out against her chest. A pint-sized woman who still has a bundled baby's shape tucked in her arms — that's a girl.
items.reading_mnemonic: 女 reads おんな and 子 reads こ, so the two known readings simply chain together into <reading>おんなのこ</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Up on the mountain trail, a small figure flexes one arm at the vending machine exactly like the <kanji>man</kanji> dragging his plow through the paddy, except his other arm is still tucked into a <kanji>child</kanji>'s swaddle, wriggling loose at his side. A miniature man who hasn't finished unwrapping yet — that's a boy.
items.reading_mnemonic: 男 reads おとこ and 子 reads こ, so the two known readings simply chain together into <reading>おとこのこ</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, by the vending machine, a hiker's toddler drops her snack and wails so hard her whole face floods the same deep, angry <kanji>red</kanji> as the ground splitting open on that hillside, glowing from the fire underneath. Nothing quiets a face that red. That furious red-faced bundle is a baby.
items.reading_mnemonic: The reading is exactly the pieces you already know: 赤 gives you the あか, and the childish ちゃん suffix tacks straight on after it, spelling out <reading>あかちゃん</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the tinny loudspeaker crackles once and a single voice booms through every aisle at the same instant, announcing a surprise scavenger hunt: onigiri, umbrellas, batteries, go. Every last customer looks up from what they're doing in the same second - not some of them, not most of them. Everyone.
items.reading_mnemonic: みんな is written exactly the way it sounds, plain kana with nothing hiding underneath, so the word simply is its own reading: <reading>みんな</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Back at the pie you already sliced into eight equal <kanji>parts</kanji> to understand it, one wedge never gets claimed - it just sits alone on the plate while Grandma Kane's cats fight over the rest. That unclaimed slice belongs to nobody else; it's yours alone, the one <kanji>part</kanji> you can never hand off. That stubborn leftover wedge is oneself.
items.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, a rower's <reading>jib</reading> - the small forward sail - swings loose and snags a stray <reading>bun</reading> right out of someone else's hands. He doesn't offer a single bite to anyone rowing beside him; that jib-and-bun grab, <reading>じぶん</reading>, is entirely his own business: oneself.

items.meaning_mnemonic: In the echoing hallway of Sei's school, gym class lets out and everyone crowds through one narrow doorway at once - shoulders, bags, elbows, all jammed together. Except one part always squeezes through first, out ahead of everything else, cutting a path for the rest of the body to follow: the head.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's shrine keeps one badly behaved llama tied up by the great bell, and it despises every visitor who gets too close, so it swings and clonks them square in the skull. The caretaker just sighs and warns newcomers the same way each time: mind <reading>a llama</reading>, or it'll crack your <reading>あたま</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat named Botan leaps onto the offering bowl and stares down at the water pooled inside it, hunting the strange animal staring back. It takes three tail-lashes before Botan realizes the intruder blinks whenever she blinks — it is her own face, staring up out of the water.
items.reading_mnemonic: A cow wanders into Grandma Kane's shrine and butts the shrine bell aside just to see what's cooking. The monk grabs the <reading>cow</reading> by the horns and yells right into its <reading>かお</reading> — but its blank face never changes.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Above the register at Koichi's konbini hangs a security frame with two little dots for pupils, tilted so it looks like it's staring you down while you pick between the onigiri and the beeping till. That frame with pupils staring back is exactly the <kanji>eye</kanji> watching every customer who lingers too long.
items.reading_mnemonic: 目 already gives you this reading on its own — め is exactly how 目 reads by itself, so the <reading>め</reading> here is that very same reading, unchanged.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Near the top of the mountain trail, that dangling flap of skin catches the sudden beep of the vending machine echoing off the rock face before your eyes even register the machine is there. The flap swivels toward the sound like it has a mind of its own — proof that the whole point of an <kanji>ear</kanji> is hearing first, seeing second.
items.reading_mnemonic: 耳 already reads みみ on its own, so the <reading>みみ</reading> in this word is that same reading, said once for the character and now doubled for the word.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a heron plants itself ankle-deep and points its long beak straight up, sniffing the air to check whether the water's too cold to cross before wading in. That beak does the one job it's built for — smelling out trouble first — which is exactly what a nose is for.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a new transfer student named Hannah presses her face to the cafeteria window, sniffing out the menu before anyone announces it. The other kids nickname her <reading>はな</reading> on the spot — that <reading>Hannah</reading>-nose never misses a smell, even through glass.

items.meaning_mnemonic: That open square is still hanging there mid-yawn, exactly as you left it — nothing has been drawn inside it, because nothing needs to be. A hole with nothing inside was already the whole idea: it's just a <kanji>mouth</kanji>, caught wide open and refusing to close until you've said the word for it.
items.reading_mnemonic: The kanji 口 already taught you both of its readings, and this word simply picks the plain <reading>くち</reading> one straight off it.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the vending machine dispenses exactly one item that day: a single chipped tooth, still faintly rattling, ejected after the last hiker crunched down on a stone hidden inside their rice ball. Everyone just runs a tongue along their own teeth, checking for the gap where a tooth used to be.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the nurse lets out one flat sound every time a kid limps in clutching their jaw — a startled <reading>ha</reading>, stretched thin like a gasp with nowhere to go. That same deadpan <reading>は</reading> is the whole word: the sound she makes over a broken tooth is the reading for tooth itself.

items.meaning_mnemonic: That same <kanji>hand</kanji> is still hanging out mid-air, wrist and all, waiting for the shake nobody's ever finished. It doesn't close, it doesn't wave — it just stays there, open-palmed, being exactly the shape it always was. That patient, unshaken shape is the word for hand.
items.reading_mnemonic: Same kanji, same lesson: 手 already gave you two readings, and this word just borrows the plain <reading>て</reading> reading straight off it.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Up on the mountain trail, that mouth-topped pair of stopped legs is moving again, planted step after step all the way to the vending machine at the top, still barking orders down at itself with every stride. Whatever plants itself like that and carries you onward — that's your <kanji>foot</kanji>, your leg.
items.reading_mnemonic: That same 足 already taught you two readings, and this word just takes the plain <reading>あし</reading> straight off it.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a man buys every onigiri on the shelf and eats them standing at the counter, one after another, until his shirt stops closing. By the last one his middle has ballooned into a round drum he has to hold with both hands — his stomach, full past reason, the only thing left worth talking about.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi watches the man's belly swell round as a spare tire and mutters he looks like he's got one strapped <reading>on a car</reading>. The man just groans <reading>おなか</reading>, patting the bulge, and Koichi decides that's as good a name for it as any.

items.meaning_mnemonic: On Sei's school sports field, the gym teacher lines everyone up and makes them stretch every part at once — arms, legs, back, neck — until the whole trembling row moves as a single shuddering unit. She points down the line and names it plainly: the body, all of it, working together.
items.reading_mnemonic: The gym teacher barks that this drill works the whole <reading>car, duh</reading> — she means the whole <reading>からだ</reading>, obviously, and nobody laughs because she's still holding the whistle. からだ, she repeats, jabbing a finger at each kid's ribs to prove her point.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one of the resident cats leaps onto a visitor's shoulders and burrows straight into the long dark strands hanging past her collar, kneading and refusing to leave. Grandma Kane just laughs, ringing the mossy steps clean, and says the cat has finally found the hair it always wanted to nest in.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane calls that shrine cat <reading>Cami</reading>, and Cami spends every visit nesting in the same visitor's <reading>かみ</reading>, purring against her scalp. Grandma Kane rings the enormous bell to shoo her off, but Cami just digs deeper into the かみ and refuses to move.

items.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a hiker finally reaches the summit vending machine and cranes forward so far to read the buttons that his head tips back on a long thin stalk, wobbling like it might snap clean off. Everyone behind him on the trail stares at that one stretched, straining neck.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the trail, the hiker wedges his head into a stone <reading>cubby</reading> beside the vending machine to get a closer look, and now his <reading>くび</reading> is stuck fast in the gap. He twists his くび side to side, but the cubby holds on tight.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A lone hiker stands at the edge of the mountain trail and lets out one enormous shout at the far canyon wall — not words, just raw sound thrown as hard as he can throw it. A beat later it comes back, fainter but unmistakably the same sound. That thrown, bounced-back sound, and nothing else, is what this word simply means: voice.
items.reading_mnemonic: The hiker is named <reading>Coe, eh</reading> — that's literally how he introduces himself, flat and dragging the vowel out. So when he shouts into the canyon and the sound flies back at him a beat later, it comes back as <reading>こえ</reading>: his own voice, thrown at rock and handed right back to him unchanged.

items.meaning_mnemonic: That tent pitched over a heaped tray — the shelter you duck into when you're hungry — gets dragged whole onto Sei's school sports field for a picnic, roof and all. The whole team ducks under it at once, and every dish sitting under that roof, from the rice down to the last pickle, gets <kanji>eaten</kanji> before the bell rings. Anything that ends up under that tent is, simply, food.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every lunch break, a scrawny transfer student named <reading>Toby Moreno</reading> materializes at Koichi's konbini and buys out the entire onigiri shelf without saying a word. The clerk has started calling out <reading>たべもの</reading> the second the bell rings, because that name and that hunger always arrive together.

items.meaning_mnemonic: That same yawning mouth wanders down to the riverbank on a hot afternoon, tips its head all the way back over the water, and doesn't stop until the whole river's worth has vanished down its throat. Food sits forgotten beside it; the only thing that gaping mouth wants now is to <kanji>drink</kanji>, and it does, all afternoon, without ever closing once.
items.reading_mnemonic: A stubborn <reading>gnome</reading> in a one-piece <reading>mono</reading> suit haunts the vending machine at the top of the mountain trail, feeding it coin after coin. Ask what he's doing up there and he just holds up a can and says <reading>のみもの</reading> — drink — like that explains everything, which, to him, it does.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the mossy steps end at a single offering bowl the cats can never quite reach: a small mound of plain white rice, steaming, set out fresh every morning. It isn't a snack and it isn't a whole feast — it's simply what's due at mealtime, the actual cooked rice sitting there and the meal built around it, both at once.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every morning a scrawny cat named Han races the shrine cats up the mossy steps for that rice bowl, and Grandma Kane leans out and yells <reading>Go, Han</reading> to cheer him on. By the time he wins, it isn't just rice anymore — it's <reading>ごはん</reading>, breakfast, served straight from the bowl he fought for.
items.description: This word literally names plain cooked rice, but in everyday speech it just as often means a full meal in general, not only the rice itself — asking someone if they've had gohan yet is asking whether they've eaten at all, breakfast, lunch, or dinner alike.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A rooster oversleeps at Grandma Kane's shrine and wakes to the sun already glaring off the enormous bell. He bolts down the mossy steps two at a time, scattering cats, because the priest sets out rice, grilled fish, and miso the instant dawn breaks — whoever reaches that tray first gets breakfast.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every dawn a groggy monk stumbles toward the shrine gate mumbling <reading>ah, sir, go, Han</reading> at the boy stacking bowls, before Han even asks what he wants: <reading>あさごはん</reading>, already getting cold on the step.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school the sports field empties for the lunch bell, and a stray dog times its raid perfectly, snatching a tray straight off the picnic table mid-sprint. Kids chase it in a lap around the track, but the dog is faster than any of them expect, gone with the whole lunch before anyone's fork is even out.
items.reading_mnemonic: The gym teacher blows the whistle at noon and roars <reading>hero, go, Han</reading> at the fastest runner, sending him sprinting after the dog. He never catches it, but by the time he's back, someone's already laid out <reading>ひるごはん</reading> for the whole team anyway.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank at dusk, a tanuki has learned exactly when the cooking fire gets left untended, and it drags the whole simmering pot toward the water to wash its paws in what's left. The family gives up chasing it along the bank and just starts cooking a second pot, because dinner has to happen eventually, tanuki or not.
items.reading_mnemonic: The father slams the door at dusk shouting <reading>bang, go, Han</reading> at the dog racing the tanuki to the pot, and by the time the door stops rattling everyone's already sitting down to <reading>ばんごはん</reading>, tanuki-free at last.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini a customer grabs the last loaf off the shelf right as the till starts beeping, panicking because the shelf is otherwise all onigiri. He hugs it like it's the only bread left in Japan, mutters thanks under the fluorescent lights, and pays before anyone else spots it.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it's read: <reading>パン</reading>, borrowed straight from Portuguese pão — no derivation needed.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer piles his arms so high with packages that he can't see over the top, and the automatic door doesn't slide open fast enough — he plows into the glass, packages skidding toward the onigiri shelf while the till keeps beeping through the whole thing. What he was hoarding, glass door and all, was meat.
items.reading_mnemonic: The butcher restocking that counter introduces himself as <reading>Nick</reading>, and every time he says it, it comes out clipped and flat, almost like <reading>にく</reading> — the customers just nod along, since that's also the word for the meat piled in front of him.

items.mnemonic_text: The swimmer on your plate: sakana.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, a fisherman casts his line for hours and reels in nothing but weeds, until a sudden tug nearly drags him into the water — he hauls back to find something flopping on the bank, gasping right alongside him. That flopping, gasping catch is the entire reason anyone stands at a riverbank all afternoon: fish.
items.reading_mnemonic: The fisherwoman working that same riverbank, <reading>Sock Anna</reading>, wades in after a lost sock and something latches onto her bare foot instead of the fabric — she yelps out the same sound as her own name, <reading>さかな</reading>, and from then on that's just the word for fish.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every morning Grandma Kane sets a fresh offering on the shrine steps, but this time it isn't rice or dried fish — it's a heap of raw produce, and the shrine cats sniff it once, turn their tails up, and stalk off toward the bell instead. Not even a temple cat will touch it. That offering nobody at the shrine wants is vegetables.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane just sighs, '<reading>ya, sigh</reading>,' every single time the cats reject her offering and slink away, and that resigned little sigh is almost exactly the sound of <reading>やさい</reading> — the vegetables piled up on the shrine steps that nobody wants.

items.meaning_mnemonic: After the last steep switchback of the mountain trail, a hiker collapses in front of the one vending machine improbably waiting at the top, expecting a cold drink — and finds every slot loaded with apples and oranges instead. Too worn out to complain, he buys one standing there. What that machine stocks at the summit is fruit.
items.reading_mnemonic: Staring at the slots, the hiker <reading>could-a moaned</reading> about the missing drinks, but he's too exhausted to do more than mutter it under his breath, and that tired, flattened mutter comes out sounding just like <reading>くだもの</reading> — the fruit waiting at the top of the trail.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the delivery truck arrives before dawn and unloads crate after crate of impossibly round, pale ovals, still warm from the truck's engine. Koichi holds one to the fluorescent light, taps it once, and it cracks open — bright yolk sliding across the counter: egg.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the fat shrine cat curls into the offering bowl every morning. Someone finally claps and shouts <reading>Tama, go!</reading> — it slinks off, revealing one warm egg underneath. That shout is the reading: <reading>たまご</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: On the sports field at Sei's school, the morning delivery crate holds little paper cartons, so cold they sweat in the sun. A kid downs one in one gulp, gets a white mustache, and holds up the empty carton proudly to the whole team: milk.
items.reading_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, the lone vending machine hums. You press the button expecting hot tea and instead a freezing carton thunks out, and someone nearby gasps <reading>Ew, new!</reading> at the chill. That gasp is the reading: <reading>ぎゅうにゅう</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You're back at the riverbank where the streams splash outward in every direction, cold spray hitting your face. Cup your hands in that spray, and the streaks resolve into something you can actually drink: <kanji>water</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Same kanji, same sound you already know from 水: <reading>みず</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, she pours something pale green and steaming into small cups for every visitor who climbs the mossy steps, cats sniffing at the tray. One sip after the climb and you understand why she never skips this step: tea.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a hot can rolls off the shelf and lands right at your feet, steam still hissing from the seam. You yelp <reading>oh, cha!</reading> as it burns your fingers picking it up. That yelp is the reading: <reading>おちゃ</reading>.
items.description: Almost always appears with the honorific prefix お attached — daily speech rarely uses the bare form alone, even though it exists in other compounds.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till beeps furiously at three in the morning as a zombie-eyed customer clutches an empty paper cup, breathing out fumes so bitter the onigiri shelf seems to lean away from him. He doesn't order food. He doesn't speak. He just raises the cup, and the cashier refills it without a word: coffee.
items.reading_mnemonic: コーヒー is written exactly the way it sounds, straight through in kana — <reading>コーヒー</reading> — nothing here to decode, just read it aloud.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the cats curled by the enormous bell always find the one jar the priest forgot to lock away. By the time you arrive for New Year's prayers, three of them are sprawled belly-up on the mossy steps, hiccuping softly, radiating that unmistakable warm reek of alcohol.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane spots the empty jar and gasps <reading>Oh, sake</reading>, her shocked cry stretching into <reading>おさけ</reading> as she chases the wobbling cats down the mossy steps, the enormous bell clanging behind her the whole way.
items.description: お酒 means alcohol in general — beer, wine, spirits, anything you drink to get tipsy — not only the rice wine English speakers picture when they hear the word sake.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The mountain trail's summit reward is one vending machine, impossibly humming after two hours of switchbacks. You feed it coins with shaking hands, and instead of water it drops a cold gold can that hisses and foams straight over your boots: beer, at the top of the mountain, before you've even sat down.
items.reading_mnemonic: ビール is written just as it's read, kana straight through — <reading>ビール</reading> — nothing to sound out beyond what's already on the can.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, someone drops a paper packet off the little footbridge, and instead of sinking it dissolves mid-air into the current, turning a whole stretch of water thick and slow, the fish drifting through it like it's honey — that's what falls into your tea as sugar.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei's homeroom teacher introduces herself as <reading>Sato</reading>-sensei, then skips the chalkboard and just pours a spoonful into her tea to prove the name: <reading>さとう</reading>, she says, tapping the packet, sweet like she is.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every dawn at Grandma Kane's shrine, the temple cats watch her fling a scoop of coarse white grains across the gate, a purifying toss meant to sting bare skin. One greedy cat licks a stray grain from the stone, recoils hard, and spends the hour draining the well dry. That sharp mineral bite on its tongue is salt.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane hands her shrine attendant Ren a sack for the purification toss. He trips on the steps, and it bursts everywhere as he yelps '<reading>She, oh!</reading>' watching grains fill his sandals — that yelp is exactly <reading>しお</reading>, salt.

items.meaning_mnemonic: It's 2 a.m. at Koichi's konbini, fluorescent lights buzzing over the onigiri shelf while the till beeps through a lull. Bored, the night clerk pulls ingredients off the shelves — instant miso, a rice ball, a squeeze of mayo — and assembles them into something new on the counter. By closing, he's turned convenience-store scraps into an actual dish: cooking.
items.reading_mnemonic: The clerk introduces himself over the counter, 'I'm <reading>Leo Uri</reading>, konbini cooking champion of aisle three.' He says his name so fast it comes out as one word — <reading>りょうり</reading> — which is exactly how you ask for cooking or a dish.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At exactly noon a bell rings through Sei's school, and dozens of <kanji>eat</kanji> tents pop up along the hallway floor — the same roof-made-of-dinner shelter you already know, one for every student ducking in to eat. Trays pile up under each roof until the bell rings again. That whole stretch, from first bite to last, is the meal.
items.reading_mnemonic: A student named Shoko checks her watch in the echoing hallway and gasps '<reading>Shock, gee</reading>, is it that late already?' — she's smelling the trays before she sees them. That gasp is exactly <reading>しょくじ</reading>: meal.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Near the top of the mountain trail, past the last switchback, hikers find the one vending machine standing improbably at the summit. Its slots hold no soda or tea — only small bags of hard, pale grains, unwashed and uncooked. A disappointed hiker buys one anyway, shakes it like a maraca, and trudges back down still hungry: uncooked rice.
items.reading_mnemonic: A hiker at the summit rattles her bag of grains and mutters '<reading>Comb</reading> through this later,' annoyed she packed the wrong snack. That mutter is exactly <reading>こめ</reading> — uncooked rice, the kind you rinse before cooking, not eat straight from the bag.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, someone leaves rice crackers by the bell as an offering. A <kanji>child</kanji> wriggles free of its wrap — arms flung wide, the exact shape that means <kanji>child</kanji> — snatches the whole plate and is found later face-down in crumbs. The monks give up on real food; now they just leave out sweets.
items.reading_mnemonic: Behind Koichi's konbini, there's a locked drawer everyone whispers about. Pry it open and you find <reading>おかし</reading> — an entire <reading>cache</reading> of sweets he's been hoarding since spring, more candy than any kid could eat in a year.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, past the improbable summit vending machine, a hiker unzips her pack instead of buying anything. Inside sits a perfectly packed rectangular box — rice, a pickled plum, a segment of grilled fish — eaten cold on a rock at the top. That neat travel box is a boxed lunch.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, Ben trips over a root and sends his lunch tumbling downhill. He chases it hollering '<reading>Ben, my toe!</reading>' — say it fast and you land on <reading>べんとう</reading>, the boxed lunch he's sprinting to save before the crows find it.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Someone moors a floating diner to a post on the riverbank so it can't drift off. A chalkboard menu hangs from the mast, and the one waiter wades out in rubber boots to deliver plates. Tourists queue on the bank just to eat somewhere that technically counts as a restaurant, even though it's really a raft with silverware.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it sounds: <reading>レストラン</reading>.
items.description: レストラン specifically means a Western-style sit-down restaurant. Casual Japanese eateries, noodle counters, and specialty food shops usually go by other names, not this word.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Sei ducks out of gym class through a gap in the fence and ends up in an impossibly quiet shop three streets over — dim lighting, one old man refolding the same newspaper, a menu of drinks nobody at school has heard of. It is a coffee shop, and gym period never felt shorter.
items.reading_mnemonic: Behind the coffee shop counter, the barista scores every espresso out of ten, and when one hits a perfect score, plants a theatrical <reading>kiss a ten</reading> on the cup before serving it. Regulars just call the place <reading>きっさてん</reading> and never ask about the ritual.
items.description: きっさてん usually points at an old-style Japanese coffee shop — dim, quiet, often decades-old — rather than a modern chain cafe.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, past the lone vending machine, a hermit crab stops dragging its blistered shell. It wedges into a hollow rock at the trail's edge, lines up four pinecones in the doorway like doormats, and won't budge again. That hollow rock, doormats and all, is officially somebody's house — the crab has made itself a home.
items.reading_mnemonic: A builder named Ei nails one crooked wall onto that same hollow rock and steps back beaming, waiting for someone to ask about the roof. Instead he throws both arms up and shouts <reading>いえ</reading>, which lands on the ear exactly like an English <reading>yay</reading>, and declares the one wall a finished house.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every evening at Grandma Kane's shrine, the stray cats pile into one shivering heap on the mossy steps — not because any cat owns the place, but because the heap itself is the point. Ask an outsider cat to squeeze in and the whole pile hisses as one; ask one inside where home is, and it just presses closer. The heap is home.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is pure kana, spelled exactly the way it sounds, so <reading>うち</reading> needs no decoding — just read it as written.
items.description: うち means home in the sense of your own group or household, not just a building. Japanese speakers use it to mark insiders against outsiders, so it can describe a company, a team, or a family circle as easily as a physical house — a nuance the English word 'home' does not carry on its own.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The swaddled <kanji>study</kanji> child, still parked under its canopy of scribbled lesson notes, gets carried to the courtyard and set at the foot of the one great <kanji>school</kanji> tree. Roots tangle around the roof of notes, a bell rings somewhere in the branches, and the courtyard fills with kids at recess — canopy and tree have grown into one building: a school.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 学 as がく and 校 as こう — chain them together (がく softens to がっ before こう) and you get exactly <reading>がっこう</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The same wide-armed stretcher who's always bragging how <kanji>big</kanji> his catch was plants himself over the swaddled <kanji>study</kanji> child's roof of lesson notes and stretches even wider, insisting the canopy is huge too. He keeps stretching until the notes swell into a whole campus of towering lecture halls — the biggest school there is: a university.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 大 as だい and 学 as がく — put them back to back, no softening needed, and you get exactly <reading>だいがく</reading>.

items.mnemonic_text: The meeting shrine of work: kaisha.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The landlord insists the view improves productivity, so the office gets hauled up the steep mountain trail — desks wedged between boulders, the printer jamming two switchbacks from the top. The boss holds the meeting by the vending machine, tapping his coffee like a whiteboard. A hiker asks if this is really a company. It is.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, <reading>Kai shares</reading> his last rice ball with a gasping hiker, then checks his watch — his 「<reading>かいしゃ</reading>」 starts at nine and he still has to jog back down. Kai shares his snacks the same way he shares deadlines: reluctantly, but right on schedule.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A rowboat flips at the riverbank, and instead of a rescue crew, a whole hospital floats out to meet it — beds lashed to buoys, an IV drip swinging from a fishing rod, a nurse checking pulses waist-deep in the current. The patient is hauled onto the nearest buoy, wrapped in a blanket, declared stable before the clipboard stops dripping.
items.reading_mnemonic: The floating buoy at the riverbank turns out to be a tiny inn — a nurse leans out of the porthole and calls it the <reading>buoy inn</reading> for short. 「<reading>びょういん</reading>」, she says, tapping the sign nailed to the mast, and the soaked patient checks in like it's a hotel with worse pillows.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The figure who's always mid-stride, legs split wide, leaning into the step, never leaves the building — he paces the lobby, stamping passbooks between strides because he won't stand still long enough to finish one. Customers behind him catch the same itch to <kanji>go</kanji> before their money finishes counting — a building built around cash that never sits still.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi restocks the onigiri shelf at 3 a.m. when a man demands gin. Koichi doesn't sell gin — he runs a konbini — but the man insists so loudly Koichi starts a private ledger, tracking yen owed for gin he never carries. <reading>Gin, Koichi</reading> mutters, ringing up onigiri instead, and the shelf becomes the block's unofficial 「<reading>ぎんこう</reading>」.

items.furigana: 郵[ゆう]便[びん]局[きょく]
items.meaning_mnemonic: The cats at Grandma Kane's shrine have turned the mossy steps into a sorting office, stacking twigs, feathers, and dead beetles beside the enormous bell. Visitors expecting incense get a paw stamping their sandal instead, like a receipt. By evening prayers the pile is sorted, labeled with cat hair, and ready for pickup.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the cats treat the mossy steps like a drop box, leaving one twig at a time beside the enormous bell. When the pile is tall enough, Grandma rings the bell, calls out <reading>you bin, cuckoo</reading>, and sorts them by size. The steps become her 「<reading>ゆうびんきょく</reading>」 — the hillside post office nobody asked for.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You step into a hall of shelves stretching past where the light reaches. Every page began the same way: someone let the sun sink over their desk while their hand kept moving, filling line after line to <kanji>write</kanji>. Multiply that by ten thousand desks and stack it under one roof — that's a library.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa the fire-breathing crow lands on the library roof and singes her own claw. Hopping in place, she does a frantic <reading>toe show, khan</reading>-style hobble past the front desk, and the librarian's endless shushing blurs her yelp into one word: <reading>としょかん</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every morning another <kanji>station</kanji> platform fills with hoofprints instead of footprints — the local horses treat the place like open pasture. Today one gallops so hard it clears the ticket gates and skids onto a departing train, mane flying. Staff gave up chasing them years ago.
items.reading_mnemonic: 駅's own taught reading carries straight over unchanged, so <reading>えき</reading> is exactly what you already know it to be.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A city block gets flattened overnight — grass paved over, buildings hauled off — replaced by flat runway under an empty stretch of sky. Nowhere to sit, nowhere to shop, just tarmac waiting for the next jet to lift into all that emptiness. That whole open, sky-swallowed lot is what people mean by airport.
items.reading_mnemonic: A clockwork cuckoo escapes its clock and takes over the tower speakers, popping out every hour to screech instead of chime. Pilots stop listening for gate numbers and taxi in the moment they hear its <reading>cuckoo</reading> call — the whole runway complex ends up named for that shout: <reading>くうこう</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A hand-painted sign hangs above one sliding door: vegetable bins spill onto the pavement, a bell over the frame jingles nonstop, and the till keeps popping open from coins going in and out all day. Nothing about the place is fancy — just one small room built around handing things to people for money. That room is a shop.
items.reading_mnemonic: A tiny shopkeeper mouse rings up every sale by squeaking the price twice, so customers just call the cramped counter <reading>mice, eh</reading> — say it fast enough and you get <reading>みせ</reading>, the shop everyone in town swears is run entirely by rodents.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A tower shop devours entire departments whole — one floor is nothing but shoes, the next is only teapots, and a man in a necktie gets trapped between six escalators that all disagree about which way is up. Every level swallows a different specialty until the whole building is just department after department stacked to the ceiling: a department store.
items.reading_mnemonic: デパート is kana spelling its own sound — say <reading>department</reading> and you've already said <reading>デパート</reading>, no decoding needed.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A shopping cart rolls out the automatic doors hauling forty bags of rice, an entire side of beef, and a wobbling pyramid of soap boxes, because an ordinary grocery run won't cut it here. One roof, every aisle, everything in bulk — the store is proud enough of the scale to call itself super for it: a supermarket.
items.reading_mnemonic: スーパー is kana spelling its own sound — say <reading>super</reading> and you've already said <reading>スーパー</reading>, nothing to derive.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's shop never closes, the till beeps without pause, and the onigiri shelf by the door restocks itself like clockwork at three in the morning. Someone pays a phone bill at the register while another customer photocopies a form, all before the entry chime finishes ringing. That does-everything, always-open little shop is a convenience store.
items.reading_mnemonic: コンビニ is kana spelling its own sound — say <reading>conveni</reading>, short for convenience, and you've already said <reading>コンビニ</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A city block gets squeezed between an office tower and a train station, so someone covers it in grass, wedges in three benches and a rusty swing set, and leaves the gate open for pigeons and toddlers to fight over the last patch of shade. That leftover square of green boxed in by concrete is a park.
items.reading_mnemonic: A gatekeeper named <reading>Cohen</reading> stands at the entrance every morning and won't lift the chain until the sun clears the trees. Kids rattle the fence chanting his name until he finally waves them onto the grass — the moment he answers is the moment the <reading>こうえん</reading> opens for the day.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Hover over that same grid again — fields squared off on the left, the straight road cutting through on the right. Now watch it fill in: roofs go up along the road, a bakery claims the corner, kids race bikes past the fields. Roads plus fields plus everyone building a life between them — that's a <kanji>town</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word borrows the reading you already learned for 町 itself — <reading>まち</reading>, no new sound to add.

items.mnemonic_text: The hall of moving pictures: eigakan.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Every night, folding chairs fill Koichi's konbini parking lot — instant ramen cups, someone's dog draped over a cooler. A bedsheet gets clipped to the delivery truck for a screen, the shutter light doubles as a projector, and the whole block settles in to watch: a cinema built out of nothing but a parking lot and a bedsheet.
items.reading_mnemonic: A giant film can rolls out of Koichi's walk-in freezer, crashes through the automatic doors, and unspools across the lot before anyone can grab it. He throws up his hands and grumbles that <reading>a giant can</reading> just opened a <reading>えいがかん</reading> right in his parking lot.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Past the mountain trail's improbable vending machine, someone has wedged a plain door straight into the rock face. Push it open and there's nothing dramatic inside — just four walls, one chair, and quiet, built for the sole purpose of finally sitting down after the climb: a room, carved out of nowhere in particular.
items.reading_mnemonic: The hiker collapses through that door, drops her pack, and sighs <reading>hay, yeah</reading> — worn out enough that even four bare walls feel like paradise. That sigh is exactly how you say <reading>へや</reading>, room, once you're finally inside one.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The bell rings at Sei's school and the hallway turns into a stampede — everyone sprinting for the same door before the next class starts. Whoever gets there first slams it shut, and the rest line up outside, jiggling, staring at their shoes: the single most fought-over room in the whole building, the toilet.
items.reading_mnemonic: Written and read exactly as it sounds, letter for letter: <reading>トイレ</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank a door stands with a huge <kanji>hand</kanji> painted on it, fingers spread wide and dripping wet. Everyone in line shakes that dripping <kanji>hand</kanji> before ducking inside to hunt for the toilet. The dripping hand is the whole point of the sign: wash first, then go — this is the restroom.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a visitor doubles over on the mossy steps and yells <reading>oh, tea-uh-rye!</reading> — the cats scatter as she sprints past the enormous bell, shouting the word for restroom: <reading>おてあらい</reading>, praying she makes it past every last cat in time.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini has one door marked staff-only, and behind it he's wedged in a battered stove, a cutting board on two beer crates, a rice cooker plugged into the drinks fridge. Customers assume it's storage, but at three in the morning he's frying eggs back there between restocking onigiri — his whole kitchen, hidden in plain sight.
items.reading_mnemonic: Behind the konbini's staff-only door, Koichi knocks over green food colouring and hollers <reading>dye the dough, oh!</reading> as it splatters across the rice cooker — the exact sound of <reading>だいどころ</reading>, the cramped little kitchen where he cooks between shifts.

items.mnemonic_text: The green space by the house: niwa.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Behind Sei's school, past the sports field, there's a locked gate nobody bothers with anymore. Squeeze through and you find a garden gone completely wild — tomato vines swallowing the old goalposts, cats sunbathing on a rusted rake nobody put away. Teachers pretend it isn't there. Everyone else just calls it the yard behind the yard.
items.reading_mnemonic: In that tangled garden behind the school, a cat pounces off the rusted rake and lands wrong, yowling <reading>knee, wah!</reading> — that garbled yelp is exactly the sound of <reading>にわ</reading>, the overgrown little yard where the school's stray cats actually live.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You keep following that winding <kanji>road</kanji> up the mountain trail, switchback after switchback, until it stops being a hiking route — a delivery scooter buzzes past, a mailbox appears at the bend, gravel turns to pavement. It isn't a trail anymore; it's somebody's street. That's the word: <kanji>road</kanji>, the ordinary road or street right outside a door.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is read exactly like the kanji you already know: 道 is <reading>みち</reading>, so no new story is needed here.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a delivery cart stalls at the water's edge, wheels churning mud. Someone drags two empty vending-machine crates out, sets them end to end across the current, and rolls the cart straight over the water without a splash. The crate-line stays there after — a bridge, built out of pure stubbornness.
items.reading_mnemonic: A cook at the riverbank burns a batch of <reading>hash</reading> browns and, furious, flings them one by one across the current. They land in a perfect line, crisp edge to crisp edge, and someone simply walks across on the hash line — which is exactly how you say <reading>はし</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini sits right on the corner, and a delivery van cuts the turn too sharp. It clips the onigiri shelf through the window, spins once, and wedges itself nose-first into the exact corner of the building — where it stays, blocking the corner entrance for the rest of the shift.
items.reading_mnemonic: The van's <reading>car door</reading> pops open on impact and won't shut again — it hangs there at the corner of the konbini like a broken wing. Koichi just tapes a sign to it: this is the corner now. That crumpled car door is exactly how you remember <reading>かど</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a lost tourist keeps ringing the enormous bell for directions. A patient officer steps out of a tiny booth by the mossy steps, cats streaming past his ankles, and points down the street to the actual police box — the booth that exists purely to rescue people from ringing the wrong bell.
items.reading_mnemonic: The officer's name badge just says Ban, and his sergeant radios him constantly: <reading>cope, Ban</reading>, another tourist's at the bell again. He sighs, straightens his booth's little roof, and steps out — that tired radio call is exactly how you say <reading>こうばん</reading>.
items.description: A 交番 is a small neighborhood police post, usually staffed by one or two officers, common on street corners and near stations — not the blue British police telephone box the English name might bring to mind. Locals stop by for directions about as often as for anything police-related.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The mountain trail is so steep that hikers stop believing in the vending machine at the top — until a taxi comes crawling up the switchbacks behind them, meter running, wheels spinning on loose gravel. It pulls up right next to the machine and idles patiently, because someone actually ordered a taxi to fetch canned coffee from the summit.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is a loanword borrowed straight from English "taxi" and written in katakana exactly as it's read: <reading>タクシー</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, something huge screeches to a stop right outside the sliding doors, tires shrieking against the curb loud enough to rattle the onigiri shelf. The doors hiss open, exhaust rolls in over the till, and a wall of tired passengers shuffles out into the fluorescent light — this rattling monster is the bus, and it stops here every hour on the hour.
items.reading_mnemonic: バス is written exactly as it sounds, so just read it as <reading>バス</reading> — the same sound as the English word <reading>bus</reading>.

items.mnemonic_text: The tree's origin, a book: hon.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At the school, Sei kneels by the tree with that single flat line marking its <kanji>origin</kanji> and presses a stack of blank paper flat against the mark. When she peels the pages away, the origin's whole shape has bled through onto every sheet, and she staples the stack edge to edge — a bound stack of someone's origin, pressed flat and readable, is exactly what a book is.
items.reading_mnemonic: 本 keeps the reading you already learned for it — read it as <reading>ほん</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Long after the <kanji>write</kanji> sun has sunk below your notebook and your hand is still moving on its own from that daily ritual, the pile of scribbled pages has grown so thick it needs its own spine. You bind the whole towering stack into one fat volume you flip through every time you're stuck on a word — a book that exists only to make writing easier: a dictionary.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa the crow swoops down, snatches the book off your desk, and squawks '<reading>じしょ</reading>!' — which sounds exactly like someone yelling '<reading>gee, show!</reading>' as he flips through it hunting for a word he can't recognize, refusing to give it back until he finds it.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, someone <kanji>new</kanji> in town stands beaming beside a fresh stack of printed pages, and every cat under the big bell presses an ear to the stack like it's a gate, straining to <kanji>hear</kanji> what's inside before anyone thinks to ask. By the time the bell rings, the whole shrine already knows what's inside those pages pressed flat — the newspaper.
items.reading_mnemonic: 新聞 keeps both taught readings back to back, so read it as <reading>しんぶん</reading> — new, then hear.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The onigiri shelf at Koichi's konbini gets restocked every hour, but the rack beside it never does — gossip pages, fishing weeklies, and a torn coupon insert all wedged into one groaning shelf the clerk just calls 'the magazine,' singular, because nobody has ever managed to tell where one issue ends and the next begins.
items.reading_mnemonic: A customer swipes the last gossip weekly off Koichi's rack, and the till beeps twice — zap, zap — before the cashier sighs, that's her again. <reading>ざっし</reading> is that double beep and sigh: <reading>zap-she</reading>, rung up on the same magazine every week.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the cats leap along the mossy steps and swat every fortune slip off the branches, until by dusk the ground is drifted white with thin square sheets — not snow, just fallen paper, blanketing the whole shrine before Grandma Kane can ring the bell.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane catches a cat pawing through the drifted fortune slips and snaps, come, me! — meaning drop it and follow her to the shrine office. <reading>かみ</reading> is that snap: <reading>come-me</reading>, aimed at a cat sitting on a pile of shrine paper.

items.meaning_mnemonic: In the echoing hallway of Sei's school, a boy chews the eraser end of a thin gray stick down to nothing, tapping the point against his desk until it snaps clean in half during the exam — the exact anxious shape and worry of a pencil.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei checks the biology closet and finds the terrarium empty — the class hamster is loose again. She sighs, empty zoo, scrawling the note with the stub left in her pencil case. <reading>えんぴつ</reading> is that sigh: <reading>empty-zoo</reading>, written before the pencil's own lead breaks.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the lone vending machine sells exactly one item no hiker asked for: a pen that leaks the instant you click it, blooming blue across your knuckles and smearing your name across the summit logbook the second you try to sign it — a pen, and now a permanent one.
items.reading_mnemonic: ペン is kana all the way through, read exactly as written and borrowed straight from English: 「<reading>ペン</reading>」 is simply pen.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini till, a customer clicks a slim plastic stick against the counter, and a tiny steel ball rolls out of the tip, dragging a thin trail of blue ink across the receipt paper. Koichi doesn't blink — that rolling ball is just how a ballpoint pen writes.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>ボールペン</reading> is pure loanword kana, written exactly as it's read, straight from the English "ball pen," so there's nothing to decode.

items.mnemonic_text: What you carry things in: kaban.
items.meaning_mnemonic: After the last bell at Sei's school, someone crams gym shoes, dog-eared workbooks, and a crumpled umbrella into one straining canvas sack, then wrestles the zipper shut over the bulge as it clears the sports field. That overstuffed sack slung over a shoulder is just a bag doing its job.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>かばん</reading> is plain kana, written exactly as it sounds, no kanji reading to derive here.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, someone wading across loses their footing, and a slim leather fold flies from their pocket mid-splash. Coins scatter into the current and bills drift downstream like paper boats, but the fold itself washes up on the bank, empty and dripping — proof that whatever it once held, it's still a wallet.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the mountain trail's lone vending machine, an old peddler unzips a battered leather fold and swears it's <reading>sci-fi</reading> tech from the future. He says the word for it, <reading>さいふ</reading>, slow and dramatic, then just buys a can of coffee like it's an ordinary wallet after all.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane is sick of craning her neck at the shrine to track <kanji>time</kanji>, so she catches the sun mid-crawl above the steps and coils its slow arc into a circle small enough to nail above the bell. Now <kanji>time</kanji> ticks around a tidy face instead of crawling across the sky — she has hung herself a clock.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer stubs his toe on the wall clock and yelps <reading>toe-kay</reading> before glaring up to see exactly how much time he wasted wincing — that wall clock is <reading>とけい</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the librarian's eyesight gives out mid-shelving, so she bends two empty onigiri wrappers from Koichi's konbini into perfect circles, wires them together with a stray chopstick, and hooks the whole rig over her ears. The blur snaps into focus at once — she has just invented glasses.
items.reading_mnemonic: A new student at Sei's school keeps insisting she isn't wearing glasses, but every teacher squints at her face and asks, <reading>Meg, uh, nay?</reading> — which is exactly how you say <reading>めがね</reading>, the glasses she is obviously wearing.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, the sky cracks open and dumps a whole second river down onto the first one. A fisherman yanks a bent bamboo frame out of his tackle box, stretches waxed paper across the ribs, and pops it open over his head just before he's soaked through — that bent, stretched frame is an umbrella.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, the rain arrives as one long <reading>cascade</reading> — clip off just the front half, said fast, and you get <reading>かさ</reading>, the umbrella the fisherman snaps open to survive it.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The lightning that split the sky over your rain-streaked window doesn't fade at the glass — it dives down a wire and into a box on the desk. Out of the earpiece pours that same restless <kanji>talk</kanji>, tongue wagging nonstop, riding pure <kanji>electricity</kanji> into your ear. That's a telephone: talk carried on a bolt of electricity.
items.reading_mnemonic: 電 already gives you でん and 話 already gives you わ — stitch them together and you get <reading>でんわ</reading>, telephone.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the new clerk Kei ties his phone to his belt with butcher's string before every shift, certain he won't survive the beeping till without it. By closing time the string has looped him to the register three times over, and everyone has stopped calling it a phone — it's just his mobile phone now.
items.reading_mnemonic: Picture the manager at Koichi's konbini shouting across the shop as the string tangles again: '<reading>Kay, tie</reading>!' — tie it down before it beeps once more. That shout is <reading>けいたい</reading>, the reading of mobile phone, the word Kei now answers to more than his own name.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The vending machine at the top of the mountain trail breaks down one rainy week, and its cracked screen fills with fuzzy grey static instead of dispensing canned coffee. Hikers keep climbing anyway, huddling round the glowing box, because somehow it has started showing Sei's sports day live from the valley below. Nobody's brave enough to unplug the trail's new TV.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>テレビ</reading> is written in kana exactly as it sounds, so the reading is simply <reading>テレビ</reading> itself — nothing to derive.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the one enormous bell hasn't been rung in months, yet the cats gather on the mossy steps every evening at six, ears flat, tails puffed. Tucked behind the bell sits a cracked wooden box quietly muttering a weather report to no one. The cats, it turns out, have been listening to the shrine's radio the whole time.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>ラジオ</reading> is written in kana exactly as it sounds, so the reading is simply <reading>ラジオ</reading> itself — nothing to derive.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a tourist raises a boxy black gadget with a glass eye at the enormous bell and shouts the thing's own name at it. The flash pops, every cat on the mossy steps freezes mid-leap, and the little screen lights up with the shot: a camera, catching cats that never agreed to sit still.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it's read, no kanji to decode — just say what you see: <reading>カメラ</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: In Koichi's konbini, beside the onigiri shelf, a customer heaves a slab of grey plastic onto the counter and starts jabbing it the way he jabs the beeping till. Half-finished English stutters out of its little speaker — pa, so, kon — until the whole register short-circuits into a glowing screen full of spreadsheets: a computer, ringing up groceries nobody asked it to buy.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it's read, no kanji hiding underneath — just the borrowed English squeezed down to fit: <reading>パソコン</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a heavy wooden seat with a tall carved back, and look closely — the carving is shaped exactly like a swaddled <kanji>child</kanji>, arms flung wide the way it always reaches. Those flung-out arms become the armrests, the swaddling becomes the seat, and the whole piece of furniture is built around that one reaching shape: a chair.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, a hiker spots the only bench and calls out to her friend, 'Ee, <reading>Sue</reading>, over here!' as she drops onto it with a groan. The two sounds run together into <reading>いす</reading> — the exact sigh of relief you make cornering the one thing at the summit built for sitting.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A moving crew wedges a single office desk through the automatic doors of Koichi's konbini because it wouldn't fit anywhere else, bolting it down beside the onigiri shelf. Now Koichi rings up rice balls sitting behind a proper desk instead of a bare register. Every clerk after him just calls it the desk.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a janitor hauls a heavy desk down the echoing hallway, grunting <reading>Sue, cooey!</reading> with every shove until the hallway chants it back. By the time the desk scrapes into the classroom, the chant has worn a groove: <reading>つくえ</reading>, the sound of a desk landing where it doesn't fit.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Two fishermen haul a wide, flat plank out of the river and can't be bothered carrying it back to camp, so they wedge it level across four boulders right there on the bank and eat lunch off it. Every trip after, they head straight for the same plank on the same four rocks. They never call it a plank again, it's their table.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is a straight loanword from the English word for table, written in kana exactly as it sounds: <reading>テーブル</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A monk lugs a stack of futons up the mossy steps of Grandma Kane's shrine, planning to store them by the enormous bell overnight. Before he finishes stacking, half the resident cats have already curled into the pile and refuse to move. He gives up, tucks a blanket round the edges, and leaves them the shrine's new bed.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is a straight loanword from the English word for bed, written in kana exactly as it sounds: <reading>ベッド</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini only has one way in: an automatic slab that slides aside the instant someone steps close, breathing out a soft whoosh right where the shop meets the street. New hires hear that whoosh and just call it what it sounds like, unchanged from English — a door.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is a loanword straight from English, written in kana exactly the way it sounds — read <reading>ドア</reading> just like the English word door that it borrows.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture someone at Grandma Kane's shrine so furious that a cat knocked over the offering bowl that they wrench open the wooden frame set into the wall and shout their outrage straight at the sky — mad, then oh, right as the frame swings wide. That opening they're yelling through, moss creeping up its sill, is a window.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane catches the cat sprawled across her offerings again and goes properly <reading>mad, oh!</reading> — the shout tears out of her as she yanks the wooden frame in the shrine wall wide open to chase it out. That startled yell is <reading>まど</reading>: the window she just threw open.

items.meaning_mnemonic: That storm-bred bolt punches through the rain and drives into a lightbulb on the ceiling, filament screaming white. Beside it, the curl of <kanji>spirit</kanji> that always rises off a hot bowl of rice streams upward too, feeding the glow. <kanji>Electricity</kanji> plus that rising energy floods the room: electricity, light.
items.reading_mnemonic: 気 already lends you Kiki's giggly き, and 電 gives you でん — line them up and you get <reading>でんき</reading>, electricity.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The vending machine at the top of the mountain trail is, inexplicably, padlocked. A hiker pats down every pocket of their khaki trousers, harder and harder, until deep in the last one something small and metal turns up — the only thing standing between them and a can of tea: the key that finally opens the lock.
items.reading_mnemonic: The hiker digs through <reading>khaki</reading> pocket after khaki pocket, patting each one flat, until the last gives up a small metal shape with a jingle. That frantic pocket search is <reading>かぎ</reading> — the key that finally unlocks the padlock chaining the vending machine shut.
items.description: In Japanese, 鍵 covers both the physical key and the lock it opens — context decides which one is meant, where English normally reaches for two separate words.

items.mnemonic_text: A copy of the truth: shashin.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a dozen cats sprawl across the mossy steps, and just as the great bell tolls, a bulb pops and freezes every yawn and twitching tail at once, the whole moment trapped flat and still forever. That frozen instant, kept for good, is a photograph.
items.reading_mnemonic: A tourist barges into the shrine's hush, camera raised, and the old priest just hisses <reading>shush in</reading> before you break it — too late, the shutter already clicked. He hands back the camera; the saved file reads simply <reading>しゃしん</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a <kanji>hand</kanji> reaches across the water and drops a folded page into a second <kanji>hand</kanji> waiting on the far bank, which folds it again and passes it to a third — the page crossing hand to hand until it reaches you, refolded and ready to read: a letter.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi wraps a sticky gummy candy inside a folded note at the konbini register and mutters <reading>the gummy</reading> as he slides it across the counter — the customer unwraps it, and taped underneath, waiting to be read, is a <reading>てがみ</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, beside the one improbable vending machine, a <kanji>hand</kanji> peels a small sticky square from a roll and presses it flat onto the corner of an envelope before shoving the envelope into the summit mailbox — the little square that lets it travel: a postage stamp.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a hiker keeps licking the vending machine's sticky squares instead of buying tea, and the vendor barks <reading>quit it</reading> — she finally buys one properly, licks it once, and presses it onto her postcard: a <reading>きって</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the vending machine on the mountain trail, you press the button for water. It grinds, hesitates, then drops a plain taped-shut carton instead, tumbling down the last few steps ahead of you. Nobody asked for this. The machine just started calling every carton a box, and now so does everyone who climbs the trail.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, Koichi wades in to cool a crate of drinks and comes out numb to the elbow. He yelps <reading>"Ha, cold!"</reading> so sharply that the fishermen nearby start calling the crate itself by that yelp, and the name sticks as <reading>はこ</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a kid staples every loose page from their bag into one brick-thick block and hauls it to class insisting it's still light. The teacher weighs it in one hand, sighs, and writes "notebook" across the cover so nobody has to argue about what to call it again.
items.reading_mnemonic: Written in kana exactly as it sounds, straight from the English word notebook — read it as <reading>ノート</reading>, no decoding needed.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's shrine cats go bare all year, until the coldest morning, when she drapes a tiny knitted sweater over every single one. They strut past the enormous bell stiff-legged, dressed head to tail, mossy steps turned runway. None of them asked for clothes, but none of them takes them off either.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a shivering customer grabs an armful of shirts off the rack and mutters <reading>"few, coo"</reading> through chattering teeth, too cold to finish a real sentence. The till beeps it through anyway, and the receipt just prints <reading>ふく</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the mountain trail, steep and endless, with that one vending machine impossibly balanced at the summit. A hiker collapses beside it, kicks off two mud-caked boots, and buys a can of tea instead of anything to eat. He drinks, sighs, and never puts the boots back on — leaves them right there under the machine as shoes for whoever runs out of nerve next.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the mountain trail vending machine, a scruffy crow named Kutsu lands on the boots someone abandoned there and calls out sharply, <reading>coo-tsu, coo-tsu</reading> — the exact sound of <reading>くつ</reading>, over and over, guarding them like his own shoes now.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture that same swaddled <kanji>child</kanji> from before, arms flung out, except Grandma Kane keeps wrapping cloth around its head for warmth, spiral after spiral, until the arms vanish under the layers and only a round knit dome pokes out the top — a hat, sitting where a baby used to be.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat hides under the knit dome sitting on the steps.
