A visitor bends to pet it and the cat explodes out, making her yelp <reading>boo-shi</reading> — the same sound as <reading>ぼうし</reading> — before she realizes the dome rolling away is only a hat.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer leans too far over the counter to grab an onigiri and his loose top catches on the price scanner by the till. The register beeps furiously, over and over, as if trying to ring up the fabric itself, until Koichi peels the sleeve free and holds up the wrinkled shirt like it just came off the shelf.
items.reading_mnemonic: シャツ is written the way it sounds — no kanji to decode, just read the kana straight across as <reading>シャツ</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the vending machine sells exactly one item: a stiff paper coat that unfolds like a cardboard crane. You climbed up in a t-shirt, so you feed it your last coins, unfold it, and stop shivering immediately. Up here, that stiff paper garment has one name and one job — it's your coat.
items.reading_mnemonic: コート is kana, so it is pronounced exactly as it looks — no kanji hiding a different sound. Read the four characters straight through and you get <reading>コート</reading>, the loanword transcription of English 'coat.'
items.description: コート is a loanword that also means "court," as in a tennis court — the two senses share one spelling and one sound, and only the surrounding sentence tells you whether someone is putting one on or standing on one.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Look up past the ceiling stretched over everyone's outstretched arms — the <kanji>sky</kanji> itself — and you'll see it has moods. When that same curling wisp of <kanji>spirit</kanji> that rises off a hot bowl of rice thickens into cloud, or thins and vanishes, the sky is telling you what's coming: today's weather.
items.reading_mnemonic: 天 already gives you てん and 気 already lends Kiki's き — stitch them together and you get <reading>てんき</reading>, weather.

items.mnemonic_text: Drops from the sky frame: ame.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You're back at the window, watching the same drops slide down the glass, one after another inside their frame. Step outside now and those drops aren't caught behind glass anymore — they're landing straight on your shoulders. What's soaking you has exactly one name: <kanji>rain</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word keeps 雨's own taught reading exactly as taught, so it reads <reading>あめ</reading> — the same sound you already tied to the drops sliding down the window frame.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, the path turns white — not sand, not ash, just cold pale flakes settling on your shoulders and melting the second they land. It piles on the vending machine's roof, on the railing, on your shoes, until the whole trail is buried under it. There's one word for that pale, cold covering: snow.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail the vending machine jams, burying a hiker under white flakes from its coin slot. She digs through the cold pile shouting <reading>you, key</reading> — hunting her dropped key — and every shout comes out sounding exactly like <reading>ゆき</reading>.
items.description: ゆき is also an extremely common Japanese given name for girls, so outside of weather talk it will usually be someone's name rather than the word for snow.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the automatic door sticks open and a sudden gust roars in, sending the entire onigiri shelf toppling and every plastic bag in the store leaping off its hook at once. He just stands at the till, beeping through the chaos, muttering that it's too much wind for one small door.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi swears the same draft <reading>causes</reading> the shelf to fall every single morning, and he's taken to yelling <reading>かぜ</reading> at the door like it's a curse word, until the whole konbini staff starts shouting it whenever a gust rolls through.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's shrine bell rings on its own one grey morning, and by the time she reaches the mossy steps, a thick grey mass has rolled in low overhead, swallowing the roofline whole and turning every cat on the steps into a silhouette. She squints up and just calls it the cloud sitting on her shrine.
items.reading_mnemonic: One of Grandma Kane's shrine cats, a fat grey tom the neighborhood calls Moe, sits on the mossy steps and coos up at the grey mass rolling over the bell. Regulars say he's only saying <reading>coo, Moe</reading>, but it comes out sounding exactly like <reading>くも</reading>, so that's what everyone calls the cloud too.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The vending machine at the top of the mountain trail sits improbably alone, no building for a mile around it, just a cable running to nowhere and a stretch of blue that starts at the machine's roof and doesn't stop. Hikers reach the summit less for the drinks than to stand there and stare straight up into all that open sky.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the summit vending machine, a hawk seen every clear afternoon <reading>soars</reading> straight up until it's a speck, and the hikers waiting on their drink call it their <reading>そら</reading> bird, because it never comes down until the whole open expanse above the machine is empty again.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the same window with a bar across it that you already know: the <kanji>sun</kanji> is climbing into the frame right now, filling the room with morning light. That one image was always doing double duty — window, bar, climbing sun — and standing alone it's already the whole word for sun and <kanji>day</kanji>, no second kanji needed to lean on.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is written with the very kanji you already read as <reading>ひ</reading>, so the sound carries straight over — no new reading to learn.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane climbs her mossy shrine steps and looks straight up: there's the same sliver she already knows, the <kanji>moon</kanji> that fattens and fades to mark off a whole <kanji>month</kanji>. Tonight she isn't tracking the calendar at all, just staring at the sliver itself — and that sliver, on its own, is simply the word moon.
items.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just the kanji's own <reading>つき</reading>, the same sound you already attached to that crescent, carried straight into the word.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi strings cheap fairy lights along the konbini ceiling, but half of them burn out by midnight, leaving a scatter of tiny bright points against black tile. Late customers buying onigiri look up and see a private sky punched with pinholes of light, one fixed point at a time. That single point of light, sitting alone in the dark, is exactly the word: star.
items.reading_mnemonic: Two hikers reach the mountain trail's summit vending machine at last light. One collapses against it, and her friend blurts <reading>Whoa, she's</reading> done — then both look up to find a single point of light waiting over the ridge: the <reading>ほし</reading> that guided the whole climb.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A fisherman leaves one bucket of water by his back door to rinse his boots, but it rains so hard overnight that the bucket overflows and never stops — by morning his whole street sits underwater, waves lapping at the mailbox. One forgotten bucket, given enough time, became an entire sea.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei wades into the riverbank current on a school trip, certain it's shallow, until the ground vanishes and cold water rushes to her shoulders. She yelps <reading>ooh, me</reading>, right before the current sweeps her toward the open <reading>うみ</reading> the river was hiding all along.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, legs burning, you stop and count peaks the old way: three ridges, the middle one tallest. Except now it isn't ink on a page — it's rock under your boots, wind in your ears, and a vending machine glowing improbably at the summit. You've hiked straight into the shape that means <kanji>mountain</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 山 keeps the same reading you already learned for the character itself — <reading>やま</reading>, the same <reading>yah-mah</reading> sound.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, you crouch to rinse your hands and watch three currents braid together exactly the way you learned to see them: three flowing lines side by side. Cup your palms and the water doesn't care about the drawing — it just runs, cold and fast, over your fingers. That current has a name: <kanji>river</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 川 keeps the same reading you already learned for the character itself — <reading>かわ</reading>, the same <reading>kah-wah</reading> sound.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one trunk splits the mossy steps clean in half, roots shoving down into the stone and branches spreading wide over the enormous bell. Cats scatter into its shade every afternoon. There's no need to explain what's growing there — trunk, roots, branches, unmistakably a <kanji>tree</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 木 keeps the same reading you already learned for the character itself — <reading>き</reading>, the same <reading>key</reading> sound, home to Kiki the tree spirit.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Under the fluorescent glare of Koichi's konbini, someone has wedged a single potted plant by the onigiri shelf: one stem leaning hard to the side, its bloom spilling clean over the pot's rim. Customers keep stopping mid-reach for rice balls just to stare at it. Stem below, blossom bursting above — a <kanji>flower</kanji> where nobody expected one.
items.reading_mnemonic: 花 keeps the same reading you already learned for the character itself — <reading>はな</reading>, the same <reading>hah-nah</reading> sound.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every evening a dog parks himself outside Koichi's konbini, nose pressed to the glass, staring at the onigiri shelf like it personally wronged him. He never begs, never barks — just stands there radiating quiet judgment until someone caves and brings one out. That silent, immovable stare is what dog means here.
items.reading_mnemonic: A new part-timer trips over the dog camped by Koichi's door and asks if he's some kind of mascot. Koichi shakes his head: he's just <reading>いぬ</reading>, plain and simple, and the easiest way to hold onto that is to hear it as <reading>in new</reading> — like he wandered in new and never left.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, cats already outnumber worshippers, but one has decided the offering bell is a toy. She swats the rope, ducks under the railing, and curls up exactly where the incense smoke is warmest, ignoring every polite attempt to shoo her off. That smug, entitled little squatter is what cat means.
items.reading_mnemonic: A visitor watches the shrine cat arch and stretch across the warm stone and winces, worried for her <reading>neck, oh</reading> — just as the cat flops flatter, completely unbothered. That half-panicked warning is the shape of <reading>ねこ</reading>, and the cat never once looks up to acknowledge it.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, past the vending machine that shouldn't be there, something small and feathered dive-bombs a hiker's rice ball straight out of his hand and is gone before he can react. He never even sees it land — just a blur, a gap in the air, and an empty wrapper. That blur is what bird means.
items.reading_mnemonic: The hiker shouts that the thing just <reading>tore</reading> his rice ball clean out of his hand, and the guide behind him laughs — everyone's shout sounds like that the first time it happens. That's <reading>とり</reading>: the sound of something snatching your lunch and vanishing before you can name it.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Sei's school announces a surprise visit from the local shelter, and by lunchtime every hallway smells like fur and nervous energy. Rabbits loose in the gym, a goat wandering near the vending machines, someone's parakeet shrieking over the PA by accident. Whatever has fur, feathers, or four legs and absolutely does not belong indoors — that's animal today.
items.reading_mnemonic: A teacher at Sei's school trips over the stray goat's hoof in the hallway and yelps <reading>though, boots</reading> as she catches herself against the wall. The goat stays entirely unbothered. Everyone agrees that yelp is the closest an English mouth gets to <reading>どうぶつ</reading>, and after today nobody forgets it.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every year on the mountain trail, the vending machine at the top freezes solid through winter — until one morning the ice around its buttons melts, a marmot pokes its head out of a burrow beside it, and the whole slope turns to mud and green shoots overnight. That sudden thaw, when everything wakes up at once, is spring.
items.reading_mnemonic: A groundhog named Haru climbs out of her burrow on the mountain trail every thaw and bellows a cheerful <reading>halloo</reading> across the valley to announce she's awake. Everyone down at the shrine started calling that first warm shout <reading>はる</reading>, and the name stuck.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, the heat gets so thick that the cicadas scream nonstop and a fat bullfrog finally can't take it anymore — it belly-flops straight into the water fully dressed in someone's abandoned sandals, sending up a wall of spray. That relentless, sweat-soaked heat that drives everyone into the river is summer.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, Koichi complains the heat is unbearable, and Grandma Kane snaps back that it's <reading>not, too</reading> — she's roasting just the same, fanning herself with a shrine pamphlet. The villagers shortened her retort to <reading>なつ</reading>, and that's the season now.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a single red leaf drifts in through the automatic door and lands square on the sensor, so the door just hangs there half-open, beeping, while more leaves blow in and pile up around the onigiri shelf until the whole floor is drifted orange. That first stubborn leaf jamming the door is autumn arriving.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the automatic door won't budge until someone finds <reading>a key</reading> taped under the onigiri shelf — it turns out to be the spare for the storeroom, left there every year once the leaves start piling up. Konbini regulars now call that leaf season <reading>あき</reading>, after the key.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the sports field freezes so hard overnight that someone's abandoned soccer ball is stuck fast to the ice, and the whole team spends morning practice tiptoeing across the frozen grass in their socks because their shoes keep sliding out from under them. That bone-deep, everything-locked-solid freeze is winter.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the frozen sports field, Sei skids into a snowbank and pops up gasping <reading>phew, you</reading> nearly took me out — his teammate had shoved him from behind. The whole team started yelling <reading>ふゆ</reading> at each other for every shove after that, all winter long.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You reach the top of the mountain trail expecting the usual lone vending machine, but instead the whole crater ahead is filled with still, glassy water stretching out to the far ridge — too big for a pond, too walled-in for the sea. You have found a lake.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the mountain trail's summit, a hiker introduces herself between gasps as <reading>Missy Umi</reading>, then points down at the water filling the crater below. Out of breath, her name and the word for what she's pointing at blur into one: <reading>みずうみ</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi restocks the onigiri shelf overnight, and by morning every wrapper is a wildly different hue — lime green, shocking pink, traffic-cone orange — clashing under the fluorescent lights. Customers stop dead in the doorway, dazzled by the sheer color of it all.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi finds a gloomy donkey named <reading>Eeyore</reading> wandering the konbini aisle. Under the fluorescent lights his gray coat lights up with every hue on the shelf, and his mournful name sounds just like the word for it: <reading>いろ</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You're still blinking from that blinding ray outside Koichi's konbini, and when your eyes finally adjust, the whole street looks bleached — the cars, the sidewalk, even the shopkeeper's apron drained of every color into the same flat <kanji>white</kanji>. That's the word for what you're staring at.
items.reading_mnemonic: This is the same 白 kanji you learned, and it keeps the same reading here: 「<reading>しろ</reading>」.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The soot from that fire settles over the village for good, and when someone finally tries to repaint the signpost, every color left in the tin has merged into a single sludge — dip the brush anywhere and it comes out the same <kanji>black</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: This is exactly the 黒 kanji you learned, keeping the same reading here: 「<reading>くろ</reading>」.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Back on the mountain trail, the crack in the ground still glows from the fire beneath the earth. Tonight that glow claws its way up past the trail, past the vending machine, until the whole hillside catches and everything you can see burns the same fierce <kanji>red</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 赤 already carries the reading you learned for it straight into this word, no detour: <reading>あか</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The sprout is still glowing over the moon, caught in that in-between shade of <kanji>blue and green</kanji>. Tonight the moonlight pulls harder than the leaves do, draining the warmth out of it until only the cool half survives — a flat, quiet, midnight blue.
items.reading_mnemonic: 青 already carries the reading あお exactly as taught, carried straight into this word unchanged: <reading>あお</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till jams and won't stop printing. Receipt after receipt spools out under the fluorescent lights, each one dyed a violent, glowing shade, until the whole counter disappears under a drift taller than the onigiri shelf — every scrap of it the exact same yellow.
items.reading_mnemonic: A canary lands on Koichi's till and pecks at the same <reading>key</reading> over and over, then hops along the counter in a tidy <reading>row</reading> of yellow feathers — key, row, <reading>きいろ</reading> — and won't budge until someone finally calls it by that color.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, a fisherman's tackle box tips into the shallows. When he fishes it back out, every hook, weight, and bobber inside has come up coated in the same slick pond algae, dripping one uniform green, until the whole box is just a soggy green mess sitting in the reeds.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a woman knocks three times on her boathouse door — <reading>me, dough, ree</reading> — and waits so long for an answer that pond algae creeps up the door itself, turning it the same green as the water: <reading>みどり</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the tea urn boils over during the morning rush, sheeting hot tea across the floor, up the onigiri shelf, and onto the ceiling tiles. By closing time everything in the shop — walls, floor, Koichi's socks — has dried into the exact same shade: brown.
items.reading_mnemonic: Picture Grandma Kane lining up cups of tea in a perfect row along the mossy shrine steps, one for every cat that shows up. A <reading>chai row</reading> is exactly the sound of <reading>ちゃいろ</reading>, and every cup in it, without exception, is the same warm brown.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The fisherman still has his arms flung wide, spread even wider today than yesterday, boasting about a catch that somehow grows a little more with every retelling. By the third telling his arms won't close in front of him at all — whatever he caught, it was <kanji>big</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 大 already sounds おお in words like this one, and き＋い are just the ordinary adjective ending, so 大きい reads straight through as <reading>おおきい</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: That same delicate hook with its two flanking dots keeps shrinking with every review, the dots drawing in closer until the whole shape looks like it might blow away in a light breeze. Nothing about it ever grows back — it stays exactly <kanji>small</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 小 already sounds ちい in words like this one, and さ＋い are just the ordinary adjective ending, so 小さい reads straight through as <reading>ちいさい</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Stand beneath that same tower with its yawning mouth of an entrance, except today the mouth is a ticket booth, and the price climbs one more floor every time you crane your neck to look up. By the top the ticket costs a fortune — the building was always both <kanji>tall</kanji> and <kanji>expensive</kanji> at once.
items.reading_mnemonic: 高 already sounds たか in words like this one, and い is just the ordinary adjective ending, so 高い reads straight through as <reading>たかい</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A heron at the riverbank refuses to use the tall bridge and instead wades under a footbridge built barely above the water. Every step forces its neck down further, until it's hunched practically flat against the current, its whole body folded so low its beak skims the surface.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the mountain trail's summit vending machine, delivery boy Ren has to duck so far under its low overhang that he grunts <reading>“he, coo, we”</reading> each time — the exact sound of <reading>ひくい</reading>, because everything up here, the ceiling included, is built low.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The woman is still kneeling safe under her own roof, and today she's turned the whole house into a shop. Rent is nothing, worry is nothing, so she chalks every price down to nothing too, hanging a sign over the door: everything in here is <kanji>cheap</kanji>, because peace of mind never cost her a thing to begin with.
items.reading_mnemonic: 安 already reads やす in cheap／peaceful, tack on the adjective ending い, and you get exactly <reading>やすい</reading> as taught.

items.meaning_mnemonic: That same person is still planted in the showroom, grinning beside their finished build, when a friend walks in and the surface throws back a mirror-perfect double of them both — two identical grinners, side by side. Nothing scuffs a mirror that clean; the whole showroom still smells of <kanji>new</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 新 already reads あたら in new, chain on し and the adjective ending い, and you get exactly <reading>あたらしい</reading> as taught.

items.mnemonic_text: Ten mouths of old stories: furui.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's shrine borrows that same mouth held up by ancient crossbeams — its bell hangs from timber so weathered the wood has gone the color of ash. Cats doze in the beam's shadow, moss creeps up every post, and the mouth beneath keeps repeating the same worn story to anyone who'll listen: this whole place is <kanji>old</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 古 already reads ふる in old, tack on the adjective ending い, and you get exactly <reading>ふるい</reading> as taught.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat sniffs the offering bowl and gives two sharp nods — one for the taste, one for the temperature — before curling up satisfied on the mossy steps. Two nods, two syllables: いい, いい. Whatever survives a cat's judgment twice over earns the simplest verdict there is — good.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it sounds, said twice over: <reading>いい</reading>.
items.description: いい is the casual, everyday word for good, but it conjugates oddly: the negative, the past, and the te-form all switch to a different stem instead of building directly off いい itself — one of the few adjectives in Japanese that bends this way.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a formal inspector in white gloves lifts each onigiri to the fluorescent light, cross-checking it against a clipboard before she'll stamp the wrapper. Nothing leaves the shelf without that stamp. This is the paperwork version of saying something is good — the one you'd write in a report, not say to a friend over the till.
items.reading_mnemonic: The inspector never just nods — she barks the verdict for the record, <reading>“Yo, E!”</reading> she calls, stamping the wrapper as she says it. That clipped, official shout is exactly how <reading>よい</reading> sounds: approval formal enough to file away.
items.description: よい is the full, uncontracted form of the same word — the one that shows up in formal speech, writing, and set phrases, while everyday conversation overwhelmingly shortens it to いい instead.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a cat knocks a straw laundry basket clean off the washing rock, and it drifts downstream with the current, contents soaking through. Nobody wades in after it. Whatever comes back out of that basket later — waterlogged, torn, ruined beyond fixing — is the exact picture of bad.
items.reading_mnemonic: The cat leans too far off the riverbank wall chasing the basket, wobbles, and topples in with a flailing <reading>“Wall, ooh-ee!”</reading> Its shriek on the way down lands close enough to <reading>わるい</reading> that everyone on the bank agrees: that fall looked bad.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, the lone vending machine has been baking in direct sun since morning. You press a palm flat against its metal side and yank it back instantly, fingers stinging. The whole trail feels like an oven today, and that vending machine is the hottest spot on it.
items.reading_mnemonic: You grab the vending machine's coin slot too fast and yelp <reading>“Ah, too!”</reading>, shaking out your scorched fingers. That yelp is basically <reading>あつい</reading> — the sound your mouth makes right before you remember mountain metal in the sun burns exactly like this.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini a customer grabs a can of oden broth straight off the warmer without checking first, yelps, and juggles it hand to hand like it's on fire, blowing on her fingers. That single reflex, grab-and-drop, is the whole word: hot, the kind you find out about by touching it.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's counter, a woman named Sue reaches for the can straight off the warmer and yelps, shaking her stinging hand and hissing the same sound twice. Hear that yelp as <reading>あつい</reading>: <reading>at Sue, ee</reading>, the exact noise she makes every single time she forgets to check first.

items.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail the vending machine hums alone in the wind, and a stray dog presses its whole body against the machine's warm metal side, shivering so hard its bark comes out broken and stuttering instead of sharp. That shudder, the cold that gets into your bones from the outside air, is the meaning.
items.reading_mnemonic: A hiker named Sam reaches the vending machine at the summit with his teeth chattering so hard the words come out garbled, over and over, until he finally zips his coat. Hear that chatter as <reading>さむい</reading>: <reading>some moo, eh</reading>, repeated until the shivering finally stops.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank someone dunks a can of juice into the current to chill it, forgets about it for an hour, and pulls it back out numb-fingered and gasping. The metal has gone shockingly cold to the touch, far colder than the air around it ever was, and that's the meaning: cold, the kind you feel through your skin.
items.reading_mnemonic: A man at the riverbank loosens his necktie in the heat and dunks the end of it in the current to cool off, then yanks it back out gasping at how it stings his fingers. That yelp is <reading>つめたい</reading>: <reading>too, my tie</reading>, dripping and cold enough to hurt.
items.description: 冷たい also describes a person, not just an object — a cold, distant, unfriendly manner. The same word that fits icy river water fits an icy attitude. This entry teaches the physical, to-the-touch sense; the personality sense is a common extension you'll run into later.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine the cats abandon the mossy steps every afternoon and pile onto the sun-warmed stone beside the bell instead, purring in a heap until the stone itself seems to purr back. That gentle, all-over warmth, never scalding, just comfortable, is the meaning.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane waves the cats off the sun-warmed stone with a cheerful farewell before heading off to buy incense, and the whole phrase comes out as one running line. Hear it as <reading>あたたかい</reading>: <reading>ah, ta-ta, kai</reading>, warm as the stone she leaves behind her.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You haul yourself up the mountain trail, drenched, and finally reach the lone vending machine at the top. Before you even press a button, its compressor exhales a blast of chilled air across the back of your neck, and the whole sweaty afternoon evaporates into one cool, refreshing breath.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the vending machine, a hiker named <reading>Suzy</reading> holds her water bottle to her cheek and sighs, dragging the word out like the cool air itself: <reading>すずしい</reading>, she says, every time the breeze finally reaches her.

items.mnemonic_text: A white-bright face of fun: omoshiroi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You step out of Koichi's konbini into that blinding <kanji>white</kanji> flash of morning sun, and just as your eyes adjust, a delivery truck reverses straight into the onigiri sign with a crash. Everyone in line stops chewing to stare, because it's suddenly the most interesting, funniest thing that's happened all week.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi surveys the flattened sign and mutters, '<reading>Oh, most royal</reading> mess I've ever seen,' and the customers by the till can't stop repeating it, laughing: <reading>おもしろい</reading>, they agree, watching him sweep up onigiri wrappers.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a substitute reads the safety manual aloud in a flat monotone for the entire period, and by the second page three students are asleep on their desks while one just counts ceiling tiles. Nothing happens, nothing changes, and that flat, empty stretch of nothing is boring.
items.reading_mnemonic: つまらない is written exactly as it sounds, kana only, nothing to decode: 「<reading>つまらない</reading>」 reads precisely the way it looks.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a dozen cats chase a dropped paper fan down the mossy steps, tumbling over each other and clanging the enormous bell by accident on the way. Visitors abandon their prayers just to watch, laughing, and that whole chaotic scramble is exactly what fun and enjoyable feels like.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane laughs so hard at the cats that she slips and lands on the steps, showing off a <reading>tanned knee</reading>, and declares between giggles that this is the most <reading>たのしい</reading> afternoon she's had all year.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the last onigiri on the shelf is about to expire right at closing time. He snatches it seconds before the till locks him out, laughing out loud in the empty, fluorescent-bright aisle. That giddy, undignified triumph over a single rice ball is what happy and glad mean here.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi clutches the onigiri and yelps <reading>Ooh, retch-she!</reading>, the exact sound of <reading>うれしい</reading> — the customers behind him in line assume it's pure joy, not the heartburn that follows right behind it.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one of the cats knocks the rope loose from the enormous bell, and it stops ringing altogether. The cats line up on the mossy steps and stare at the dead bell like mourners at a funeral, not one of them moving. That flat, drawn-out stillness is what sad means here.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane sighs over the silenced bell, <reading>kahh, nuh, sheesh</reading> — nearly the sound of <reading>かなしい</reading> itself, as if the whole shrine were groaning out the word for sad.

items.mnemonic_text: No room in the heart: isogashii.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the final bell rings and she is somehow expected to be three places at once: the sports field, the office, and the echoing hallway, all before the gate locks. She sprints the same loop between them so many times she forgets which errand she already finished. That constant, overlapping scramble is what busy means here.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei pants <reading>ease over, gosh, she!</reading> jogging past the sports field for the third time — close enough to <reading>いそがしい</reading> that it's basically her out-of-breath way of saying busy.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Partway up the mountain trail, a cow wearing a muzzle plants its hooves at the steepest switchback and refuses to go one step further, not even toward the vending machine improbably waiting at the top. Coaxing it up that last stretch turns out to be nearly impossible, which is what difficult means here.
items.reading_mnemonic: The hiker groans <reading>muzzle-cow-she!</reading> at the stubborn animal — near enough to <reading>むずかしい</reading> that it becomes her word for anything this hard, from then on.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat drops a whole fish at her feet like it's nothing — no hunting story, no fuss, just here you go. She barely blinks. Everything about the exchange takes no effort at all, the easiest gift she's ever received.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane offers the cat a plate of sushi in return. It just shrugs, like accepting would say <reading>yeah, sushi</reading>, sure, whatever — refusing would take effort it doesn't have. That shrug is the sound of <reading>やさしい</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the bleachers were built so close to the hallway wall that runners can high-five the kids at their lockers without leaving the track. No gap, no jog required — just reach across mid-stride. That's how it feels when something sits within arm's reach without you moving your feet.
items.reading_mnemonic: A student presses her cheek to the hallway window, eye to eye with the bleachers just beyond the glass — <reading>cheek, eye</reading> close, nothing between them but the pane. That's the sound of <reading>ちかい</reading>, near enough to fog the glass.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The vending machine at the top of the mountain trail is so far away that by the time you reach it, the drink inside has gone flat from age. Every switchback just reveals another switchback waiting behind it. The summit never gets closer, only farther.
items.reading_mnemonic: Near the summit, a hiker stubs her toe on a root and yelps <reading>toe, ee!</reading> — the echo bounces off ridge after ridge, because the peak above her is <reading>とおい</reading>, so far that the echo outlasts the climb itself.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a leaf drops onto the current and is gone before it finishes falling — past the washing stones, under the bridge, out of sight in one blink. Nothing on that water ever holds still long enough for a second look.
items.reading_mnemonic: A boy leaps off the riverbank shouting <reading>hi-yah!</reading> and is already underwater before the shout finishes echoing off the far bank — that's the speed of <reading>はやい</reading>, gone before the sound catches up to him.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Same sun-over-the-stick you already know: it's cresting the horizon so <kanji>early</kanji> that your alarm hasn't even gone off. You're blinking awake in a grey pre-dawn kitchen, coffee not ready, socks mismatched — the sun got here first, and now everything today has to start this <kanji>early</kanji> just to keep up with it.
items.reading_mnemonic: This is just 早（はや）plus the い ending, the reading you already know, giving you <reading>はやい</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture someone hauling a shopping cart up the mountain trail, swearing they'll reach the vending machine at the top in five minutes. Forty minutes later they're still only halfway, one wheel catching on every root. By the time they finally arrive, the machine has sold its last can and the sun is already going down.
items.reading_mnemonic: Meet Ozawa, still dragging that cart. Every time someone yells at him to hurry, he just sighs, '<reading>oh, so</reading> tired,' stretching the words out to stall for time — and that long, dragging drawl is exactly the sound of <reading>おそい</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: That same bearded elder from before is leaning on his stick atop Grandma Kane's mossy shrine steps. His <kanji>long</kanji> beard doesn't stop at his sandals — it keeps pouring down step after step until it pools at the bottom, where the shrine cats have started napping in it. Nobody has ever found the end of that beard, because it just keeps going, absurdly <kanji>long</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Just 長（なが）plus the い ending, the reading you already know, giving you <reading>ながい</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till beeps and spits out a receipt that stops after two centimeters, cut off mid-word before the total even prints. The clerk tugs at the paper, but that's all there is — the roll's been swapped by mistake, and every single receipt today comes out stubby, clipped, cut short.
items.reading_mnemonic: Jika, the new clerk, tries to introduce herself, but the till keeps beeping over her: '<reading>Mi, Jika</reading>—' is all that gets out before she's cut off. Her own clipped name is the whole lesson — that stubby, chopped-off sound is <reading>みじかい</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane climbs the mossy steps expecting another cramped little shrine room, but the doors swing open onto a courtyard so wide the enormous bell looks like a pebble sitting in the middle of it. The cats scatter in every direction because there's finally room to run. She just stands there with her arms out, turning in a slow circle: wide, spacious, wide, spacious.
items.reading_mnemonic: A tiny hero marches up Grandma Kane's steps expecting a cramped little shrine and instead finds a whole valley behind the gate, room enough to get lost in. He plants his flag and shouts so the cats can hear it too: <reading>hero</reading>, <reading>ひろい</reading>, this place just keeps going.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi restocks the onigiri shelf until the aisle behind it chokes down to nothing — one shoulder in, one shoulder out, and the till starts beeping because somebody's stuck sideways. He wedges a mop bucket into the last gap out of spite and now there isn't even room to breathe: narrow, cramped, narrow, cramped, nobody move.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sammy tries to squeeze past the onigiri shelf sideways and gets wedged solid between two racks while the till keeps beeping at him for no reason. <reading>Sammy</reading> can't move an inch, and everyone shuffling past just mutters the same thing at him: <reading>せまい</reading>, せまい, you picked the worst aisle.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Someone dumps a waterlogged stone lantern on the riverbank and asks for help hauling it home. Two people grab opposite ends, knees buckling, boots sinking a little deeper into the mud with every step, and the third person just watches them struggle: heavy, heavy, heavy, put it down before someone's back gives out.
items.reading_mnemonic: He tries to lift the waterlogged lantern off the riverbank by himself and it doesn't budge a centimeter. <reading>Oh my</reading>, he wheezes, letting it thud straight back into the mud — <reading>おもい</reading>, this thing is おもい, somebody else grab the other end already.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Sei sprints across the sports field hauling what should be a heavy gym bag, except someone swapped the weights inside for empty juice cartons overnight. He practically floats down the track, arms pumping, feet barely tapping the ground between strides: light, light, light, he could carry ten of these.
items.reading_mnemonic: Cara chases Sei down the echoing school hallway with the swapped-out gym bag and can't believe how little it weighs on her shoulder. <reading>Cara</reading>, we're winning this race, she yells back at him, we're so <reading>かるい</reading> today, かるい as air.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi flips every switch behind the register at once, and the whole konbini goes nuclear — onigiri wrappers glowing white, the beeping till suddenly readable from across the parking lot. A moth outside faints on the spot. That's the only word for it: bright, blindingly, hopelessly bright.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi shields his eyes and gasps <reading>"ah, car, ooh-ee!"</reading> — the nonsense his blinded brain makes of <reading>あかるい</reading> — as the fluorescents blaze so hard they're visible from the street outside.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's enormous bell goes silent at dusk, and the mossy shrine steps dissolve into shadow so complete you hear the cats climbing before you ever see them. You feel your way up by touch alone, one hand on stone you can't find with your eyes. That's the word for pitch-black: dark.
items.reading_mnemonic: A cat yowls <reading>"coo, why…"</reading> somewhere on the shrine steps — the sound that scratches itself into your head as the reading <reading>くらい</reading> — right before it vanishes completely into shadow, leaving only its voice behind.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, someone microwaves a lopsided onigiri that by all rights should be a disaster. Instead steam curls off it like it came from a five-star kitchen, and three strangers stop scrolling their phones just to watch you eat it. That's what delicious means here.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is written exactly the way it sounds — just say <reading>おいしい</reading>, no kanji hiding a different reading underneath.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the vending machine improbably parked at the top of the mountain trail, you buy the last can — mystery flavor, no label — and immediately regret existing. Your face does something involuntary. That single working button might be a war crime. That's bad-tasting.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is written exactly the way it sounds — just say <reading>まずい</reading>, nothing to derive, nothing hiding underneath.
items.description: Beyond food, まずい is also the everyday word for a situation gone wrong or awkward — closer to "uh-oh, bad" than to bad cooking. Someone muttering it while staring at a spilled drink or a missed deadline is using this same word, not talking about taste at all.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a delivery van dumps a whole pallet of sugar sacks onto the onigiri shelf. One bag splits open and buries the till in white dust. The cashier can't help scooping a fingerful straight off the counter — it's pure, blinding sugar, nothing else. That's what sweet tastes like.
items.reading_mnemonic: A woman at Koichi's konbini bites into what she assumes is a plain rice cracker and gasps <reading>ah my</reading>, eyes watering — it's actually a sugar candy in disguise. Her gasp is exactly the sound of <reading>あまい</reading>, sweet.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A hiker reaches the vending machine improbably parked at the top of the mountain trail and buys the only can left. The first sip is a wall of salt, like drinking the ocean. Two steps later the chili catches up and torches the back of her throat. She sits down hard on a rock, fanning her mouth. That drink was spicy, and it was salty.
items.reading_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, a jeep pulls alongside the hiker, and the driver leans out and offers her a ride: <reading>car ride</reading>, he calls, grinning around a mouthful of chili peppers. That's the sound of <reading>からい</reading>, spicy, salty.
items.description: This word covers two distinct sensations English keeps separate — spicy-hot (a chili pepper) and salty (over-salted soup). Which one a speaker means comes entirely from context, not from the word itself.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, someone has left a bicycle half-buried in the mud, its wheels crusted brown, a plastic bag snagged on the handlebars flapping in the current. A heron lands on the seat, takes one look at the muck dripping off every spoke, and flies straight back off without touching it. Even the heron won't go near something that dirty.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, Grandma Kane spots the mud-crusted bicycle and asks who left it there. A boy points at his friend and blurts <reading>Kit, uh, not I!</reading> — which is exactly how you say <reading>きたない</reading>, dirty.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A new gym teacher shows up at Sei's school looking barely older than the students, sprinting laps around the sports field twice as fast as anyone else and still bounding up the bleachers two at a time after the whistle blows. The staff room can't agree on whether to call him sir or classmate. Everything about him says young.
items.reading_mnemonic: In the echoing hallway, Sei radios a teacher on an old <reading>walkie</reading>-talkie to ask why the new gym teacher looks like a student. The reply crackles back: he just is <reading>わかい</reading>, young.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the enormous bell has been struck by centuries of visitors until every corner has worn away entirely — no edges, no angles, just one smooth curve running all the way around it. The monks pat it fondly and call it perfectly round.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a fat cat refuses to leave the bell stand, curling tighter every time a visitor claps. The old monk sighs, 'you get <reading>more roly</reading> every day' — and that mumbled phrase is how you remember <reading>まるい</reading>, round.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, that sprout's glow from over the moon drifts downstream every evening, staining the whole current the same impossible shade until the water looks like liquid moonlight. Fishermen call it the <kanji>blue</kanji> hour, and standing knee-deep in it, they're right — it's blue.
items.reading_mnemonic: 青 already gives you あお, and い just adds the plain い ending, so 青い is simply あお plus い — <reading>あおい</reading>, no extra story needed.

items.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, that same fire-lit earth keeps cracking uphill until it reaches the vending machine improbably parked at the summit. The heat gets to the cans inside, and they burst open, spilling <kanji>red</kanji> soda down the rocks like slow lava.
items.reading_mnemonic: 赤 already gives you あか, and い just adds the plain い ending, so 赤い is simply あか plus い — <reading>あかい</reading>, nothing more to work out.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Back at Koichi's konbini, that same blinding morning ray never fades — it keeps hitting the onigiri shelf until every wrapper on it bleaches to the exact same shade of <kanji>white</kanji>. The till keeps beeping uselessly, unable to tell one product from another anymore.
items.reading_mnemonic: 白 already gives you しろ, and い just adds the plain い ending, so 白い is simply しろ plus い — <reading>しろい</reading>, no story required.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The village elder tosses one more log onto that sooty communal fire, and a startled cat bolts straight through the ash pile chasing a moth. It streaks across every wall and rooftop on its way out, smearing soot over the parts the smoke hadn't reached yet, until the whole huddled village is stained one uniform <kanji>black</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just 黒（くろ）with the ending い tacked on, giving you exactly 「<reading>くろい</reading>」.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A hiker on the mountain trail stops at the summit vending machine, wraps both arms around it, and simply picks the whole humming thing up off its concrete pad to shake loose a stuck can. Nobody films it. Nobody comments. He just sets it back down and keeps walking, unmistakably strong.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the mountain trail's summit, the same hiker hoists the vending machine overhead one-armed and lets out a flat, matter-of-fact roar — “<reading>TSU-YO-EE</reading>!” — the sound the whole trail now associates with anyone that <reading>つよい</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi tries to twist the cap off a bottle of tea at the konbini counter and simply cannot do it. He braces the bottle against the register, grits his teeth, asks the customer behind him for help. She opens it without looking up from her phone, one twist, done. He was just weak.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a character wading across the stepping stones gets his ankles knocked out from under him by the current and pitches sideways into the shallows, letting out a thin, defeated “<reading>yo-wa-ee</reading>” as he goes down — the sound that means someone's <reading>よわい</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's enormous shrine bell has come loose from its beam and is swinging lower with every gust, grazing the heads of the cats sunning themselves on the mossy steps below. Nobody's fixed it yet. Everyone who visits just learns to duck first and pray second — the whole shrine is quietly dangerous.
items.reading_mnemonic: As the bell swings past, an old priest at the shrine throws an arm out to stop a visitor from walking under it, hissing “<reading>ah-boo-nigh</reading>!” under his breath — the exact warning shape of 「<reading>あぶない</reading>」, said before anything actually falls.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a stray kitten totters down the mossy steps, misjudges the very last one, and rolls the rest of the way, ending up flat on its back among the resident cats with all four paws in the air. Nobody laughs. Nobody could. It is somehow the single cutest thing that has ever happened on those steps.
items.reading_mnemonic: かわいい is already exactly what it sounds like — kana straight through, with no kanji hiding a different pronunciation underneath, so the word you say and the word you read are simply 「<reading>かわいい</reading>」.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Somewhere on the steep mountain trail, a hiker stubs bare toes on the vending machine's metal base and folds instantly in half, hopping in a tight circle with both hands clamped around the foot, teeth gritted, unable to manage a single word except the one that means painful.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the sliding door snags his necktie just as he steps through, yanking him back against the onigiri shelf. He yelps 「<reading>いたい</reading>」, wrestling the <reading>tie</reading> free from the still-beeping door, no dignity left in the fluorescent glare.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a kid presses against the sports-field fence eyeing another team's shiny new ball, arms not quite reaching through the wire, face doing all the talking. Nobody has to ask what that expression means — wanting something you can't yet have looks the same on everyone.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, Grandma Kane eyes the far bank where the mushrooms grow thick and sighs 「<reading>ほしい</reading>」 to no one in particular — '<reading>oh, she</reading>' really does want to cross, and the current is just fast enough that wanting has to be enough for today.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi rings up the same rice ball at his konbini every single evening, though the shelf is stocked with a dozen other kinds. He doesn't compare, doesn't browse — just walks straight past the beeping till to the one he always gets, because some things you're simply fond of and no substitute will do.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail in midwinter, Sei straps skis on right by the vending machine and grins 「<reading>すき</reading>」 before pushing off downhill — the crunch of the <reading>skis</reading> against fresh snow is the sound of someone doing exactly what they love.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the till keeps beeping over the same soggy egg sandwich nobody buys. A customer picks it up, wrinkles her nose, and shoves it back onto the shelf for the third time today. The clerk sighs and admits the whole town has quietly decided this sandwich is disliked.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane holds up a shrine key and swears it opens the bell tower, but it's obviously the wrong one — a <reading>key lie</reading> if she's ever told one. The cats hiss at her fib. Everyone at the shrine mutters 「<reading>きらい</reading>」 about that key, because nobody trusts a liar's key twice.

items.meaning_mnemonic: That <kanji>hand</kanji> you'd normally hold out for a shake instead shoots straight <kanji>up</kanji>, higher than everyone else's, catching every ball a street juggler throws without even glancing at it. The crowd realizes this hand belongs to someone truly skillful — good at whatever it touches.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the edge of the mountain trail, a keeper named <reading>Joe's zoo</reading> trains a monkey to pour tea without spilling a drop. Hikers stop climbing just to watch, murmuring 「<reading>じょうず</reading>」 every single time the cup fills clean to the brim.
items.description: Used to praise someone else's skill — saying this about your own ability comes across as boastful, so speakers reach for a different word when the skill being described is their own.

items.meaning_mnemonic: That same <kanji>hand</kanji> that should hold steady instead droops <kanji>down</kanji> below the table, fingers trembling as it fumbles the teacup and sends it crashing to the floor. Everyone at the table agrees: this hand is unskillful, hopelessly bad at absolutely everything it touches.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa the fire-breathing crow tries to toast a marshmallow and instead sets the whole power line ablaze, dropping the charred stick into the river below. The other birds start calling him a total <reading>hater</reading> of marshmallows, squawking 「<reading>へた</reading>」 every time he lights another one on fire.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's rice bowl breathes out that same curling <kanji>spirit</kanji> steam every morning, but today it rises so fast and so high it nearly knocks the bell clean off its hook. She grins — a bowl steaming that lively means the person eating it is healthy and lively too.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kiki the tree spirit hands a hiker a glowing <reading>Gen key</reading> that unlocks nothing but pure energy — one turn and the hiker springs up the mountain trail without even panting. The trees whisper 「<reading>げんき</reading>」 every time someone uses it and comes back bursting with life.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the mossy steps lead up to one enormous bell that nobody dares ring — even the cats stop mid-stride and flatten their ears, padding past on silent paws so nothing disturbs the hush. Not a chime, not a meow, not a footstep. That held-breath stillness is quiet.
items.reading_mnemonic: A cat named Shizuka naps under that same enormous bell, and visitors tiptoe past whispering '<reading>she's-zoo-kah</reading>, don't wake her' so as not to break the hush. That whispered warning carries 「<reading>しずか</reading>」.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini at midnight should be dead quiet, but tonight the till won't stop beeping, the onigiri shelf is being raided by a dozen elbowing customers, and somebody's abandoned grocery cart is still spinning in the doorway. Noise stacked on noise stacked on noise — that overflowing racket is lively / bustling.
items.reading_mnemonic: Back at that same beeping till, a whole herd of yaks squeezes past the onigiri shelf, their knees banging the shelf with every step — '<reading>knee-gear yaks</reading>,' the clerk mutters, watching the chaos spread. That crowded racket is 「<reading>にぎやか</reading>」.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, one battered vending machine stands against the mist — and someone climbs all the way up every single morning just to wipe its dusty glass front until it gleams, though nobody has ever explained why. Spotless glass, spotless coin slot, spotless everything, on a trail where nothing else is. That is pretty / clean.
items.reading_mnemonic: きれい is written and read exactly as it looks, straight kana with no hidden reading to derive — just remember 「<reading>きれい</reading>」 as is.

items.mnemonic_text: A name that exists everywhere: yuumei.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school sports field, one student's <kanji>name</kanji> gets called over the loudspeaker so many times — first place, then an encore, then again for the yearbook photo — that it starts echoing down the hallways on its own, and strangers who never set foot on that field find themselves repeating it too. A name that outgrows the mouth that gave it is famous.
items.reading_mnemonic: That echoing name reaches Koichi's konbini, where the clerk overhears it and starts to say '<reading>you may</reading>—' before catching himself, unsure if he's even allowed to say something so well-known out loud. That awkward almost-permission carries 「<reading>ゆうめい</reading>」.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a tourist misses the mossy top step and goes down hard, shin cracking on stone. Before they finish wincing, an old woman appears from nowhere, hoists them up, and walks them the rest of the way to the bell, never once mentioning her own bad knees. That unasked-for shin-saving is what kind means here.
items.reading_mnemonic: The old woman introduces herself as she dusts off the tourist's shin: <reading>shin, set to</reading> help, always, she says, like it's a permanent setting. The tourist repeats it back slowly — <reading>しんせつ</reading> — and it sticks, because she really was set to kind from the moment she saw the fall.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi hires a new clerk named Ben who reorganizes the whole konbini overnight. Every shelf now holds exactly what the last customer needed — umbrellas by the door on rainy days, batteries by the toy aisle, a charger built into the counter itself. Nobody has ever had to ask Ben for anything twice. That's what convenient means.
items.reading_mnemonic: Regulars started saying <reading>Ben, really</reading> — as in, Ben, you've really outdone yourself this time — every time they found the exact thing they needed exactly where they needed it. Say it fast enough and <reading>べんり</reading> just falls out of your mouth, konbini bag already in hand.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The vending machine atop the mountain trail has one working button, and it dispenses only cold soup on the hottest day of the year. Hikers queue anyway since it's the only machine for two hours either way, and every one of them mutters the same thing on the way down. Nothing up there works the way it should. That's inconvenient.
items.reading_mnemonic: What they mutter is <reading>phew, Ben</reading> — cursing whoever named the trail's contractor, Ben, who clearly never climbed it himself. Wheeze it out at the summit and you've basically said <reading>ふべん</reading>, the exact word for a machine that's more trouble than it's worth.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Sei's school lets out early with no explanation, and the hallway that's usually echoing with footsteps goes completely silent. Sei sits alone on the steps with an entire afternoon and nothing scheduled in it, swinging a bag back and forth just to have something to do. An empty stretch with nowhere to be — that's free time.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei texts a friend just one word: <reading>he, ma</reading> — short for hey, ma, guess what, she's about to waste the whole afternoon. Drag those two sounds together and it's <reading>ひま</reading>, said by someone who has absolutely nothing to do and all day to do it in.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A delivery moped skids on the mountain trail and crashes into the vending machine at the top. Before you can flinch, the <kanji>big</kanji> fisherman-armed giant from next door steps out, catches both moped and driver in one arm like nothing happened, and sets them upright without spilling a single dented can. Nothing here needed fixing. That's all right.
items.reading_mnemonic: Dai the giant baby stomps through Grandma Kane's shrine and topples the enormous bell with one diaper-swipe. The priest just repaints the dented bronze — a quick <reading>dye job, boo</reading> — while Dai claps and babbles <reading>だいじょうぶ</reading>, certain the bell was never actually broken.

items.mnemonic_text: A big change of trouble: taihen.
items.meaning_mnemonic: On Sei's school sports field, the <kanji>big</kanji> stick-figure kid takes a running start for the long jump, sails clean over the sandpit, and flattens the snack stand and half the scoreboard on landing. The coach just stares at the wreckage, clipboard still raised. That kind of day is what this word means: tough, awful.
items.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, Dai grabs a passing hen and moors his raft by simply <reading>tying the hen</reading> to it as an anchor — except the hen just paddles off, dragging raft and giant baby under. Soaked and sinking, Dai wails the only word that fits: <reading>たいへん</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the vending machine improbably parked on the mountain trail, an old peddler unrolls a blanket covered in buttons — red, teal, one just paint-spattered — insisting every single one does something different. You press three at random and get juice, a whistling kettle, and a burst of confetti. Nothing on that blanket matches anything else. That is the entire idea of various.
items.reading_mnemonic: A parrot at Koichi's konbini refuses to say any word once — it repeats everything twice, tilting its head each time like it's testing a new shade of the same phrase. Ask it to name anything and out comes the doubled echo, <reading>いろいろ</reading>, sounding just like calling a <reading>hero, hero</reading> across the aisle.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Two identical customers walk into Koichi's konbini at the same moment, in the same jacket, reaching for the same drink on the same shelf. The clerk rings up one barcode, scans the second item out of habit, and gets an identical receipt down to the second. Everything about the two of them matches, right down to the yawn.
items.reading_mnemonic: A hiker reaches the vending machine at the top of the mountain trail and meets his own look-alike standing there already — same scar, same missing jacket button. Startled, he blurts his twin brother's name like a catchphrase, <reading>oh, Naji</reading>, which is exactly how the reading <reading>おなじ</reading> sounds, twin and echo both.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A new clerk at the library re-folds every origami crane the kids abandon on the returns desk, squaring each corner twice before setting it down straight. She bows to a stack of overdue books like they're guests arriving late. Nothing about her is rushed — every motion is polite, every motion is careful.
items.reading_mnemonic: The other clerks nickname her <reading>tay-nay</reading> for how she irons every library ticket flat before filing it, and the sound became the word itself: <reading>ていねい</reading>, meticulous and polite, exactly the way she squares those corners.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat that normally swats everything off the mossy steps stops mid-swat, sits down, and just stares at one stone lantern glowing gold in the evening light. Even the cranky, destructive cats agree on this one: it's lovely, it's wonderful, it's worth sitting still for.
items.reading_mnemonic: That same cat gets nicknamed <reading>sue-tech</reading>, because anything shiny short-circuits her, and she freezes at the lantern glow while everyone around her mutters <reading>すてき</reading> before she can even blink.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Two teams line up on opposite banks of the river, rope pulled taut between them, boots dug into the mud, each side straining directly against the other's pull. Neither team gives an inch — that dead-even standoff, everyone pulling the opposite way from everyone else, is exactly the picture for opposite, against.
items.reading_mnemonic: The referee, nicknamed <reading>hun-tie</reading> because his necktie unravels every time he blows the whistle, screams <reading>はんたい</reading> whenever one team yanks in the exact opposite direction from the other.

items.mnemonic_text: Head off down the crossroads: iku.
items.meaning_mnemonic: That stick figure who's always mid-stride, the one who can never <kanji>go</kanji> two seconds without moving to the next place, finally shoulders a bag and walks straight out the door one morning. You watch the doorway swing shut behind them. That's the whole word: to go.
items.reading_mnemonic: It's simply the taught <reading>い</reading> reading of 行 that Koichi already uses, plus く, spelling out <reading>いく</reading> exactly as the kanji already taught you.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the crossroads, the tree spots someone trudging up the mountain trail, footsore and ready to quit, and doesn't wait politely — it stretches a branch out like a beckoning arm and hauls them under its shade before they can even ask. That's the tree's whole personality: it never chases anyone anywhere, it only ever makes people <kanji>come</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 来 already gives you く and る gives you る, so to come lands on <reading>くる</reading> exactly as those two pieces already taught you to say.

items.mnemonic_text: Sweep up and go home: kaeru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The same weary traveler from 帰's story finally reaches the little house, drops the walking stick on the step, and collapses through the door without even taking off his shoes. That homeward pull was never about the walking — it's the whole shape of <kanji>return</kanji>, and once it starts pulling, stopping halfway was never on offer.
items.reading_mnemonic: 帰 already supplies かえ here and る supplies る, so return home comes out as <reading>かえる</reading> — the same reading you learned for 帰, just running straight into the verb ending.

items.mnemonic_text: Take food to the mouth: taberu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini is closing, and the last customer ducks under the peaked tent-roof from 食's story — the shelter built entirely out of dinner, rice and side dishes heaped under the eaves. There's nothing else you can do under a roof like that but sit down where you're standing and <kanji>eat</kanji>, so that's exactly what closing time forces on him.
items.reading_mnemonic: 食 already gives た, べ gives べ, and る closes it out, so to eat becomes <reading>たべる</reading> exactly as those three pieces already spelled it.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, the food radical sits beside that same gaping, thirsty mouth from 飲's story, but now it's not just hanging open — it's tipped straight back over the water, gulping in one long pull. No plate ever touches those lips, only river water pouring straight down, and that greedy tilt-and-gulp is what it means to <kanji>drink</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 飲 already gives の and む gives む, so to drink lands on <reading>のむ</reading> exactly the way those two pieces spell it out.

items.mnemonic_text: Eye on legs going to look: miru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>eye</kanji> that stood up on legs is exhausted from all its walking, so it stops in the middle of the road and just stands there. It doesn't blink, doesn't turn away, doesn't do anything else at all — it just plants its legs and looks. That is all this word ever asks of you: to <kanji>see</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 見（み）＋る（る）gives you <reading>みる</reading>, the readings you already know stacked together.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Kiki the tree spirit presses her <kanji>ear</kanji> against the <kanji>gate</kanji> of the shrine one more night, straining to catch the whispers behind it. But tonight she can't just stay quiet about it — she raps on the wood and demands to know what they're saying. Pressing an ear to a gate gets you two things: you listen, and eventually you have to <kanji>ask</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kiki the tree spirit giggles every time the wind <reading>kicks</reading> up, which is the only signal she needs to start <reading>きく</reading>ing at the gate again.

items.mnemonic_text: Let the tongue tell it: hanasu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a <kanji>mouth</kanji> keeps releasing stacked lines of <kanji>speech</kanji> across the water, one slab after another, while right beside it a <kanji>tongue</kanji> wags nonstop, egging it on for more. Between the two of them the water is drowned out entirely — this is what it sounds like when someone won't stop <kanji>talking</kanji>. That endless back-and-forth is what it means to speak.
items.reading_mnemonic: Hana, a heron who wades the riverbank, opens her long beak and lets out a honk that sounds exactly like <reading>はな</reading>, then finishes it off with a brisk <reading>す</reading> snap of her bill — together that's <reading>はなす</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a stone <kanji>mouth</kanji> carved into the old bell pushes out one neat stacked layer of <kanji>speech</kanji> every time a cat brushes past it, like it's reading off a single fixed line it memorized decades ago. It never adds anything, never explains, it just delivers that one word again and again. That single fixed word, pushed out and done, is what it means to <kanji>say</kanji> something.
items.reading_mnemonic: Ichi the shrine cat only ever meows one clipped sound, a flat <reading>ee-oo</reading> that the cats around the bell have started imitating, and that sound is exactly <reading>いう</reading>.

items.mnemonic_text: Sell words to your eyes: yomu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini till goes quiet — the merchant has abandoned his onigiri shelf and is hunched over the register receipt instead, lips moving syllable by syllable down the tiny print. Wares untouched, eyes locked on the page, mouth shaping every line he isn't selling. That hunched, silent scanning is the whole picture of learning to <kanji>read</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 読 already gives you よ, and the ending む stays む, spelling out <reading>よむ</reading> exactly as taught.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every evening at your desk the sun sinks below your notebook exactly like it always does, and the instant its last light fades your hand starts moving on its own, filling line after line in the dark with no lamp to help. That daily blackout scribbling, repeated night after night, is the whole ritual of learning to <kanji>write</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 書 already gives you か, and the ending く stays く, spelling out <reading>かく</reading> exactly as taught.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You spot something you want and reach for the cowrie shell that's stood in for money since forever, laying it flat on the counter and sliding it across before you can lose your nerve. Shell handed over, prize now in your other hand — that whole exchange, shell for object, is exactly what it means to <kanji>buy</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 買 already gives you か, and the ending う stays う, spelling out <reading>かう</reading> exactly as taught.

items.mnemonic_text: Lay goods on the stand: uru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture that same street vendor leaning back on his two kicked-out legs, sign propped above his stacked goods, still shouting prices at everyone who walks past. He never once stops to hand over money himself — only to unload what's piled in front of him onto whoever stops. That relentless shouting-and-unloading is exactly what it means to <kanji>sell</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 売 already gives you う, and the ending る stays る, spelling out <reading>うる</reading> exactly as taught.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every dawn, an old monk climbs Grandma Kane's mossy shrine steps at the exact same unhurried pace, one bell-toll per step, never rushing even when the temple cats race past him. Visitors say they could set their watches by him. That plodding, deliberate, one-foot-after-the-other pace up the steps is exactly what this word means: to walk.
items.reading_mnemonic: The tourists nickname the shrine monk 'the <reading>rook</reading>,' since like a chess rook he only ever creeps one square forward. Every morning the cats chant his rhythm up the mossy stairs: <reading>あるく</reading>, あるく, あるく, one slow step at a time.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Sei is already late for practice when the coach spots him at the classroom door. There's no time to warm up, so he just bolts, straight down the echoing hallway and out onto the sports field, arms pumping, shoes slapping tile and then grass. The coach doesn't even blink. That flat-out, no-warning sprint across the field is to run.
items.reading_mnemonic: As Sei rockets across the field, the announcer's shout comes out garbled through the loudspeaker — all anyone hears is <reading>ha-shee-roo</reading>, over and over, close enough to <reading>はしる</reading> that the whole team starts using it as their word for tearing across the grass.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi falls face-first into the river trying to grab a floating onigiri wrapper before it drifts past Grandma Kane's shrine steps. He can't touch the bottom, so he flails, arms churning, head barely above the current, refusing to let go of the wrapper. That desperate, arms-churning motion through water is to swim.
items.reading_mnemonic: Watching him thrash, the cats lined up on the shrine steps cheer him on with what sounds like <reading>oh-yo-go</reading>, as if urging 'oh, go, go!' — close enough to <reading>およぐ</reading> that Koichi adopts it as his own victory shout every time he drags himself back to shore.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, a cat sunning itself beside the vending machine is startled by a hiker's dropped can, and it doesn't just scurry off — it launches clean over the machine in one motion, all four paws leaving the ground at once. That single clean launch off the ground, whether across a gap or straight up, is to fly or jump.
items.reading_mnemonic: As the cat sails over the machine, it clips a tuba someone left leaning against it, and the horn lets out a low <reading>toh-buh</reading> honk mid-air — the exact sound the hikers now shout as <reading>とぶ</reading> every time that cat launches itself again.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You fell asleep leaning against the onigiri shelf at Koichi's konbini, and the till starts beeping nonstop over a jammed barcode. The noise won't quit, so you peel your eyes open, stagger upright, and blink at the fluorescent lights. That beeping is the whole story: to wake up, to get up.
items.reading_mnemonic: Oki the night clerk always oversleeps at Koichi's konbini. Every morning the manager shouts <reading>おきる</reading>, get up, and jangles the shutter key — <reading>oh, key</reading> — until Oki finally rolls off the floor and opens the store.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You've hiked all the way up to the vending machine at the top of the mountain trail, and the climb wrecks you completely. You slump down against its warm hum, eyes shutting before you even decide to rest, and don't move again until morning. That collapse against the machine is what it means: to sleep.
items.reading_mnemonic: A hiker called Near always collapses <reading>near</reading> the mountain vending machine, murmuring <reading>ねる</reading> before he even finishes sitting down, and by dawn he's still curled against its warm hum, dead to the world.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, two frozen visitors drop straight onto the mossy steps, planting themselves on the same patch of ground exactly like before, refusing to move an inch closer to the bell. Cats pile onto their laps and pin them there. That's exactly what it means to <kanji>sit</kanji> — plant yourself and stay.
items.reading_mnemonic: This one is regular: 座 keeps its すわ reading and gets る tacked on, giving you <reading>すわる</reading> exactly as taught.

items.meaning_mnemonic: On Sei's echoing sports field, the coach blows the whistle and every player plants their feet on the ground exactly like before, refusing to budge an inch, rooted upright in a straight line. Nobody sits, nobody wobbles — the whole team just <kanji>stand</kanji>s there until the whistle blows again.
items.reading_mnemonic: This one is regular: 立 keeps its た reading and gets つ tacked on, giving you <reading>たつ</reading> exactly as taught.

items.meaning: to rest / take a day off

accepted_answers.answer_text: to rest / take a day off

items.meaning_mnemonic: You reach the top of the mountain trail expecting the vending machine, but the same <kanji>rest</kanji> person is still slumped against the tree, arms crossed, a note pinned to the bark reading back tomorrow. Everyone else keeps hiking past; this one has turned a five-minute breather into calling off the whole day. That is 休む: to rest, to take a day off.
items.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just 休（やす）＋む stacked exactly as taught, giving <reading>やすむ</reading> with nothing new to derive.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi unlocks the konbini at six to find last night's clerk still behind the till, sleeves rolled, restocking the onigiri shelf for the fourth time since closing. He offers to send her home; she just points at the line forming outside and grabs another crate. Some people rest between shifts. She has never once learned how — she just works.
items.reading_mnemonic: The new clerk at Koichi's konbini won't leave the <reading>hot rack</reading> of oden warming by the till, muttering <reading>はたらく</reading> under her breath as she flips skewers past midnight, refusing every break Koichi offers.

items.mnemonic_text: Force yourself to learn: benkyou suru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Sei stays in the echoing hallway of her school long after the sports field empties, hunched under a flickering light, filling page after page of a workbook while the caretaker locks each classroom around her. She isn't waiting for a practice or a friend to finish up — she's just studying, alone, until every problem on the page is solved.
items.reading_mnemonic: A new exchange student at Sei's school bows low over his desk and swears to his teacher, <reading>Ben, Kyoto, sure</reading>, naming both his hometown and his promise in one breath, then opens his notebook and starts <reading>べんきょうする</reading>, filling page after page until the hallway lights click off around him.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one persistent cat has taken to shadowing her every move — copying exactly how she rings the enormous bell, sweeps the mossy steps, and bows twice before the altar. Nobody assigned it a lesson; it simply watched an expert long enough to learn from her, one gesture at a time.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane names the shrine cat <reading>Nara</reading>, after the old temple town where she trained as a girl, since it watches her rites with such focus. Every dawn it edges closer to her heels, and by autumn the visitors swear the cat has started to <reading>ならう</reading> her exact bow.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the resident cat keeps hooking a paw around the base of the enormous bell, testing whether today is the day it tips. Grandma Kane never shouts. She crouches down and taps the stone beside it, over and over, every morning, until the cat starts copying the tap instead of shoving. Patient repetition until someone else can do it themselves — that is what it means to teach.
