items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane repeats the tapping so many mornings that the cats start yowling it back at her, a flat little <reading>おしえる</reading>, oh-shee-eh-ru, and the tourists on the mossy steps swear it sounds exactly like <reading>oh, she'll</reading> — she'll keep doing this forever, patiently teaching.
items.description: 教える covers more than formal instruction — it also means simply telling or informing someone of a fact, like giving directions to a station. The English gloss undersells how broad the everyday use is.

items.mnemonic_text: Divide it and grasp it: wakaru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The knife comes down again, splitting the pie into its eight wedges, but this time you actually taste one <kanji>part</kanji>, and the whole recipe suddenly makes sense: the cinnamon, the density, why it took so long to bake. Only once you've tasted that one part does it truly click — that click is what it means to understand.
items.reading_mnemonic: 分（わ）とかる（かる）がつながって、<reading>わかる</reading> — the readings you already have for 分 line up exactly to give you 「<reading>わかる</reading>」.
items.description: わかる pairs with が, not を — the thing you understand is grammatically the subject, closer to "it becomes clear to me" than "I understand it." Reaching for を here is a common learner slip.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, the vending machine at the summit restocks like magic — until you catch the delivery man radioing ahead to a friend at dawn. Once you've seen him do it, you can't pretend not to anymore; the secret clicks into place and stays there. That sudden, permanent click, the moment the secret becomes yours, is what it means to know something.
items.reading_mnemonic: A shrew has been staking out those delivery crates for weeks and finally works out that the truck always arrives at dawn. <reading>しる</reading>, it seems to squeak, sounding just like <reading>shrew</reading> — now it knows exactly when to dart in before the machine even opens.
items.description: 知る marks the moment something becomes known, not the ongoing state of knowing it — for an ongoing "I know," learners need the continuous て-form instead of this plain form standing alone.

items.mnemonic_text: Turn it over in the mind: kangaeru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school sports field, the visiting kangaroo mascot stops mid-hop and just stands there, chin dipped, replaying the coach's instructions before committing to a single bounce. It refuses to move again until it has turned the play over enough times to be sure. Working something out fully before acting on it is what it means to think something through.
items.reading_mnemonic: The mascot pauses so long that the crowd starts chanting <reading>かんがえる</reading>, kan-ga-eh-ru, which to the visiting parents sounds exactly like <reading>kangaroo</reading> — and it really is one, still working through the play call before it dares to jump.
items.description: 考える describes working through a problem step by step — reasoning, weighing, deciding — rather than a passing feeling or fleeting thought. Reach for this one when actual mental effort is involved.

items.mnemonic_text: A thought in the heart: omou.
items.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail you stop dead at the vending machine that has no business being up there, staring at the buttons without pressing any of them for a full minute. Your friend asks what's wrong. Nothing's wrong, you say — you're not doing anything, you're just standing here working through what you think and feel about a can of hot coffee.
items.reading_mnemonic: Further up that same trail a cow blocks the path and just stares. You stare back, it stares back, and it finally lets out one flat moo. The only thing that comes out of your mouth in reply is <reading>おもう</reading> — that same flat, thinking exhale, an <reading>oh, moo</reading> for whatever's turning over in your head.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the new hire gets handed the entire onigiri shelf and told to have every position memorized by closing time. He stands under the fluorescent lights reciting shelf slots to himself, ignoring the beeping till, until the whole shelf is burned into his skull. That's what memorizing something for good actually takes.
items.reading_mnemonic: He does it by muttering the same flat chant at the shelf, over and over, all shift: oh, bore, you, oh, bore, you. By closing time the chant has worn a groove straight into his memory, and what's left in his mouth is <reading>おぼえる</reading> — the sound of an <reading>oh, bore, you</reading> repeated until it sticks.

items.mnemonic_text: Let it slip the mind: wasureru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one of the cats buries the spare bell clapper under the mossy steps, fully intending to dig it back up. It naps in the sun instead. Days later it noses around all the identical mossy steps with no idea which one, the whole plan having genuinely gone out of its head.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane crouches by the steps and asks the cat plainly: was you really the one who buried it? The cat just blinks, having forgotten the entire errand. That blank <reading>was you, reru</reading> stare, empty of any answer, is exactly <reading>わすれる</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school sports day, one kid volunteers for every single event before anyone else can answer: relay, tug-of-war, clean-up, all of it. By the final whistle he's just standing in the middle of the field doing the next unasked-for thing, because doing is the only setting he owns.
items.reading_mnemonic: する is written exactly the way it sounds, plain kana with nothing to decode — just <reading>する</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a tadpole flops onto a lily pad and refuses to leave. It sits there so long its tail shrinks and legs sprout, and by sunset it hops off the pad a frog. Nobody ever catches the exact moment it happens — one thing just quietly turns into another. That quiet turning, tadpole into frog, is to become.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it's read, containing 「<reading>なる</reading>」.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini has one onigiri that has sat on the same shelf for three years. It hasn't rolled off, spoiled, or been restocked — it is simply, stubbornly present, the way a rock or a receipt or a vending machine is present. Nothing with legs, nothing that breathes, just an object taking up space. That plain, unmoving presence is to exist.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it's read, containing 「<reading>ある</reading>」.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's shrine has a cat that has lived among the mossy steps for as long as anyone remembers. It breathes, blinks, occasionally swats the enormous bell, proof that something living is here, right now, unlike the stones around it. That ongoing presence, breath and all, is to exist.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it's read, containing 「<reading>いる</reading>」.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the vending machine finally appears, and the hiker who has been dreaming about it for two hours locks both arms around it like it might disappear. She doesn't buy anything from it, she just holds it, arms full of cold metal and victory, refusing to let go. That grip is to hold, to have.
items.reading_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, the hiker's boot skids on a patch of moss. She grabs another clump of <reading>moss, too</reading>, both fists closing around it so she doesn't tumble down the slope. Holding two fistfuls of moss, too, that grip is <reading>もつ</reading>, the sound of hands that refuse to let go.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A hiker's hand shoots out for the last can of coffee sliding off the vending machine tray. The lid rim catches her sleeve and tears a clean slit through the fabric before the can lands in her palm. She doesn't stop to check the damage. She just needed to take the can, grab it before anyone else could.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a fat calico waits till no one's looking, then leaps onto the tray and <reading>tore</reading> a rice cracker off the plate before Grandma can shout. The bell swings from the impact. That cat has taken more crackers than anyone, and everyone calls the theft by its sound: <reading>とる</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A boy borrows the last bat from the school equipment shed and swings so hard at the first pitch that the handle snaps clean in half. He shrugs, jogs to get the spare, and swings that one too. Nobody taught him to be gentle with things — only that if it exists in that shed, you use it until it's someone else's problem.
items.reading_mnemonic: The school somehow owns one elderly cow, kept behind the sports field for reasons nobody remembers. When the mower breaks, the coach ropes her to the cart and hollers to use the cow — students hear <reading>tsu-cow</reading>, and it sticks: that's exactly what's happening, they <reading>つかう</reading> the cow to drag the cart.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, someone has spent all afternoon weaving wet reeds into a raft, tying each bundle with more reeds pulled from the mud. It wobbles, it leaks a little, but it floats when she pushes it past the shallows. She didn't find a raft down here. She built one, piece by piece, from whatever the river handed her.
items.reading_mnemonic: A cuckoo at the riverbank spends the whole morning weaving twigs into a nest, calling its own name the entire time it works — <reading>cuckoo</reading>, <reading>つくる</reading>, over and over, like it's narrating the job. By evening the nest holds together on its own, twigs it wove into something it made from nothing.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The delivery man arrives before sunrise and hauls up the konbini's rusted shutter by hand because the motor's dead again. His shoulder aches by the third pull, but the gap widens, fluorescent light spilling onto the sidewalk, onigiri shelf glowing behind the glass. He just keeps pulling until there's enough gap to walk through.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every morning the same delivery man hauls up Koichi's shutter by hand, and every morning his shoulder <reading>aches</reading> a little more by the third pull. He mutters the same sound through gritted teeth as the gap finally widens enough to walk through — <reading>あける</reading> — the ache and the opening worn into the same groove.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every evening at Grandma Kane's shrine, the last visitor leaves and the ancient gate groans on its hinges. The caretaker leans her whole weight into it until the two heavy halves meet with a dull clang, sealing the mossy steps off from the night and the cats out. That final clang is the meaning: to close.
items.reading_mnemonic: The caretaker's name is Shizu, and when she shimmers the bronze gate shut at dusk, the metal catches the last orange light and seems to glow all along its seam. She <reading>shimmers</reading> it closed every single night — say <reading>しめる</reading> and picture that glowing gate swinging to.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a broken keychain flashlight sits in the discount bin by the register until a bored customer clips two fresh batteries onto its back and thumbs the switch. The little bulb sputters, then catches, glowing steady in his hand. That double motion — snapping something onto a thing and waking it up — is the meaning: to turn on, to attach.
items.reading_mnemonic: つける is written in kana exactly as it sounds, with no kanji hiding underneath: <reading>つける</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the summit vending machine's fluorescent panel flickers and dies in a gust of wind at the exact moment a hiker rubs yesterday's chalk arrow off the rock beside it with his thumb. Bulb dark, chalk gone, both within the same breath of wind — that's the meaning: to turn off, to erase.
items.reading_mnemonic: The ranger who patrols the mountain trail is named Kesu, and hikers joke that wherever he walks, lights die and marks vanish behind him. Whisper <reading>けす</reading> and picture him snapping his equipment <reading>case</reading> shut — every switch he touches goes dark, every chalk line under his boot disappears.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the teacher stacks a mountain of ungraded homework by the door until the pile itself looks ready to <kanji>exit / leave</kanji> on its own. Rather than wait for that, she shoves the whole stack out into the hallway and drops a permission slip in the mailbox besides — anything that needs to go, she takes out and sends. That's the meaning: to take out, to send.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei, the fastest kid at school, <reading>dashes</reading> for the door the instant the bell rings, worksheets flying out of his open bag behind him. Teachers have started calling it his name for the move: <reading>だす</reading> — always mid-dash, always flinging something out as he goes.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the little figure who ducks under doorways to <kanji>enter</kanji> on its own is stalling by the onigiri shelf. You plant a hand on its back and shove — bent double, it goes through anyway, disappearing into the back room. You didn't just watch it enter this time; you made it happen. You put it in.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, Eri catches a slippery <reading>eel</reading> that keeps trying to escape. She has one hand free and a bucket ready, so before it can wriggle off she says '<reading>いれる</reading>' and drops it straight in.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, you forgot your umbrella and it's pouring. The priest keeps a bin of spares by the mossy steps and lets you take one, no questions, as long as you understand it's not a gift — you're borrowing it, and it goes back tomorrow.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one of the temple cats treats a fallen toy <reading>car</reading> like the greatest find ever, dragging it around all day — but by evening it always drops it back on the steps, because even a cat instinctively knows how to <reading>かりる</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, everyone forgets a pencil at some point, and there's always one kid by the window who has extras. She holds one out without a word, already expecting it back before the bell rings — that's exactly what it feels like to lend something.
items.reading_mnemonic: At school, Sei <reading>casts</reading> a glance at her spare pencil, then slides it across the desk to a friend who forgot theirs, saying '<reading>かす</reading>' — a quick loan she fully expects back by the end of class.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the till beeps and beeps at a customer already halfway out the door, arms full of onigiri he never scanned. The clerk has to haul him back by the collar before he'll dig out his wallet. Nobody leaves that counter until the beeping stops — you always have to pay.
items.reading_mnemonic: The clerk hauls him back by the collar, shouting that he'll <reading>haul</reading> him to the register himself if he has to. Coins finally hit the counter. The whole scrambling scene is <reading>はらう</reading> — to pay.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane sits on the mossy shrine steps with her hands folded, cats draped over her feet like she isn't going anywhere. Whatever she's expecting hasn't come yet, so she just sits, still as the bell beside her. That stillness, held on and on without complaint, is what it means to wait.
items.reading_mnemonic: A cat wanders up and tries to strike a <reading>match</reading> against the shrine bell, hoping to hurry things along, but Grandma Kane doesn't even blink. She's content to <reading>まつ</reading> as long as it takes.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Two people come around the same bend of the riverbank from opposite directions, both staring at the water instead of the path, and walk straight into each other. They stumble apart, startled, and there's nothing left to do but say hello. That collision, two people suddenly face to face, is what it means to meet.
items.reading_mnemonic: They collide so hard both yelp <reading>ow</reading> at once, then just stand there rubbing their foreheads and laughing. That startled little run-in by the river is <reading>あう</reading> — to meet.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, a tiny torii gate stands guard in front of the lone vending machine. You duck your head low, just like the ducking figure who taught you to <kanji>enter</kanji>, and step through the narrow gate into the clearing — the machine already humming, waiting.
items.reading_mnemonic: 入 already gave you the reading はい, so adding plain る spells out 「<reading>はいる</reading>」 directly.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school the bell rings and the hallway fills instantly, everyone funneling toward the same doorway like those two stacked mountains finally toppling outward under their own height. There's no lingering once the peaks give way — the whole crowd is already <kanji>exit / leave</kanji>, headed out.
items.reading_mnemonic: This one's regular: 出 gives で and る just adds the ending, together spelling out <reading>でる</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school the whole class lines up for the field-trip bus, but one boy refuses to sit until he's counted every seat twice. The driver revs the engine, the line surges forward, and the boy finally hops aboard as the doors hiss shut behind him. That's what it means to ride, to board.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the driver bellows one rule before the bus leaves: <reading>no rule</reading> about pushing. A boy who never listens hops on anyway, and the driver sighs, muttering <reading>のる</reading> under his breath as the doors close on him again.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, an old fisherman poles his boat back to shore, but his cat refuses to get off, digging its claws into the plank. He tips the boat until the cat has no choice, and it tumbles onto the mud with an offended yowl. That's the picture: reluctant, undignified, but off.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, the ferryman's cat is named <reading>Oriel</reading>, and every evening she refuses to disembark until he tips the boat. He mutters <reading>おりる</reading>, already off himself, as she finally splashes onto the mud beside him.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a mossy stone bridge arches over the carp pond, and an old monk crosses it every morning at the exact moment the bell tolls, timing his steps to the sound. One morning he pauses to feed the pond cats, forgets the bell, and has to hustle to cross before it stops ringing.
items.reading_mnemonic: The monk crossing the bridge is nicknamed <reading>Walter</reading> by the tourists, and Grandma Kane calls out <reading>わたる</reading> every morning to hurry him across the mossy stones before the bell finishes tolling.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Inside Koichi's konbini, a shopping cart with one stuck wheel refuses to go straight, swerving hard into the onigiri shelf every time it nears the corner. The clerk gives up steering it normally and yanks it sideways right at the corner, spilling rice balls everywhere as it finally turns.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the clerk yells <reading>mug a roo</reading> every time the cart nearly rams a customer, and the wheel screeches <reading>まがる</reading> as it swerves around the corner just in time, rice balls flying off the shelf behind it.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Toto the door-to-door turtle grinds up the mountain trail with his shell stacked full of sample doors, aiming for the vending machine at the top. Right at the steepest switchback he plants one foot flat against the gravel and freezes — the same <kanji>stop</kanji> pose the trail already taught you — and won't haul his doors another step until someone flags him down.
items.reading_mnemonic: 止（と）＋ま＋る spell out <reading>とまる</reading> exactly the way you already learned to read 止 — the readings just fall into place, no new story needed.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, out on the sports field, a hedgehog referee named Hazy Maru raises the starting horn over a line of runners. Nobody steps forward, nobody says go — the instant the horn sounds, the race just begins on its own, runners lurching off before they've even decided to move. That's what beginning looks like when nothing and nobody has to make it happen.
items.reading_mnemonic: Hazy Maru raises the horn and bellows <reading>Ha, Jimmy, Maru!</reading> across the field before anyone can move, and the racers bolt not because he counted down but because his shout already sounded like the race starting itself: <reading>はじまる</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Behind the register at Koichi's konbini, a raccoon clerk named Meru Jimson grips the ancient till with both paws and physically shoves its lever forward, forcing the beeping to life stroke by stroke. Nothing in this shop starts on its own — she has to begin it herself every morning, hauling the whole shift into motion by hand before a single customer walks in.
items.reading_mnemonic: The clerk grunts <reading>Ha, Jimmy, Meru!</reading> every single morning as she wrenches the till's lever down, and regulars have started timing their onigiri run to that grunt — the sound that means she's deciding, on purpose, that the day is now <reading>はじめる</reading>.

items.mnemonic_text: It comes to an end: owaru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the mossy steps go quiet and the cats freeze mid-stretch the instant the enormous bell rings its last, sagging note. Nobody rings it twice — that single dying note is the whole signal that whatever was happening on those steps is done, over, finished, and everyone on the steps knows to stand up and leave.
items.reading_mnemonic: One particular shrine cat, Ru, yowls <reading>Oh, wow, Roo!</reading> every time that last bell note dies away, startled it's really over. The yowl blurs into <reading>おわる</reading> — the sound of the exact moment the ceremony ends and Ru stops caring about any of it.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the ancient payphone by the door refuses to connect unless you shout the right word into the receiver before dialing. Everyone in line has learned the trick by now: say it loud, then the call goes through. Mumble it, and the line just stays dead — you have to properly make the call.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it sounds, so there is nothing to decode — just read <reading>かける</reading> straight through and that is the whole reading.

items.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a fallen vine blocks the only path to the vending machine at the top. Someone has already sliced clean through it in one motion — the two halves swing apart like saloon doors — and past the gap, the thirsty hikers finally reach the machine. The vine had to be cut before anyone could pass.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kiroo the kangaroo guards that same mountain vine. When a hiker gets close, she rears back and yells '<reading>KEY-roo</reading>!' before one clean kick slices the vine in half — it is her signature move, and hikers now mutter <reading>きる</reading> to themselves before every cut, copying the kangaroo's battle cry.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the gym locker room has one communal hoodie that never gets folded — it just gets pulled straight over whoever walks in first, backwards, arms flailing through the wrong holes. By the time the whistle blows, someone is standing there with the top half properly on, however wrong it looks underneath.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kiroo the kangaroo also keeps a spare hoodie in Sei's locker room, and every morning she wrestles it over her head shouting '<reading>KEY-roo</reading>!' with one ear stuck in a sleeve. Students now mutter <reading>きる</reading> under their breath while dressing, copying the muffled cry from inside the hoodie.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a raccoon refuses to wade in without stripping down first, peeling a mud-caked jacket off one shoulder at a time and flinging it onto a rock before dog-paddling across. Every animal downstream waits for the splash that means the jacket is finally off and the crossing has begun.
items.reading_mnemonic: That riverbank raccoon has a name — the other animals call her <reading>Newgoo</reading> for the sound her claws make peeling wet fabric, a slow squelch like <reading>ぬぐ</reading>. Every time she strips the muddy jacket off before diving in, she drags the sound out long and slow, and the name stuck.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a raccoon drags in a bicycle caked in mud, dunks it under the current, and scrubs the frame with a fistful of gravel until every speck lifts off and the metal shines wet in the sun. Rinse, scrub, repeat — that's washing.
items.reading_mnemonic: The raccoon holds the dripping bike over its head and announces <reading>a raw</reading> deal, since scrubbing stripped the paint clean off. Down at the riverbank they just call the whole scene <reading>あらう</reading> now.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At school, the recess bell rings and the whole sports field erupts — kids chasing a rolling ball, someone doing cartwheels into the sandpit, a stray dog that snuck through the gate joining every game at once. Nobody keeps score. Nobody stops. That's playing.
items.reading_mnemonic: A kid trips mid-cartwheel, lands face-first in the sandpit, and lets out <reading>a sob</reading> — then laughs and does it again on purpose. The whole field starts calling that stunt <reading>あそぶ</reading> for the rest of recess.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat leaps onto the giant bell rope and yowls straight down the mossy steps, scattering pigeons off the roof. A second cat joins in an octave higher, then a third, until the whole shrine sounds like a badly rehearsed choir. That's singing.
items.reading_mnemonic: The lead cat lets out a long, warbling <reading>oo-ta-oo</reading> into the bell rope, and by the second verse every cat on the mossy steps is repeating that exact howl — <reading>うたう</reading> — like a chorus line nobody auditioned for.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a pigeon gets trapped between the automatic doors as they slide open and shut, and starts hopping side to side to dodge them, wings out, feet shuffling under the fluorescent lights by the onigiri shelf. The beeping till never stops. That's dancing.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi waves a hand at the pigeon and complains about the <reading>odor</reading> it's kicking up mid-shuffle, feathers and dust everywhere. He starts calling the whole routine <reading>おどる</reading> whenever it happens again.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a heron dives for a fish, misses, and cartwheels straight into the mud. It stands back up wearing a lily pad like a hat, holding a look of total dignity, as if nothing happened. That straight-faced dignity in total defeat is what gets you — you cannot help it, you laugh, then grin the whole walk home.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the mossy shrine steps, a street performer named <reading>Wara</reading> attempts to out-sing the enormous bell. It is so off-key that even the cats flee, and Grandma Kane doubles over, unable to stop laughing — <reading>わらう</reading>, over and over, until she's wiping her eyes.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You reach the vending machine improbably parked at the top of the mountain trail, dig out your last coin, and watch it get swallowed with a smug beep and no snack in return. Legs shaking, throat tight, staring at that blinking screen — this is the exact moment your face crumples and you start to cry.
items.reading_mnemonic: Halfway up, a hiker named <reading>Knox</reading> kicks the machine that ate his coin, and it just rings hollow, like a knock on an empty door. He slides down against it and finally lets himself <reading>なく</reading>, sobbing into his sleeve while the machine blinks on, indifferent.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Deep on the back shelf of Koichi's konbini, past its printed deadline, the oldest onigiri finally gives out — filling gone grey, wrapper gone limp, the little countdown sticker flashing red one last time before going dark. Koichi bows his head over it for a solid ten seconds. It has died.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the register, Koichi taps the flashing sticker and mutters that <reading>she knew</reading> this one wasn't going to make it. He logs it in his little notebook of onigiri that <reading>しぬ</reading> before their shift ends, tally after quiet tally, page after page.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The same shoot that broke through the earth in the story of <kanji>life</kanji> keeps climbing past where anyone was watching, until one morning it splits its last husk open in the sun and unfurls a leaf nobody planted. No ceremony, no announcement — something that wasn't there yesterday is simply, suddenly alive: it has been born.
items.reading_mnemonic: At school, Sei is put in charge of the class tomato plant, certain nothing will come of it. Weeks later she sprints down the hallway insisting <reading>you're merely</reading> looking at a seed one day, and then — <reading>うまれる</reading> — a whole red tomato hangs off the vine she swore was empty.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture someone circling apartment listings for months, rejecting every one — too small, too loud, too far from the shrine — until one day they just stop circling. They unpack the boxes, hang a calendar on the wall, and stay put. That's the gap between visiting somewhere and actually living there: eventually you settle in and reside.
items.reading_mnemonic: A hulking <reading>sumo</reading> wrestler wanders into Grandma Kane's shrine one afternoon, likes the mossy steps and the cats, and simply never leaves. He builds a tiny hut by the bell and starts paying the shrine rent every month. That's <reading>すむ</reading> — to live, to reside.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You're packing for a weekend trip and your friend keeps grabbing things off the shelf — a hairdryer, three paperbacks, a spare umbrella. You take each one back and set it down: not necessary. Then you get to the phone charger and stop. That one you keep. That's the line between wanting something and actually needing it.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, a lost <reading>eel</reading> flops out of a hiker's water bottle, gasping — it needs water right now or it's finished. The hiker jams coins into the improbable vending machine, and the eel wheezes out the sound of its own need: 「<reading>いる</reading>」.

items.meaning_mnemonic: That <kanji>see</kanji>-eye on its pair of little legs wanders off one day and climbs to the very top of a hill, right out in the open. Now it doesn't matter who looks up — from the village, from the school field, from the riverbank — that eye is standing right there in plain sight. It's stopped just doing the looking and started being the thing everyone can look at: visible.
items.reading_mnemonic: 見（み）＋える gives you 「<reading>みえる</reading>」 regularly — the same み you already know from 見, plus the える ending this whole verb family wears.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Your ear is still pressed against that cold gate from before, straining for whispers — except this time you don't have to strain. The sound comes straight through the wood on its own: footsteps, a slammed door, someone calling your name, all loud enough to reach you without you having to <kanji>hear</kanji> for it. When sound arrives like that, unbidden, it's simply audible.
items.reading_mnemonic: 聞（き）＋こえる gives you 「<reading>きこえる</reading>」 regularly — the same き you already know from 聞, carried straight into this verb.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the curry machine glitches. Instead of dropping the packet into the bin like it does for everyone else in line, it swivels, hums, and fires a steaming pouch of curry straight into your hands — skipping every other customer, no request made, no line waited in. Nobody arranged it. Something simply gave itself to you.
items.reading_mnemonic: くれる is pure kana — no kanji to decode — so just sound out <reading>くれる</reading> as the curry machine's hiss: say <reading>curry-roo</reading> fast and you have it exactly right.
items.description: This verb only works when the giving benefits you or your in-group — someone does something for your side. A different verb covers everyone else giving to a third party, so it's easy to reach for this one in the wrong direction as a beginner.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, she fills a basket with rice cakes and works her way down the mossy steps, pressing one into the hands of every visitor she passes — the family by the bell, the tourists taking photos, even the cats sprawled on the stones. She doesn't keep a single cake back for herself. By the bottom step the basket is empty and everyone else's hands are full.
items.reading_mnemonic: あげる is written exactly as it sounds — read the basket-emptying rhythm as <reading>あげる</reading>, matching the bounce of a <reading>kangaroo</reading> hopping down the steps handing things out.
items.description: This verb covers giving outward — you or your group giving to someone else. It carries a faint sense of conferring a favor, which can sound presumptuous aimed at someone clearly above you; a more humble word is expected in that direction.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, a heron stands perfectly still while the current drifts small fish toward its beak. It never wades in, never chases, never hunts — it just waits at the same spot every morning, and the river keeps delivering. Everything the heron eats today, something else caught for it first.
items.reading_mnemonic: もらう is pure kana, read straight through: sound out <reading>もらう</reading> as the heron's stomach grumbling <reading>more, ow</reading> each time a fish arrives late.
items.description: This verb marks receiving, and it stretches beyond objects — you can 'receive' a favor or an action someone did for you, not just a physical thing. The person you received it from is the one who benefited you, which trips learners moving directly from English 'get.'

items.meaning: to be able to / be done

accepted_answers.answer_text: to be able to / be done

items.meaning_mnemonic: On the sports field at Sei's school, a kid who's wiped out on the skateboard deck all week finally lands the trick clean in front of the whole class. The board goes still under their feet — quiet, no more falling, no more trying. It's not luck; they can do it now, and the trick itself is finished.
items.reading_mnemonic: できる is pure kana — sound it out as <reading>できる</reading>, the crowd's murmur when the trick lands clean: <reading>deck-hero</reading>.
items.description: This word also functions as the potential form of the verb 'to do,' so it can mean either 'able to do something specific' or simply 'possible' depending on context. The thing that's possible is marked differently than a normal direct object, which trips learners used to English's straightforward 'can.'

items.meaning_mnemonic: You set your umbrella down for one second on the mossy steps of Grandma Kane's shrine, and when you turn back there is only a cat sitting in exactly that spot, looking innocent. The umbrella is not behind the cat, not under the cat, not anywhere. It has simply stopped existing. That is what it means to lose something.
items.reading_mnemonic: The shrine cat on Grandma Kane's mossy steps has one trick: she'll <reading>knock loose</reading> any offering balanced near the edge, and once it slides past the bell into the dark underneath, the shrine keeper just sighs and says <reading>なくす</reading> — it's gone, no use looking.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The eye that stood up on legs to <kanji>see</kanji> everywhere finally spots what it's after. It stops walking, plants its legs flat on the ground, and refuses to budge until you notice what it's staring at. That sudden dead stop, legs locked, eye fixed — that's the exact feeling of finding something you'd been hunting for.
items.reading_mnemonic: The reading is built straight from what you already know: 見（み）plus the verb ending つける, giving <reading>みつける</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the vending machine dispenses a paper crane instead of a drink. The hiker who buys it doesn't keep it — she opens her hand and lets the wind carry it down the switchbacks, waving until it's gone. Not keeping something, but launching it off toward someone else: that's what it means to send, to see off.
items.reading_mnemonic: A ranger at the mountain trail radios down every hiker who passes the summit, calling them her <reading>oak crew</reading>, and each evening she watches them go, waving from beside the vending machine until the trail is empty — that daily goodbye ritual is <reading>おくる</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a turtle has apparently opened a ferry service: every evening it surfaces with someone's forgotten sandal balanced flat on its shell, swims it dead straight across the current, and leaves it on the far rock before turning back for the next one. Nobody asked it to. It just carries things from one bank to the other, and that's the whole job.
items.reading_mnemonic: Fishermen at the riverbank cheer <reading>Ha, Cobo!</reading> every time the turtle noses a lost sandal off the rocks and paddles it across dead level, and once it lands safely on the far side, they call the whole ferry-run <reading>はこぶ</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the onigiri shelf holds forty identical triangles, and the till keeps beeping impatiently. A tired shopper stands frozen, picking one up, putting it back, picking up another, until she finally commits — she has to choose, and the beeping won't stop until she does.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, <reading>a rabbit</reading> hops up the mossy steps, surrounded by cats, and must pick just one to sit with. It circles them twice, muttering <reading>えらぶ</reading>, choosing, before flopping down beside the one-eared tabby.

items.mnemonic_text: Hold it up to see: miseru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The eye that grew legs doesn't just wander off to <kanji>see</kanji> things for itself — sometimes it marches straight up to you, plants itself in front of your face, and refuses to leave until you've looked too. Dragging what it saw over so someone else can see it as well is exactly what it means to show something.
items.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just 見 as <reading>み</reading> plus the ending せる tacked on, giving you <reading>みせる</reading> straight from the reading you already know for “see”.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Sei stands at one end of the empty sports field and cups his hands to shout across it. His voice ricochets down the echoing hallways behind him, bouncing off lockers, doubling back twice before anyone comes running — that's what it takes to call someone from clear across the school, to invite them over.
items.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, someone wades in too deep and calls out <reading>yo-boo</reading> for help, the sound skipping across the water until it lands as <reading>よぶ</reading> — close enough that everyone within earshot comes running to invite themselves into the rescue.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the one vending machine refuses to drop its can, jammed sideways in the slot. A hiker rocks it, kicks the base twice, and jiggles the coin return until the can finally thuds free — the machine works again, fixed and repaired, ready for the next exhausted climber.
items.reading_mnemonic: Back at Koichi's konbini, the till breaks mid-beep and Koichi mutters <reading>now, Sue</reading>, which is exactly what it sounds like — <reading>なおす</reading> — before Sue crouches under the counter with a screwdriver and gets it running again.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A hiker named Tomo reaches the vending machine at the top of the steep mountain trail just as the sun drops. His legs refuse another step down, so he unrolls a mat beside the machine, uses his backpack as a pillow, and settles in to stay overnight, listening to the machine hum its one lonely song until morning.
items.reading_mnemonic: Tomo stands frozen on the dark trail, torn between climbing down and waiting for dawn. He mutters, 'I'll stay till <reading>tomorrow</reading>' — the cold swallows his words into one sound, exactly like <reading>とまる</reading>, and he plants his boots and doesn't move again.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat spots the enormous bell rope dangling above and decides the bell tower looks like a throne. Paw over paw, it hauls itself up the mossy steps, then straight up the rope, refusing to stop until it's perched on the bell's crown surveying the cats below — that relentless paw-over-paw haul is what it means to climb.
items.reading_mnemonic: Nobu, the shrine cat's owner, snaps at a neighbor asking to borrow his ladder: '<reading>No, borrow</reading> nothing — watch this instead.' He hauls himself up the mossy steps hand over hand, the whole climb echoing through the cats as one long <reading>のぼる</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini stocks a hundred kinds of onigiri, and today he's misplaced the exact one he wants. He paces the fluorescent-bright aisles, checks behind the beeping till, digs through the shelf twice — turning the whole store over just to search for a single rice ball he's sure is still there.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi narrates his own hunt like a soap opera, sweeping a hand across the onigiri shelf: '<reading>Saga's</reading> search for the missing rice ball continues...' he announces to no one, and every time he says it, the line comes out sounding exactly like <reading>さがす</reading>.

items.mnemonic_text: Set them in a row: naraberu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Sei's gym teacher makes everyone line up their shoes along the sports field before practice — heel to heel, toe to toe, not one pair crooked. Sei spends ten minutes nudging sneakers into a perfectly straight row, and that patient shove-and-shuffle down the line is exactly what it means to line up.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei's gym teacher marches down the row of crooked sneakers shouting '<reading>No rebels</reading>!' at anyone out of line, and the command comes out clipped and fast, landing on everyone's ears as <reading>ならべる</reading> before they scramble to straighten their shoes.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail your legs give out, so you cup your hands and shout the whole message to the hiker just above you. She shouts it to the next, who shouts it to the next, until it reaches the vending machine waiting at the summit and prints out your exact sentence. Nobody up there invented anything — they only passed it on unchanged. That uphill, word-for-word relay is what it means to convey or tell.
items.reading_mnemonic: A tutor is stationed halfway up that same mountain trail, relaying every word radioed down from the summit vending machine without changing a syllable of it. Say her job fast — tutor, tutor — and it collapses into <reading>つたえる</reading>, the <reading>tutor</reading> whose only task is passing the message on exactly as it was given.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Sei's teacher lobs a question across the sports field like a ball, slow and looping, and it takes forever to come back. But when it does, it isn't a mumble — it's one clean shout that cracks down the echoing hallway and lands exactly where it's supposed to. That single confident shout, sent back only once someone is sure of it, is what it means to answer.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the kid everyone calls Kota is a hero for one reason: he's always first to shout back when the teacher lobs a question across the field. Say it fast — Kota, hero — and it flattens into <reading>こたえる</reading>, the <reading>Kota, hero</reading> whose reputation depends on never letting a question sit unanswered.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine you climb the mossy steps, grab the rope on the enormous bell, and haul it down hard enough to scatter every cat on the grounds. That's the only way anyone up there notices you've got something to ask — the bell itself answers nothing, it just announces that a question is on its way. That deliberate, rope-hauling demand for attention before you ever open your mouth is what it means to ask a question.
items.reading_mnemonic: One particular shrine cat has a trick: it sits bolt upright and bats the bell rope over and over until Grandma Kane comes running to see what it wants. Bark its command fast — sit, summon — and it flattens into <reading>しつもんする</reading>, the cat's own way of demanding that someone come answer it.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The storm outside Koichi's konbini keeps cutting the lights, and every time the <kanji>electricity</kanji> flickers back on, the till phone is already ringing with some caller mid-sentence, still going, spinning story after story down the wire as if the connection had never dropped at all. Electricity carrying someone's endless <kanji>talk</kanji> straight into your ear — that's what it means to phone.
items.reading_mnemonic: でんわする is just the readings you already know, stacked in order: 電 as でん, 話 as わ, plus する tacked on the end — read them straight through and you get <reading>でんわする</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>go</kanji> stick figure — legs split wide, one arm swinging forward — never settles for a single step out the door. He straps on a pack and keeps swinging that same arm through town after town, station after station, never breaking stride. Repeating the going, over and over, day after day, without ever stopping to unpack: that ceaseless, restless going is what it means to travel.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Koichi</reading> hangs a CLOSED sign over the till for the first time in years, laces his boots by the onigiri shelf, and walks out past the beeping doors — the konbini king is finally going to <reading>りょこうする</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>buy</kanji> reach — cowrie shell out, slid across the counter — doesn't stop at one purchase. Basket after basket, shell after shell, the hand keeps reaching, sliding, reaching again, aisle after aisle, until the counter is buried under shells. That endless string of buying, one purchase chasing the next with no end in sight, is what it means to shop.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Kaa</reading> dive-bombs the konbini roof, hops down the onigiri aisle, and grabs everything with one wing, puffing flames at anything reduced-price. Koichi sighs and rings it up — a whole crow's <reading>かいものする</reading> spree, till smelling faintly of scorched feathers.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every evening a stray dog checks the same three streets in the same order — the bakery, the vending machine, the bridge — not hunting for anything, just walking them because the walking itself is the point. No errand starts the loop and no errand ends it; it just circles the block and lets itself back home. That aimless, looping stroll, taken for its own sake, is what it means to take a walk.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Sanpei</reading>, a retired ferryman with no boat left to row, shows up at the riverbank anyway, hands in his pockets, ambling the bank and back for no reason but the ambling. He calls this slow circuit his <reading>さんぽする</reading>, same tide-slow lap, every evening.

items.mnemonic_text: Tidy it all up: souji suru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Every cat at Grandma Kane's shrine tracks paw-prints across the moss, and every morning she attacks the steps with a broom twice her height, scattering leaves, sweeping cobwebs off the enormous bell, scrubbing stone until it shines — that relentless morning ritual is what it means to clean.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane scrubs the mossy shrine steps and barks at a lounging cat, <reading>Soap, geezer, sure!</reading> — her raspy shout for <reading>そうじする</reading>, and the cat finally slinks off so she can finish cleaning.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every basket of clothes at the riverbank ends the same way: someone dunks the pile in the current, scrubs a shirt against a flat rock, and chases a runaway sock bobbing downstream before it drowns — the whole soggy, splashing chore of getting clothes clean is doing the laundry.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a fisherman wades in to net a runaway sock and hollers <reading>Send sock, sure!</reading> — his gruff cry for <reading>せんたくする</reading>, as he wrings it out and pins it up to dry with the rest of the wash.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi drags a portable stove behind the onigiri shelf and starts frying eggs directly under the beeping till, ash drifting onto the rice balls, customers stepping over the smoke to pay — until the whole fluorescent-lit konbini smells like dinner, because that chaos is cooking.
items.reading_mnemonic: Behind the counter at Koichi's konbini, a rigged hot-plate catches fire under the onigiri shelf, and Koichi just shrugs at the blaze, <reading>Roary, sure!</reading> — his deadpan answer for <reading>りょうりする</reading>, tossing another egg into the flaming pan anyway.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Somebody has to haul crates up the steep mountain trail to refill that one improbable vending machine at the summit, every single day, rain or shine, boots blistering, back aching under the load — that grinding, thankless climb up and back down again is what work means.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every day the delivery hiker trudges up the mountain trail to restock the summit vending machine, stubs her boot on its base, and yelps — the trail crew just sighs, <reading>She got toe!</reading>, their running joke for <reading>しごと</reading>, because it happens on every shift.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture Sei's school clanging its bell for third period. Every desk snaps upright at once, notebooks flip open, and forty pens move in the same held breath as the teacher starts writing on the board — that shared, synchronized scramble to take down everything before the bell rings again is exactly a class, a lesson.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a substitute teacher named Joog Yo shows up juggling three yo-yos down the aisle to keep everyone awake. The class starts chanting his name, <reading>じゅぎょう</reading>, like a cheer, because his <reading>juggle-yo</reading> act is the only reason anyone survives third period.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every night, Koichi finds a fresh stack of workbooks wedged onto the onigiri shelf, exactly where the rice balls should be — someone keeps swapping snacks for problem sets nobody asked for. He bags them for customers anyway, grumbling that unfinished pages waiting for you at home, whether you want them or not, is exactly what homework is.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the beeping konbini till, a tired student shakes a single die over his stack of worksheets, muttering <reading>しゅくだい</reading> every time it lands, hoping the number will somehow do his <reading>shook-die</reading> homework for him before Koichi rings him up and shoves him out the door.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the mossy steps fill every February with silent students ringing the one enormous bell, clapping twice, and begging the cats for luck. The weight of it all — one bell, one prayer, one date circled on the calendar for weeks — is exactly what an exam is: the single test everything has been building toward.
items.reading_mnemonic: A student rings Grandma Kane's enormous bell so hard a cat topples off the railing, then stands there muttering over and over, <reading>しけん</reading>, convincing herself <reading>she can</reading> pass tomorrow's exam if the bell just rings back loud enough.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, hikers find one improbable vending machine that only accepts jokes — feed it a bad enough pun and it judges you before dispensing a drink. That single machine standing between you and relief, checking whether you measure up before it lets you pass, is exactly a test.
items.reading_mnemonic: テスト is a loanword from English "test", written and read exactly as it sounds: <reading>テスト</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A boy chains his own ankle to his desk every night in the school hallway, papers piling knee-deep, refusing to unlock the cuff until dawn. A pigeon roosts on his head and won't leave either, staring at the pages until they stop turning. Neither of them moves until every problem is solved — that grinding, chained-in effort is study.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every night before he chains himself down, the boy mutters the same quiet oath: '<reading>Ben, cue, oh</reading>, no distractions.' Said fast, it slides into <reading>べんきょう</reading> — the sound of him swearing himself back to the desk.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the lone vending machine doesn't dispense drinks anymore. Every button jams, spits out a folded riddle instead, and demands you solve it before it will even consider a refund. Hikers arrive thirsty and leave with an armful of only more of these — unanswered questions and problems, stacked one on top of the last.
items.reading_mnemonic: A sticker on the machine reads, in block letters: '<reading>MONDAY</reading> deliveries only — no drinks.' Grumbled enough times on the hike back down, that word wears smooth into <reading>もんだい</reading>, the exact sound of every problem the machine caused.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A fisherman at the riverbank refuses to reel in anything until the river tells him something back. He shouts a question at the current, waits, and eventually a smooth stone washes up at his boots with a single word scratched into it. He pockets the stone before he even looks at the fish — to him, that scratched stone is the answer.
items.reading_mnemonic: The fisherman is named Kota, and every time a stone washes up he reads the word aloud, then tacks on his own tic: '<reading>Kota, eh?</reading>' Said quickly on the riverbank, that slurs into <reading>こたえ</reading> — his own name fused with the answer he just fished out.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one particular cat never blinks — it just stares at whatever offering was left on the mossy steps, as if grading it. Visitors have taken to leaving notes asking the cat what it's thinking. It never answers, but everyone leaves convinced that unblinking stare carries the real point of the offering — its meaning.
items.reading_mnemonic: A girl named Emi visits the shrine daily just to ask that cat what its stare means. She never gets an answer, only ends up muttering her own name back at it — '<reading>Emi</reading>, me, again' — until the sound wears down to <reading>いみ</reading>, the word she's really been chasing all along.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The mouth is still stacking layers of speech, but this time it doesn't stop where a single sentence would end — it keeps piling layer on layer, far past what one thought needs. That endless stack of <kanji>say</kanji> becomes an entire language, and every layer in it, taken alone, is a word.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's cat drags a tiny stolen <reading>coat</reading> across the shrine steps, and the temple goat trailing behind lets out one flat <reading>baa</reading> like a complaint. Coat, baa — say it fast and you get <reading>ことば</reading>, the word for word itself.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini awning juts out over the sidewalk to greet you before you're even through the door — that's <kanji>front</kanji>, the part that always meets you first. Duck under it and Koichi leans out to fill the gap over his mouth with the one word that was missing: his <kanji>name</kanji>. Front first, then the name.
items.reading_mnemonic: 名 gives you な and 前 gives you まえ, joined exactly as taught into <reading>なまえ</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the mountain trail's lone vending machine, every button is carved with dense, stroke-packed marks instead of pictures — no plain lines anywhere, just rows of intricate symbols crammed into a space built for a simple picture. Whatever you call that whole crowded family of written characters, this word is it: kanji.
items.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, a general named <reading>Khan</reading> wades in to rinse his coat and plants a boot on a rock hidden under the current — he yelps a startled <reading>gee</reading> loud enough to scatter the herons. Khan's gee: <reading>かんじ</reading>, the word for the crowded characters on the sign he still can't read.

items.meaning_mnemonic: On Sei's sports field the coach gives up on straight chalk lines and starts dragging the chalk into loose, looping curves instead — no sharp corners anywhere, just soft rounded strokes bending back on themselves. That rounded, curling script the coach just invented by accident is exactly what this word names: hiragana.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is written exactly the way it's read, all in kana: <reading>ひらがな</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the exhausted night clerk restocks imported snacks and refuses to write in curves. Every foreign product label gets stamped out in blocky, straight-edged letters, like they were sliced with a paper cutter instead of drawn by hand. That sharp, angular script reserved just for foreign words is katakana.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it sounds, 「<reading>カタカナ</reading>」.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a transfer student's mouth won't stop — one open mouth stacking speech on speech, then another mouth joining in, piling word after word into a whole <kanji>language</kanji>. But every syllable that tumbles out is rolled and foreign, all flat vowels and hard Rs the local kids can't place. That foreign stack of speech is English.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a hiker who speaks nothing but English barks <reading>Hey, go!</reading> at the stragglers by the summit vending machine. His clipped accent squashes the shout into the very sound of <reading>えいご</reading>, and that's the reading that's stuck to English ever since.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the shrine steps, dawn breaks and the <kanji>sun</kanji> climbs straight through the gate's window bar, marking a fresh day. Beside it, the tree's origin line still points to the very <kanji>origin</kanji> everything grew from, pressed flat into an ancient book. Then mouths start chanting, stacking speech on speech into a whole <kanji>language</kanji>, spoken over that book, in the land where the sun began. That stacked, sun-born tongue is Japanese.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank crossing, a drill-sergeant crane paces the stepping stones shouting orders: <reading>Knee! Hon! Go!</reading>, bend the knee, grip the handle, go. Villagers repeat the barked count until it blurs into one word, <reading>にほんご</reading>, and that's the reading that sticks whenever someone names the language.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the mountain trail's summit, the <kanji>sun</kanji> breaks through the vending machine's fogged window first thing each morning, same as it climbs through any window with a bar across it. Below, the tree's <kanji>origin</kanji> line still marks the very root everything grew from, the first page of the story. Sun rising first over the origin of it all: that's the name given to the whole nation, Japan.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till beeps out a stuttering three-note tone every time the register opens, <reading>knee, hone, go</reading>, and the night clerk swears it's saying <reading>にほん</reading> at him on every single sale. Say it three times fast and you'll hear it too.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The person from the slanted gate keeps walking, past their own fence, until the open air runs out at someone else's <kanji>country</kanji> — walls so tall they wrap an entire nation. They step through the gap still headed <kanji>outside</kanji>, and now they're standing in a foreign country.
items.reading_mnemonic: This one's regular: 外 already reads がい and 国 already reads こく, so stacked together they simply give you <reading>がいこく</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the teachers get summoned into the echoing hallway every Friday, and nobody wants to go. The moment the doors seal shut, someone always groans one flat, defeated "geez." That groan is the whole room's opinion of the meeting they're now stuck in.
items.reading_mnemonic: Picture a teacher named Kai standing at the front of that same sealed hallway. He claps twice and says, "Kai, geez, let's begin" — and the room slumps. Say it fast and you get <reading>かいぎ</reading>: the <reading>Kai, geez</reading> ritual that kicks off every meeting nobody chose to attend.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A yak on the mountain trail solemnly holds out one sock to you and refuses to let go until you swear to bring the other one back next week. That solemn oath — the yak's one sock held hostage until you keep your word — is a promise, an appointment you can't wriggle out of.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the mountain trail's lone vending machine, a yak grips one of your socks between its teeth and won't return it. It grunts <reading>やくそく</reading> — say "<reading>yak, sock</reading>" fast enough and that's exactly what it sounds like — until you promise to meet it there again next week for the other one.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Right before you lift that solid little roof and uncover the stash of gleaming nuggets, someone clears their throat politely — a soft "oh" announcing what's coming. Then out comes the precious <kanji>gold</kanji> that's been tucked away safe underneath, introduced now with the respect it deserves: money.
items.reading_mnemonic: お is the polite "o" prefix and 金 already reads かね, so together they simply give you <reading>おかね</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Someone frames a photo of the <kanji>go</kanji> stick figure — caught mid-stride, one arm swinging forward, legs split over unfamiliar ground — and pins it above their desk like a promise. It isn't him going right now; it's the single, saved-up going still waiting to happen, the whole journey folded into one still frame. That pinned promise of a future going is a trip.
items.reading_mnemonic: Behind the register, <reading>Koichi</reading> tapes up one photo: himself atop the mountain trail, out of breath beside that improbable vending machine. He taps it every morning and says the word, <reading>りょこう</reading> — the one trip he ever took.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You walk into Koichi's konbini planning to grab one thing, but the cowrie shell in your hand won't stop moving — you <kanji>buy</kanji> the onigiri, then the drink, then the umbrella by the door, sliding shell after shell across the till until your arms are full of bags. That endless chain of buying, one thing after another, is shopping.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa the fire-breathing crow perches above Koichi's konbini, bags overflowing, screeching <reading>かいもの</reading> — it lands on your ear like <reading>kie, moan, oh</reading>, her call every time she swoops down to buy one more thing.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Sei's school field has one announcer who only ever learned a single English word, so before every event — race, ball game, swim meet — he grabs the microphone and bellows スポーツ, because that one borrowed word already covers every game you could name: sports.
items.reading_mnemonic: スポーツ is a loanword written exactly the way it sounds, straight from English into kana: <reading>スポーツ</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's enormous bell doesn't just clang once — every cat in the yard has learned to time its own yowl to the ring, overlapping into layers of tone until stray clangs and cat wails resolve into something with rhythm. Noise agreeing to become rhythm like that is music.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a frog named Onga croaks the same three notes on a loop, <reading>おんがく</reading>, until the herons start swaying to the beat; his call sounds exactly like <reading>on, gah, coo</reading>, and that's the sound everyone nearby now associates with music.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You're stuck at a bus stop in the rain, and the drugstore across the street has a demo screen in its window that never turns off — passersby keep pausing mid-stride, faces lit blue, unable to look away from the flickering rectangle. That instinctive freeze, everyone briefly captured by a moving picture, is a movie.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the mountain trail's summit vending machine, an owl waits every night, wingtips tapping, unmistakably <reading>eager</reading> — because that machine's one nightly trick is flickering a movie across the rock face, and eager is exactly the sound of <reading>えいが</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, a hiker collapses in front of the lone vending machine and won't take another step. Her friend starts humming, then breaks into a full song about the cold drinks waiting at the summit. By the second verse the hiker is back on her feet, still humming, powered entirely by the song.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the vending machine, her friend keeps saying <reading>you oughta</reading> sing along before every button press, until the hikers are chanting it back in rhythm — <reading>oughta</reading>, <reading>oughta</reading> — and the phrase warps into <reading>うた</reading>, the machine's tinny jingle playing the actual song.

items.meaning_mnemonic: In the echoing school hallway, someone taped up a drawing so bad the paper itself seems embarrassed to hold it. Every student who passes stops, tilts their head, and produces the exact same reaction — because what's supposed to be a horse has four legs, three ears, and no clear idea which end is which.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei stops in the hallway, squints at the taped-up drawing, and says only <reading>え</reading> — one flat syllable, the same sound as the English <reading>eh</reading> you'd give a joke that didn't land. Every classmate who passes does the same thing, the hallway filling with confused, one-note え's.

items.meaning_mnemonic: That same mouth still hasn't stopped, and now its stories have an audience: the cats at Grandma Kane's shrine gather on the mossy steps every evening because one of them just won't quit <kanji>talking</kanji>, spinning fresh <kanji>stories</kanji> about a fish the size of the bell. Nobody's ever proven a word of it, but nobody leaves either.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every time the storytelling cat starts up again, Grandma Kane calls out from the steps, <reading>Hannah, she</reading> really said that? — and the phrase blurs into <reading>はなし</reading>, the very story the whole shrine has gathered on the mossy steps to hear.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, one customer plants himself at the register and asks about every single item on the shelf — the onigiri's expiration, why the till beeps twice, whether the till itself has feelings. Koichi answers thirty of these before the line behind reaches the door, and there's no sign of them stopping.
items.reading_mnemonic: Watching them pile up, Koichi mutters to the next person in line, <reading>she's too much</reading> — and the words blur into <reading>しつもん</reading>, the very thing holding up his till: one more question, then another, then another.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Momo, the konbini clerk, hates chaos. Every dropped umbrella, chipped mug, and lost sock that wanders onto her counter gets a paper tag and a spot on the shelf, no matter what it is. She never asks what it means or why it's there — a thing is a thing, and every thing gets labeled and shelved.
items.reading_mnemonic: Momo stamps each tag with a flat moan: "moooono." Customers assume she's exhausted, but it's just her filing chant — one long <reading>moan</reading> for every <reading>もの</reading> she catalogs, thing after thing after thing.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the gossip cat drags in a folded cot every evening and refuses to say a word until you're sitting on it. Only then does she report the day's matters — who fought, who left an offering, what toppled off the shelf — never a solid object you could hold, only something that happened.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every night the cat pats the cot twice before she'll talk, announcing the news with a soft double knock: "<reading>こと</reading>, <reading>こと</reading>" — the same sound as tapping a <reading>cot</reading>, her signal that a matter is about to be reported.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, past the lone vending machine, a toucan named Toco stubs her toe on the exact same rock every single hike. She stops, taps it twice, and declares that spot the place — not the trail, not the view, just the one stubbed patch of ground she keeps returning to.
items.reading_mnemonic: Toco's toe finds the same rock every hike, and she barks out her toe-corral: <reading>ところ</reading> — <reading>toe-corral</reading> — the small fenced-in place at the top of the trail that belongs only to her stubbed toe.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a fisherman raises his hoe like a compass whenever someone asks which way to wade across. He never points with his hand — only the hoe, tilted toward whichever direction the current looks calmest that day — and that single tilt is the only answer anyone gets.
items.reading_mnemonic: He grunts one flat <reading>ほう</reading> as the hoe swings — the same clipped sound as saying <reading>hoe</reading> with your mouth barely open — and that grunt-and-tilt is the whole direction anyone needs at the crossing.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A customs officer refuses to ever say the word "person" — it's beneath the dignity of his line. Instead he stamps each passport with a flourish and announces "next, esteemed guest," bowing a fraction lower for the elderly and exactly the same for everyone else. That stiff, formal way of naming someone is the word itself.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a tailor sets up shop by the onigiri shelf, snipping fabric with a huge <reading>cutter</reading>. Every customer who walks in gets bowed to and called "esteemed <reading>かた</reading>" before he measures their shoulders for a suit nobody asked for.
items.description: As "person," 方 is a polite, formal register word — used to respectfully describe someone else (a customer, a stranger, an elder), not to refer to yourself or to talk casually about friends.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You already know the gate with its two doors thrown open, the sun hanging low and trapped in the gap between them. Now a duck waddles up to that same gate and refuses to pass — it just paces back and forth in the strip of light, unwilling to leave the <kanji>interval / between</kanji> the two doors. That pacing, caught-in-the-middle strip of light is the word: an interval, the between.
items.reading_mnemonic: 間 already gives you the reading directly — the same one from the kanji's own gate-and-sun story, so 「<reading>あいだ</reading>」 is simply what you say.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A hiker climbs the mountain trail for hours, certain the summit is impossibly far, only to trip over the vending machine at the top and realize it's the same one he passed at the trailhead. He'd walked in a circle the whole time. Whatever he'd been trudging toward was nearby the entire climb — he just never looked over his shoulder.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, a <reading>cheeky cook</reading> has set up a stall serving free noodles to anyone who insists the summit is <reading>ちかく</reading> — nearby — even though they've clearly been climbing for hours. He never corrects them; free noodles for the delusional.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one cat claims the mossy step by the bell, and a second cat — never asked, never invited — plants itself immediately beside the first, close enough their tails touch. Every single day it's the same two steps, side by side, the second cat permanently attached to whichever step the first one picks. That fixed, right-beside-you position is what the word means.
items.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>tawny</reading> cat has taken over the step <reading>となり</reading> — right next to — the shrine bell, and hisses at anyone else who tries to sit there, as if the neighboring step belongs to it alone.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The runner is still frozen mid-stride, string trailing off his heel from a race that never seems to end. Now picture the whole pack has finished and gone home, and he's still out on the empty course, a few permanent steps back from where everyone else stood. That's his spot for good — <kanji>behind</kanji> the group, always trailing after.
items.reading_mnemonic: An <reading>usher</reading> at Sei's school assembly grabs every latecomer at the door, and instead of the empty front seats, walks them all the way to the back — <reading>うしろ</reading> — where they stand behind the whole crowd for the rest of the ceremony.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture that storefront awning again, jutting out over the sidewalk with its two-legged display stand planted beneath it. It's built to be the very first thing anyone sees, standing out in <kanji>front</kanji> of the shop, met <kanji>before</kanji> a single customer crosses the threshold. Whatever greets you first, whatever juts out ahead of everything else, is the front — the before.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word just carries over the kanji's own reading: 前 is read <reading>まえ</reading>, exactly as already taught.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The spear is still lodged dead center in that open square, exactly where you first pictured it — but now imagine trying to yank it back out and finding the square won't let go, gripping tight around the blade buried in its <kanji>middle</kanji>. Whatever's skewered that way isn't sitting near an edge; it's held fast, tucked <kanji>inside</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 中 keeps the reading you already learned for it: <reading>なか</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: That same figure is still at the slanted gate, one foot already past the threshold — but now picture them finally committing, both feet clearing the fence, the gate swinging shut behind them for good. Whatever was inside is someone else's problem now; they're standing in the open air, fully and firmly <kanji>outside</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 外 is read <reading>そと</reading>, exactly the reading already taught for this kanji.

items.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a goat drags the vending machine past the summit, still climbing — its hooves pointing the same way as that little mark rising off the ground: skyward. It won't stop until there's nothing left <kanji>above</kanji> it but open sky, which is exactly <kanji>up</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The word takes exactly the reading you already know from the kanji itself: 上 is read <reading>うえ</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, someone balances a shelf mid-air while doing the laundry, and the little mark dangling off underneath it stops waiting — it drops, plop, straight into the current. Everything about that shelf still leans toward the space it fell from: <kanji>down</kanji>, <kanji>below</kanji> the surface, gone.
items.reading_mnemonic: The word takes exactly the reading you already know from the kanji itself: 下 is read <reading>した</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer jams an arm into the vending slot up to the elbow, fishing after a stuck onigiri — the same fingers-into-open-mouth shape as before, working itself free all over again. It's always the dominant one doing this kind of stunt, which is why that grabbing hand is the <kanji>right</kanji> one.
items.reading_mnemonic: The word takes exactly the reading you already know from the kanji itself: 右 is read <reading>みぎ</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, in the middle of shop class, someone braces a carpenter's square hard against a plank so it won't slip while a friend saws — the same tensed grip as before, the arm that isn't doing the cutting. That steadying arm is always the one on the <kanji>left</kanji>, holding everything still so the other hand can work.
items.reading_mnemonic: The word takes exactly the reading you already know from the kanji itself: 左 is read <reading>ひだり</reading>.

items.mnemonic_text: Backs turned to the cold: kita.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The two figures are still on that frozen bench, spine to spine, too stubborn to face the wind. A postman trudges by and asks which way is <kanji>north</kanji>. Neither turns around — they just jab a thumb back over the shoulder, into the gale that's been freezing them all along, and that's your answer.
items.reading_mnemonic: 北 already gives you this exact sound for the place name, so you just say <reading>きた</reading> straight from what you learned.

items.meaning_mnemonic: That tent is still pitched with its wind chime jingling under the roof, planted on the sunniest patch of ground you could find. You keep dragging the stakes further and further along, chasing the warmth, until the chime is going nonstop in the soft breeze — and dragging a tent that far only points one way: <kanji>south</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 南 already carries this reading for the place name, so that's the sound you use here too: <reading>みなみ</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every morning that same tree at the horizon snags the sun in its branches again, right on schedule. You watch it happen daily: the sun claws its way through the tangle, breaks free, and you know exactly which direction you're facing when it does — <kanji>east</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 東 already gives you this exact word's sound, so you just say <reading>ひがし</reading> straight from what you learned.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every dusk that squat cage fills up again, wings folding in one after another as the birds settle for the night. You count them home each time the sun dips the exact same direction, and that direction is always <kanji>west</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 西 already carries this reading for the place name, so that's exactly what carries over here: <reading>にし</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Han the half-and-half chef takes the pie his knife already split into eight <kanji>part</kanji>s and lines up exactly four of them — the fat exclamation point standing dead center, its two legs kicked out even on both sides. Four parts here, four parts there: a clean, mirrored <kanji>half</kanji> on every plate he serves.
items.reading_mnemonic: 半分 simply combines the readings you already know: 半 read as はん plus 分 read as ぶん gives you <reading>はんぶん</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the new monk doesn't leave one coin behind. He tips the entire offering box onto the mossy steps, sweeps every last piece into his sack, and pats the empty box twice to prove it: nothing remains inside. He took the whole thing, every part of it — that's the idea.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's shrine keeps a monk on offering duty, and he only has one rule, chanted at every visitor: <reading>Zen-boo</reading> — give it all. He turns the donation box completely upside down and shakes it until the last coin drops. That chant is <reading>ぜんぶ</reading>, and it means the whole thing, nothing left inside.
