items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini restocks the onigiri shelf every morning, but today the delivery truck backs up too far and dumps three times the usual order. Onigiri spill off the shelf, stack on the floor, and pile up by the register until Koichi can't see the counter anymore. Customers wade through rice triangles just to check out — that's not a stocking error, that's a lot.
items.reading_mnemonic: たくさん is written exactly the way it sounds, kana only, nothing to decode: <reading>たくさん</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You've already watched someone take a bite out of small: slice one more dot off that hooked little shape and next to nothing survives. Pinch what's left between two fingers — that scrap, that residue, the near-nothing you can still hold onto — is exactly <kanji>few</kanji>. A little is whatever remains after almost everything else is gone.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sho, the tiny stage magician, never asks the crowd for much. Before every trick he holds up one white-gloved finger and requests just <reading>a skosh</reading> of hush, a skosh of powder, a skosh of anything at all. That signature request is <reading>すこし</reading> — a little, exactly his size, never more.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer asks to sample every rice ball on the shelf before buying one, but takes only the tiniest sliver off the corner of each — never a real bite, just a taste. The clerk restocks behind him without noticing anything's missing. That's the whole trick of asking for just a little: barely there, gone before you'd call it a bite.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is spelled in kana exactly as it's read, with no kanji to decode: <reading>ちょっと</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, one umbrella turns up in the lost and found every rainy week, and every student swears, straight-faced, that it belongs to someone else — never mine, always another person's. By the end of term nobody remembers whose it actually was, just an endless chain of pointing at whoever's standing nearby. That endless deflection is the word: other.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a peddler named Hoka the hawker never sells you anything from his own cart — he waves you further up the path, insisting you buy from the other hawker instead. Every climber ends up chasing an <reading>hoka</reading> who doesn't exist. His name says it plain: <reading>ほか</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, two cats that look identical fight nonstop, so she builds a low wall down the middle of the mossy steps just to keep them apart — one bowl on each side, one nap spot on each side, one bell on each side. Everything about their lives gets divided into its own separate portion, one and then another entirely. That's the word.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the shrine, one cat named Betsy refuses to share the steps with the others — she claims her own patch of moss, apart from every cat there, hissing if anyone crosses the line. Grandma just shrugs and calls her the <reading>べつ</reading> cat, plain as the sound of her own name: <reading>Betsy</reading> stays separate, always.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Someone collapses on the school sports field, forehead burning, and the same swirling wisp you've seen rise off a hot bowl of rice now curls up off their skin instead — their <kanji>spirit</kanji> visibly leaking out into the air with every ragged breath. The nurse takes one look at that steam and doesn't even need to ask what's wrong: illness.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kiki the tree spirit catches a chill on the mountain trail, and her usual giggle turns into a rasping cough that shudders through the branches, ending in a weak, wheezy <reading>b'yo-key</reading> sound — <reading>びょうき</reading> — the same puff of spirit as always, just worn thin by illness.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Sei collapses face-down on the school field after the last sprint of practice, soaked in sweat. A cold wind knifes across the grass the instant she stops moving, and by evening she's shivering under three blankets with a raw throat and a fever — a cold caught in one gust of wind.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei's coach wraps her scraped knee in gauze at the edge of the field, and the wind — <reading>かぜ</reading> — snatches the loose end and flaps it like a flag. She hisses '<reading>gauze</reading>' through her teeth, kaze, the same wind that left her sick the next morning.
items.description: 風邪 is written with the same character as 風, 'wind' — colds were traditionally believed to be carried in on a bad wind, which is also why the everyday expression for catching a cold literally means 'to be hit by wind.'

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the medicine shelf sits past the onigiri, a lonely row of blister packs nobody touches — until 2 a.m., when someone stumbles in hacking and coughing, sweeps the whole row into a basket, and pays without a word. That row of boxes is the medicine.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi restocks the shelf with only a <reading>cursory</reading> glance, tossing boxes on by feel. A customer mumbles '<reading>くすり</reading>, please' without looking up either — both of them running on autopilot at 2 a.m., neither one fully awake.

items.mnemonic_text: A drawing of the land: chizu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Partway up the mountain trail, a hiker stalls at an unmarked fork, digs a single folded sheet out of her pack, and traces the dotted line with her finger all the way to the vending machine waiting improbably at the summit. That creased sheet in her hands is the map that gets her there.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the fork she unfolds it and mutters '<reading>cheese zoo</reading>' under her breath — her own private trick for the sound — tracing the line with one finger: '<reading>ちず</reading>, cheese zoo, don't you dare blow away now.'

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank crossing, the ferryman won't push off until every passenger hands him a small paper stub, torn cleanly in half at the perforation. No stub, no ride across — that torn scrap clutched in your hand is the ticket.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, the ferryman drops each torn stub into a rusty tin he calls his '<reading>key pool</reading>,' clinking it in with a grin and calling out '<reading>きっぷ</reading>, another one for the pile' before shoving off.

items.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, Koichi refuses to leave any bag at the bottom, so he hauls all of them past the vending machine at the summit, knees creaking louder with every step. By the time he collapses at the top, all anyone can see is baggage — two duffels, a rolled tent, and Koichi somewhere underneath it all.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi reaches the vending machine at the trail's summit and groans, 'need... motsu... one more step,' shifting the duffel on his shoulder. A hiker behind him hears only <reading>にもつ</reading> — sounds just like <reading>need-motsu</reading> to her, watching him stagger under all that luggage.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, the overhead cart — that boxy frame with its axle drawn straight through, the <kanji>vehicle</kanji> shape you already know — gets struck by the same jagged bolt that cracks out of the rain-soaked sky, feeding it pure <kanji>electricity</kanji>. Sparks race down the axle and the whole cart screams off along the tracks, electrified into a train.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>でんしゃ</reading> is just 電's でん plus 車's しゃ said back to back — the readings you already know, joined.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Outside Koichi's konbini, under the buzzing fluorescent sign, that same overhead cart shape — axle through the middle, wheels flanking each side, the boxy frame all around — rolls up to the beeping till lane itself, engine running. Nobody laid a track out here, just four wheels parked on the apron: a <kanji>car</kanji>, plain and simple.
items.reading_mnemonic: This is the same 車 you already read as くるま, so the word for car is simply <reading>くるま</reading> — the reading you learned with the kanji itself.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the overhead cart shape — axle through the center, wheels braced on either side, the same boxy frame you already know as a <kanji>vehicle</kanji> — comes loose from its cart body and rolls itself up the mossy steps on just its two wheels, wobbling past the enormous bell while cats scatter. No engine, no rails, just those wheels pedaling themselves uphill: a bicycle.
items.reading_mnemonic: A cat at Grandma Kane's shrine watches the wheels totter past the bell and yowls, 'jitters... shaa!' as they nearly tip into the moss. That startled <reading>jitters-sha</reading> cry is exactly how you say bicycle: <reading>じてんしゃ</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The restless figure who can't stand still — always mid-stride, always about to <kanji>go</kanji> somewhere — sprints down a runway and just keeps going, faster and faster, until the ground drops away entirely and he's roaring into the sky strapped inside an airplane.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi, the konbini king, gets impatient waiting for delivery trucks, so he buys a tiny plane. Swooping over the store, he yells his restock call — <reading>"HEE, GO KEY!"</reading> — and that shout becomes <reading>ひこうき</reading>, the sound of his little airplane roaring past overhead.

items.meaning_mnemonic: An otter drags every barrel and plank he can find onto the riverbank, lashing them together into a lopsided raft before the current rises further. He shoves off with a broom for a paddle — proof that any floating hunk of junk counts as a ship the moment it carries someone somewhere.
items.reading_mnemonic: The ferryman blows through a battered <reading>funnel</reading> to signal departure, and the honk that comes out lands squarely as <reading>ふね</reading> — the noise every boat on this river makes before it pushes off from the dock.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Follow that dangling tail that always points <kanji>below</kanji> the shelf, down past the floor, down past the foundations, until you're standing on a platform lit by flickering tubes with a train roaring in out of the dark — the subway is just where below finally bottoms out.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa perches on the power line above the entrance grate and coughs out a puff of flame that echoes down into the tunnel: <reading>"CHEE! KUH! TETSU!"</reading> the workers below holler back, and that ringing call becomes <reading>ちかてつ</reading>, the sound of trains ducking underground every morning.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A hamster spins its wheel in tight, dizzying circles while its keeper stands by with a clicker, tallying each lap out loud. Nobody cares how far the hamster actually traveled — only how many circuits it completed, because that count is the only thing anyone bothered measuring: times, plain and simple.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every time the hamster finishes a loop, a referee named <reading>Kai</reading> blows his whistle and marks a tally on his clipboard, shouting the same syllable each time so it's unmistakable: <reading>かい</reading> — one more time counted, one more circuit done.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A vending machine at the top of the mountain trail dispenses nothing but pebbles, buttons, and dice — one at a time, plink, plink, plink. A hiker feeds it coins just to watch the tiny things drop, because that machine only deals in <kanji>small objects (counter)</kanji>, and it refuses to give you anything bigger.
items.reading_mnemonic: The hiker mutters "<reading>ko</reading>-<reading>ko</reading>-<reading>ko</reading>" every time another <reading>こ</reading> pebble clatters into the tray, counting them off one clunk at a time, her breath fogging the cold mountain air as the tray slowly fills up.

items.mnemonic_text: Count of long thin things: hon.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till has jammed with a single receipt spooling endlessly onto the floor — a long white ribbon of paper, thin as the line marking a tree's roots. The clerk keeps stacking these long unrolled strips like planks, and pretty soon he's counting them the same way he'd count <kanji>books</kanji>: as long objects (counter).
items.reading_mnemonic: 本 already reads ほん from book / origin, so the counter for long objects keeps that same reading: <reading>ほん</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane is fanning herself at the shrine with what she insists is one paper fan, except the wind keeps peeling it apart into more and more identical flat sheets, scattering across the mossy steps. The cats bat each sheet flat against the stone, and she ends up having to tally the whole scattered stack as <kanji>flat objects (counter)</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: One cat pins a sheet down and lets out a flat, dragged-out "<reading>maaai</reading>" every time another one lands, so Grandma starts counting them by that cry: <reading>まい</reading>, <reading>まい</reading>, <reading>まい</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, Sei is trying to wash one stray cat, but it wriggles free and suddenly there are three more identical stray cats streaking off between the rocks, all soaked and furious. She gives up chasing them individually and starts tallying the whole dripping mob as <kanji>small animals (counter)</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every time a cat darts past her soaked sleeves, Sei yelps "<reading>hick</reading>!" in surprise, and by the third one darting past the rocks she's just counting the startled yelps out loud: <reading>ひき</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Jin the friendly giant ducks through the door of Koichi's konbini, and a whole line of customers files in behind him, each one a <kanji>person</kanji> striding forward on the same two legs you learned before. Jin taps each striding person on the shoulder as they pass, tallying them one after another — which is exactly what you do when you count people.
items.reading_mnemonic: Jin has to duck so low under the konbini doorframe that the effort squeezes out a groan — a long, rattling <reading>にん</reading> that shakes the onigiri shelves. Koichi just sighs and starts counting customers by Jin's groans instead of a clicker: one groan, one <reading>neen</reading>, one person through the door.

example_sentences.japanese: 学校に先生が三人います。
example_sentences.english: There are three teachers at the school.
example_sentences.furigana: 学[がっ]校[こう]に先[せん]生[せい]が三[さん]人[にん]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 私の家族は四人です。
example_sentences.english: There are four people in my family.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の家[か]族[ぞく]は四[よ]人[にん]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 公園に子供が五人いました。
example_sentences.english: There were five children in the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 公[こう]園[えん]に子[こ]供[ども]が五[ご]人[にん]いました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the librarian stacks returned homework workbooks so high on one cart that the bottom shelf buckles and the whole tower slides across the echoing hallway floor, spine over spine, until it rams the trophy case. She doesn't reshelve them — she just counts how many books fell, one after another, in that same skidding stack.
items.reading_mnemonic: Satsuki, the school librarian, keeps a wooden clapper by the returns cart, and every time a stack of books topples she snaps it once for each one: <reading>さつ</reading>, <reading>さつ</reading>, like a strict little <reading>salt</reading> shaker sprinkling counts over the mess instead of cleaning it up.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は本を三冊買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought three books.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は本[ほん]を三[さん]冊[さつ]買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 図書館で本を二冊借りました。
example_sentences.english: I borrowed two books from the library.
example_sentences.furigana: 図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]で本[ほん]を二[に]冊[さつ]借[か]りました。

example_sentences.japanese: 机の上に雑誌が一冊あります。
example_sentences.english: There is one magazine on the desk.
example_sentences.furigana: 机[つくえ]の上[うえ]に雑[ざっ]誌[し]が一[いっ]冊[さつ]あります。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Dai the giant baby crawls into the school's echoing gym and finds it full of vending machines, washing machines, and one ancient arcade cabinet lined up like toys. He shoves each one an inch across the floor with one finger, giggling, and by the time he's bored he's pushed every single machine in the building at least once.
items.reading_mnemonic: Dai the giant baby gets bored of shoving machines and starts headbutting them instead, and each thud rings out as a deep <reading>だい</reading> that rattles the gym windows. The teachers just count machines by counting thuds — one <reading>die</reading>-like boom per dented vending machine.

example_sentences.japanese: 部屋にテレビが一台あります。
example_sentences.english: There is one TV in the room.
example_sentences.furigana: 部屋[へや]にテレビが一[いち]台[だい]あります。

example_sentences.japanese: 家に新しい自転車が二台あります。
example_sentences.english: There are two new bicycles at home.
example_sentences.furigana: 家[いえ]に新[あたら]しい自[じ]転[てん]車[しゃ]が二[に]台[だい]あります。

example_sentences.japanese: 会社にパソコンが何台ありますか。
example_sentences.english: How many computers are there at the company?
example_sentences.furigana: 会[かい]社[しゃ]にパソコンが何[なに]台[だい]ありますか。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane lines up cups of water along the mossy shrine steps for the cats, refilling one from the well every time a cat drinks it dry, over and over until the whole row is gone again. She never counts the cats — she counts the cups she's had to refill, one cupful after another, until the well runs low.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every time a cat drains a cup on the shrine steps, Grandma Kane lets out a tired little sigh that comes out as <reading>はい</reading>, the same sigh she uses when someone asks her something she'd rather not answer — a flat, resigned <reading>hi</reading> as she reaches for the well again.

example_sentences.japanese: 朝、お茶を三杯飲みます。
example_sentences.english: In the morning, I drink three cups of tea.
example_sentences.furigana: 朝[あさ]、お茶[ちゃ]を三[さん]杯[ばい]飲[の]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女はコーヒーを二杯飲みました。
example_sentences.english: She drank two cups of coffee.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]はコーヒーを二[に]杯[ばい]飲[の]みました。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎日、水を何杯飲みますか。
example_sentences.english: How many glasses of water do you drink every day?
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]日[にち]、水[みず]を何[なに]杯[ばい]飲[の]みますか。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a vending machine bolted to the mountain trail, one machine bolted onto every single level as hikers climb. They count out loud passing each one: first machine, second, third, all the way to the summit. By the top nobody's counting mountains anymore — they're counting floors (counter), one per machine.
items.reading_mnemonic: A guy named <reading>Kai</reading> gets stuck in a tiny elevator wedged into the mountain trail, one vending machine bolted to every floor. Each time the doors ding open he groans his own name, <reading>かい</reading>, half greeting and half complaint, so the sound sticks to every floor that clicks past.

example_sentences.japanese: 私の部屋は二階です。
example_sentences.english: My room is on the second floor.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の部屋[へや]は二[に]階[かい]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 図書館は三階にあります。
example_sentences.english: The library is on the third floor.
example_sentences.furigana: 図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]は三[さん]階[かい]にあります。

example_sentences.japanese: レストランは何階ですか。
example_sentences.english: What floor is the restaurant on?
example_sentences.furigana: レストランは何[なに]階[かい]ですか。

items.mnemonic_text: Count of years of age: sai.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the mossy steps are lined with birthday candles instead of stone lanterns, one candle burning on every step. The shrine cats trot past blowing each one out in turn, and the shrine keeper explains he isn't counting steps at all — he's counting years old (counter), the same tally kept every birthday.
items.reading_mnemonic: A shrine cat blows out the last candle on the mossy steps and lets out an exhausted <reading>さい</reading>, a long <reading>sigh</reading> that sounds exactly like the word. The shrine keeper nods along — every sigh marks one more year old, so the sound and the tiredness are stuck together for good.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は十八歳です。
example_sentences.english: He is eighteen years old.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は十[じゅう]八[はち]歳[さい]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 妹は五歳です。
example_sentences.english: My younger sister is five years old.
example_sentences.furigana: 妹[いもうと]は五[ご]歳[さい]です。

example_sentences.japanese: あなたは何歳ですか。
example_sentences.english: How old are you?
example_sentences.furigana: あなたは何[なん]歳[さい]ですか。

items.meaning_mnemonic: On Sei's sports field, runners line up wearing paper bibs pinned on backwards, and the coach marches the row jabbing each one straight — first, second, third — until the whole line stands in strict number / order. Nobody has run a single step yet; the entire scene is just about getting that order right.
items.reading_mnemonic: The coach straightening everyone's bibs wears her hair in a tight <reading>ばん</reading>, and every time she barks out a runner's number the <reading>bun</reading> bobs in time, bobbing down the whole line. That bobbing bun is how you remember ばん means number and order.

example_sentences.japanese: 私の部屋は五番です。
example_sentences.english: My room is number five.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の部屋[へや]は五[ご]番[ばん]です。

example_sentences.japanese: あのバスは何番ですか。
example_sentences.english: What number is that bus over there?
example_sentences.furigana: あのバスは何[なに]番[ばん]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 私の切符は三番です。
example_sentences.english: My ticket is number three.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の切[きっ]符[ぷ]は三[さん]番[ばん]です。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the microwave beeps and someone keeps sliding in the same lump of dough, cranking the dial past a new temperature mark and checking it once, twice, three times before it's ready. Each check is one pass at a certain heat, and stacking up those passes is exactly what times / degrees means.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi keeps muttering <reading>ど</reading> under his breath while pressing more <reading>dough</reading> into the microwave, and it comes out sounding exactly like the English word. Every mutter marks one more attempt at the right heat, which is how ど ends up meaning times and degrees.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は一度その公園に行きました。
example_sentences.english: I went to that park once.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は一[いち]度[ど]その公[こう]園[えん]に行[い]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は三十度で暑いです。
example_sentences.english: Today it's thirty degrees, so it's hot.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は三[さん]十[じゅう]度[ど]で暑[あつ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼はその歌を二度歌いました。
example_sentences.english: He sang that song twice.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]はその歌[うた]を二[に]度[ど]歌[うた]いました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You already know this shape: a single shiny coin flattened into a square frame, round enough to pass for a <kanji>circle</kanji>. That coin never needs to be anything grander — one coin sitting in one frame is worth exactly one <kanji>yen</kanji>, and it always has been.
items.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just the kanji's own taught sound: 円 is read <reading>えん</reading>, exactly as you already learned it for the coin in its square frame.

example_sentences.japanese: これは千円です。
example_sentences.english: This is a thousand yen.
example_sentences.furigana: これは千[せん]円[えん]です。

example_sentences.japanese: パンは二百円でした。
example_sentences.english: The bread was two hundred yen.
example_sentences.furigana: パンは二[に]百[ひゃく]円[えん]でした。

example_sentences.japanese: 財布に五千円あります。
example_sentences.english: There is five thousand yen in my wallet.
example_sentences.furigana: 財[さい]布[ふ]に五千[ごせん]円[えん]あります。

items.meaning_mnemonic: That same scarecrow is still out there, sleeves gone gray, having watched the rice fall and rise through one full circuit of sun and frost. It never counts the seasons one by one — it only marks the moment its whole slow watch loops back to where it started, and that single loop is a <kanji>year</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just the kanji's own taught sound: 年 is read <reading>ねん</reading>, the same one you already learned for the scarecrow's yearly watch.

example_sentences.japanese: 日本に三年住んでいます。
example_sentences.english: I've been living in Japan for three years.
example_sentences.furigana: 日本[にほん]に三[さん]年[ねん]住[す]んでいます。

example_sentences.japanese: 大学で四年勉強しました。

example_sentences.furigana: 大[だい]学[がく]で四[よん]年[ねん]勉[べん]強[きょう]しました。

example_sentences.japanese: 会社で二年働きました。
example_sentences.english: I worked at the company for two years.
example_sentences.furigana: 会[かい]社[しゃ]で二[に]年[ねん]働[はたら]きました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: That same crescent moon now hangs painted above the calendar taped beside Koichi's till, one wedge inked in for every lap it makes across the sky. Shoppers glance up between onigiri runs to see which wedge is lit, using the moon exactly as before — just to name the <kanji>month</kanji> instead of the night.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi refuses to update that calendar one day at a time — he's too <reading>gutsy</reading> for that. Once every full moon he tears off an entire wedge in one motion, grunting <reading>がつ</reading> as the paper rips clean away.

example_sentences.japanese: 何月に日本へ行きますか。
example_sentences.english: What month are you going to Japan?
example_sentences.furigana: 何[なに]月[がつ]に日本[にほん]へ行[い]きますか。

example_sentences.japanese: 二月は寒いです。
example_sentences.english: February is cold.
example_sentences.furigana: 二[に]月[がつ]は寒[さむ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 兄は三月に生まれました。
example_sentences.english: My older brother was born in March.
example_sentences.furigana: 兄[あに]は三[さん]月[がつ]に生[う]まれました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the caretaker never repaints the mossy steps one moon-turn at a time. He waits, letting several full turns of the <kanji>month</kanji> stack up unnoticed among the cats, then tallies the whole stretch off in a single breath before finally ringing the bell.
items.reading_mnemonic: The shrine cats have grown <reading>cagey</reading> about the caretaker's tenure, counting his moon-turns in murmurs of <reading>かげつ</reading> each time another stretch gets added to his tally before the bell ever rings.

example_sentences.japanese: 日本語を三ヶ月勉強しました。
example_sentences.english: I studied Japanese for three months.
example_sentences.furigana: 日本[にほん]語[ご]を三[さん]ヶ[か]月[げつ]勉[べん]強[きょう]しました。

example_sentences.japanese: 母は二ヶ月会社を休みました。
example_sentences.english: My mother took two months off from work.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]は二[に]ヶ[か]月[げつ]会[かい]社[しゃ]を休[やす]みました。

example_sentences.japanese: 六ヶ月で新しい言葉をたくさん覚えました。
example_sentences.english: In six months I memorized a lot of new words.
example_sentences.furigana: 六[ろく]ヶ[か]月[げつ]で新[あたら]しい言[こと]葉[ば]をたくさん覚[おぼ]えました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the caretaker watches the <kanji>sun</kanji> climb through the window-with-a-bar each morning and chalks one mark onto the great bell for that <kanji>day</kanji>. The temple cats keep swatting the marks off the bronze, so she starts over, one sunrise at a time, tallying days like coins dropped in a jar.
items.reading_mnemonic: Regular reading — 日 was already taught as <reading>にち</reading>, and that's exactly the reading this word keeps, unchanged.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は何日ですか。
example_sentences.english: What's today's date?
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は何[なに]日[にち]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 来月の十一日に友達と会います。
example_sentences.english: I'll meet a friend on the 11th of next month.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]月[げつ]の十[じゅう]一[いち]日[にち]に友[とも]達[だち]と会[あ]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 今月は三十日まであります。
example_sentences.english: This month has 30 days.
example_sentences.furigana: 今[こん]月[げつ]は三[さん]十[じゅう]日[にち]まであります。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Partway up the steep mountain trail, you retrace the boxy calendar loop of the <kanji>week</kanji> with one finger, looping toward the vending machine glinting at the summit. Each loop finished, the gate's caught sliver of sun marks the <kanji>interval</kanji> before the next starts, and by the top you've climbed through several whole weeks of loops.
items.reading_mnemonic: Regular reading — 週（しゅう）plus 間（かん）simply combine, giving you <reading>しゅうかん</reading> straight from readings you already know.

example_sentences.japanese: 来週から三週間、休みます。
example_sentences.english: I'll take a three-week break starting next week.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]週[しゅう]から三[さん]週[しゅう]間[かん]、休[やす]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 二週間、日本語を勉強しました。
example_sentences.english: I studied Japanese for two weeks.
example_sentences.furigana: 二[に]週[しゅう]間[かん]、日本[にほん]語[ご]を勉[べん]強[きょう]しました。

example_sentences.japanese: 何週間、旅行しますか。
example_sentences.english: How many weeks are you traveling for?
example_sentences.furigana: 何[なに]週[しゅう]間[かん]、旅[りょ]行[こう]しますか。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, the <kanji>sun</kanji> crawls across the sky the way it does at the shrine, ticking off <kanji>hours</kanji> like a clock reflected in the water. Between one splash of laundry and the next, the gate-shaped gap of caught sunlight marks the <kanji>interval</kanji> you were gone, and you realize you've lost several whole hours just watching the current.
items.reading_mnemonic: Regular reading — 時（じ）plus 間（かん）simply combine, giving you <reading>じかん</reading> straight from readings you already know.

example_sentences.japanese: 毎日二時間勉強します。
example_sentences.english: I study for two hours every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]日[にち]二[に]時[じ]間[かん]勉[べん]強[きょう]します。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日三時間映画を見ました。
example_sentences.english: Yesterday I watched a movie for three hours.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]三[さん]時[じ]間[かん]映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 何時間待ちましたか。
example_sentences.english: How many hours did you wait?
example_sentences.furigana: 何[なに]時[じ]間[かん]待[ま]ちましたか。

items.mnemonic_text: The hour on the clock: ji.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till clock is nothing but that same <kanji>sun</kanji>-in-a-window face from the shrine, glowing under fluorescent lights instead of sky. The beeping till freezes the instant the hand lands square on a number, and Koichi calls out that exact moment — not a stretch of <kanji>time</kanji>, just the single instant the sun-face points to.
items.reading_mnemonic: Regular reading — 時 was already taught as <reading>じ</reading>, and that's exactly the reading this word keeps, unchanged.

example_sentences.japanese: 授業は二時に始まります。
example_sentences.english: Class starts at two o'clock.
example_sentences.furigana: 授[じゅ]業[ぎょう]は二[に]時[じ]に始[はじ]まります。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は十時に寝ます。
example_sentences.english: I go to sleep at ten o'clock.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は十[じゅう]時[じ]に寝[ね]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 三時に友達と会います。
example_sentences.english: I'm meeting a friend at three o'clock.
example_sentences.furigana: 三[さん]時[じ]に友[とも]達[だち]と会[あ]います。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi slices the onigiri timer at the konbini into wedges instead of watching the clock, and each <kanji>part</kanji> he shaves away is a <kanji>minute</kanji> he can finally <kanji>understand</kanji> has passed — three wedges gone, three minutes counted.
items.reading_mnemonic: The counter reading is simply 分's own taught reading 「<reading>ふん</reading>」 carried straight over, so counting minutes uses the same sound you already know.

example_sentences.japanese: 二分待ちました。
example_sentences.english: I waited two minutes.
example_sentences.furigana: 二[に]分[ふん]待[ま]ちました。

example_sentences.japanese: 何分歩きますか。
example_sentences.english: How many minutes do you walk for?
example_sentences.furigana: 何[なに]分[ふん]歩[ある]きますか。

example_sentences.japanese: 五分で終わりました。
example_sentences.english: It finished in five minutes.
example_sentences.furigana: 五[ご]分[ふん]で終[お]わりました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Partway up the mountain trail, a hiker's runaway balloon slips its string and drifts higher than the vending machine at the summit, then higher than the whole ridge — it doesn't stop until it's the very mark of <kanji>up</kanji> itself, floating above everything below it: to go up, rise.
items.reading_mnemonic: On that same trail, a hiker named Agatha grabs the balloon's string by mistake and is yanked skyward, yelling 「<reading>あがる</reading>」 as she rises past the summit — the sound of her cry, <reading>ah-ga-roo</reading>, is exactly how you say to go up, rise.

example_sentences.japanese: 猫が机の上に上がりました。
example_sentences.english: The cat climbed up onto the desk.
example_sentences.furigana: 猫[ねこ]が机[つくえ]の上[うえ]に上[あ]がりました。

example_sentences.japanese: 雨が上がって、公園で遊びました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat swats the offering shelf until the charm hanging beneath it swings loose, dropping further and further past the mossy steps — everything about it points one way, straight <kanji>below</kanji> where it used to sit: to go down, fall.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa the fire-breathing crow perches on the shrine's bell rope, but her weight drags it lower and lower until it dips past the mossy steps — she squawks a mournful 「<reading>さがる</reading>」, her cry sounding just like <reading>saga-ru</reading>, as she watches herself sink: to go down, fall.

example_sentences.japanese: 川の水が少し下がりました。
example_sentences.english: The river's water level dropped a little.
example_sentences.furigana: 川[かわ]の水[みず]が少[すこ]し下[さ]がりました。

example_sentences.furigana: 危[あぶ]ないですから、みんな後[うし]ろに下[さ]がりました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a kid raises his hand so high above his desk it nearly brushes the ceiling, then keeps going — hoisting his chair, his bag, even the wastebasket until everything in the room sits <kanji>above</kanji> where it started: to raise.
items.reading_mnemonic: In the echoing hallway, the same kid hoists the trophy case higher, grunting 「<reading>あげる</reading>」 with each heave, the sound landing right on <reading>ah-geh-roo</reading> — pure effort to raise something up.

example_sentences.japanese: 学生は手を上げました。

example_sentences.furigana: 学[がく]生[せい]は手[て]を上[あ]げました。

example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は声[こえ]を上[あ]げました。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は頭を上げました。

example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は頭[あたま]を上[あ]げました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The shelf from 下 tilts, and the crate riding on it slides toward that dangling mark, sliding <kanji>down, below</kanji> the shelf's edge until it's about to hit the floor on its own. Before that happens you grab the crate and lower it yourself, hand over hand, taking it down deliberately instead of letting gravity finish the job.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa the fire-breathing crow perches above Koichi's konbini loading dock, puffing little flames as a signal. The clerks call back "<reading>oh, rose</reading>!" mishearing his screech for a flower, but they still know to <reading>おろす</reading> the delivery crates, lowering box after box off the truck onto the pavement.

example_sentences.japanese: 銀行でお金を下ろします。

example_sentences.furigana: 銀[ぎん]行[こう]でお金[かね]を下[お]ろします。

example_sentences.furigana: 車[くるま]から荷[に]物[もつ]を下[お]ろしました。

example_sentences.furigana: 机[つくえ]の上[うえ]から本[ほん]を下[お]ろしてください。

items.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a hiker's phone slips loose from an unzipped pocket and tumbles by itself past the vending machine, bouncing down switchback after switchback with nobody chasing it. Nobody pushed it, nobody dropped it on purpose — it just goes, all the way down into the ravine below, entirely on its own.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a tanuki named Otchi loses his footing on the loose gravel and yelps "<reading>ouchy</reading>!" as he tumbles past the vending machine. His cry is how you remember <reading>おちる</reading>, the verb for anything that simply falls on its own.

example_sentences.japanese: 財布が道に落ちました。
example_sentences.english: My wallet fell onto the road.
example_sentences.furigana: 財[さい]布[ふ]が道[みち]に落[お]ちました。

example_sentences.japanese: 木から花が落ちました。
example_sentences.english: A flower fell from the tree.
example_sentences.furigana: 木[き]から花[はな]が落[お]ちました。

example_sentences.japanese: 鍵が机から落ちました。
example_sentences.english: The key fell off the desk.
example_sentences.furigana: 鍵[かぎ]が机[つくえ]から落[お]ちました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a boy juggling erasers by the sports field takes aim and flings one straight down onto his rival's shoe, on purpose, then strolls off whistling. Nobody trips him, nothing slips — he means to send it down, and that deliberate act of sending something down is the whole word.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a boy named Otto stands at the sports field fence and shouts "<reading>oh, toss</reading> it here!" before yanking the ball straight down out of the air himself. That shout is how you remember <reading>おとす</reading>, the verb for deliberately dropping something.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は財布を落としました。
example_sentences.english: I dropped my wallet.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は財[さい]布[ふ]を落[お]としました。

example_sentences.japanese: 猫が机の上から本を落とした。

example_sentences.furigana: 猫[ねこ]が机[つくえ]の上[うえ]から本[ほん]を落[お]とした。

example_sentences.japanese: 女の子はお菓子を落とした。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one of the many cats steals an offering plate from beneath the enormous bell, but the mossy steps make for a terrible getaway. Guilt, or maybe just clumsiness, wins out, and by dawn the cat has quietly carried the plate all the way back to the exact spot it took it from.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat flings a fish bone past the enormous bell, and every time it sails back into her paw the bell gives one clean "<reading>kay-essu</reading>" clang. That clang is <reading>かえす</reading>, the sound of something coming right back to where it started.

example_sentences.japanese: 図書館で借りた本を返します。
example_sentences.english: I'll return the book I borrowed from the library.
example_sentences.furigana: 図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]で借[か]りた本[ほん]を返[かえ]します。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達にお金を返しました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank the current is too fast to wade, so instead of crossing yourself you stretch out and hand the umbrella straight across to the woman waiting on the far bank. She catches it one-handed, dry the whole time — you didn't cross the river, you handed it over.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat drags a stray pot of stew up the mossy steps and dumps it at your feet. '<reading>What a stew</reading>,' you mutter — <reading>わたす</reading> — as Grandma Kane scolds you for feeding the shrine cats her prized dinner.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は友達に本を渡しました。
example_sentences.english: I handed my friend a book.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は友[とも]達[だち]に本[ほん]を渡[わた]しました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You wake with the sun already high, sprint to Sei's school still wearing one shoe, and skid into the echoing hallway just as the bell finishes its last ring. Every other seat is filled, every face turned toward the door, toward you, standing there late.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei tears down the mountain trail toward school, trips over a root by the lone vending machine, and yells '<reading>oh, curry!</reading>' as his lunchbox bursts open — <reading>おくれる</reading> — arriving with rice down his shirt and the bell already silent.

example_sentences.japanese: バスが遅れています。
example_sentences.english: The bus is running late.
example_sentences.furigana: バスが遅[おく]れています。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は学校に遅れました。

example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は学[がっ]校[こう]に遅[おく]れました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The last train chimes its warning right outside Koichi's konbini, and you abandon your basket mid-scan, shove past the onigiri shelf, and pelt for the platform doors as they begin to slide shut. There's no time left to think — only to hurry.
items.reading_mnemonic: A cat bolts down the mossy steps of Grandma Kane's shrine for no reason at all, and you chase after it shouting '<reading>easy, go, easy, go!</reading>' — <reading>いそぐ</reading> — sprinting the whole way down before the enormous bell finishes its first toll.

example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は急[いそ]いで学[がっ]校[こう]へ行[い]きました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini till is buried under boxes he can't shift alone, so you hold up your <kanji>hand</kanji>, fingers spread the way you always picture it, and slide it under the heaviest crate just before it tips. You're not doing his job for him — you're only lending a <kanji>hand</kanji>, which is exactly what helping means.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the sports field at Sei's school, your friend can't lift the net alone, so you jog over saying '<reading>let's do</reading> this together' — <reading>てつだう</reading> — and grab the other end before he drops it.
items.description: 手伝う specifically means pitching in on a task that's mainly someone else's — helping with chores, homework, or work — rather than a general word for rescuing or assisting in any sense.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You are locked out of your apartment in the rain, keys sitting in plain view on the kitchen counter through the window, phone dead, neighbor not home. You stand under the awning testing the same doorknob for the tenth time, and this exact useless loop is the meaning: to be troubled.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the vending machine on the mountain trail, a scruffy kangaroo blocks your way, its fur knotted with burrs. You crouch down and <reading>comb a roo</reading> right there on the gravel, and the line of hikers behind you groans, thoroughly <reading>こまる</reading> at the wait.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The supply cabinet at your office has exactly one stapler, and by Friday afternoon it is simply gone — not broken, not borrowed, gone. items.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, a woodpecker hammers the same dead branch for hours until it finally splits and topples into the current. The birds go quiet — <reading>knock, no more</reading> — and the fisherman sighs: whatever was there has become <reading>なくなる</reading>, gone for good.

items.meaning_mnemonic: After the birthday party ends and the last guest waves goodbye, one lonely slice of cake sits alone on the table, uneaten, crumbs scattered everywhere else. Everyone else got their piece and left; only this slice stayed behind. That staying-behind, the leftover, is the meaning: to remain.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the last onigiri on the shelf turns out to be a display fake with <reading>no core</reading> — just rice on the outside, hollow within. Koichi leaves it sitting there past closing, the one item that never sells: it simply <reading>のこる</reading>, remains, night after night.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You watch an intersection from the corner for a full minute: the light is red, then amber, then green, then back to red, cars stopping and starting each time. Nothing about the pole itself moves, yet everything it signals is different every time you look. That shifting-in-place is the meaning: to change.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school sports field, someone drives a tiny toy car through a puddle shaped exactly like a <reading>car wash</reading>, and it rolls out a completely different color than it went in. Sei blinks at the repainted car and mutters that everything on this field has just <reading>かわる</reading>, changed.

example_sentences.furigana: 天[てん]気[き]が変[か]わりました。

example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は少[すこ]し変[か]わりました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a courier frog named Kaera swaps one basket for another on every crossing — rice one way, laundry the other, never both at once. She doesn't just move things, she changes what's in someone else's hands entirely. That deliberate swap is what the word teaches: something changes because someone changed it.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaera the frog announces each swap with a croak that sounds like <reading>かえる</reading> — the vendors nearby just call her <reading>Kaera</reading>, and the name stuck to the sound itself.
items.description: This is the transitive verb — you change something (someone changes their mind, changes the schedule), always with an object. There's a separate intransitive partner meaning something changes on its own; that one takes a different reading, so don't reach for this word when nothing did the changing.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は名前を変えました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one of the countless cats leaps for a moth and misses, slamming into the enormous mossy bell instead. The whole hillside goes still for a second, then the bell answers — one huge sound rolling down the steps. Nobody rang it on purpose; it simply rang, sound arriving as a consequence, not a choice.
items.reading_mnemonic: The shrine cat is named <reading>Naru</reading>, and when she yowls at the bell it answers with a tone the locals swear sounds just like her name — <reading>なる</reading> — echoing down the steps every time.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Near the top of the steep mountain trail, the one lonely vending machine keeps its light on all night, a single bright square glowing over the dark ridge. Hikers exhausted from the climb spot it from three switchbacks away before anything else on the mountain — the machine's whole purpose, up here, is simply to shine.
items.reading_mnemonic: The hiker who restocks that machine is named <reading>Hikaru</reading>, and climbers joke that both he and the machine do the same job on that ridge: <reading>ひかる</reading>, shining so you don't miss the top.

example_sentences.japanese: 夜、空に星が光っています。
example_sentences.english: At night, stars shine in the sky.
example_sentences.furigana: 夜[よる]、空[そら]に星[ほし]が光[ひか]っています。

example_sentences.japanese: 暗い部屋で猫の目が光りました。
example_sentences.english: The cat's eyes shone in the dark room.
example_sentences.furigana: 暗[くら]い部屋[へや]で猫[ねこ]の目[め]が光[ひか]りました。

example_sentences.furigana: 朝[あさ]、川[かわ]の水[みず]が光[ひか]っていました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Inside Koichi's konbini, the ceiling mascot's stuffing has sprung a slow leak, and tufts drift down over the onigiri shelf like a private snowfall that never reaches the door. The till keeps beeping through it as customers brush fluff off their shoulders. Whatever comes down from above, steadily and without asking, is what falls.
items.reading_mnemonic: Customers call that drifting stuff the mascot's <reading>fur</reading>, and the clerk mutters the word every time it happens — <reading>ふる</reading> — since in this konbini it never rains, it just falls.
items.description: This verb is reserved for rain and snow falling from the sky — it doesn't extend to objects falling in general, so don't reach for it when something merely drops or tips over.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は雨が降っています。
example_sentences.english: It's raining today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は雨[あめ]が降[ふ]っています。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日、雪がたくさん降りました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi finds the drink-cooler's price sticker curling up at the corner, licks the back of a fresh one from the roll, and presses it down flat against the glass with his whole palm until every corner is glued flat. items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi keeps a toy <reading>harpoon</reading> by the register and spears each curling flyer clean onto the corkboard so it stays flat, muttering <reading>はる</reading> under his breath with every satisfying thunk.

example_sentences.japanese: 手紙に切手を貼りました。
example_sentences.english: I stuck a stamp on the letter.
example_sentences.furigana: 手[て]紙[がみ]に切[きっ]手[て]を貼[は]りました。

example_sentences.japanese: かばんに写真を貼ります。
example_sentences.english: I'll stick a photo on my bag.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane crosses the mossy shrine steps every morning with a saucer of milk, choosing the exact same paw-worn stone by the enormous bell and setting it down without a wobble, right where the cats expect it. That precise, deliberate setting-down is putting or placing something exactly where it belongs.
items.reading_mnemonic: She lowers the saucer onto a gnarled root of <reading>oak</reading> jutting from the shrine steps, whispering <reading>おく</reading> each time like a little rule for where things go.

example_sentences.japanese: 机の上に辞書を置きます。
example_sentences.english: I put the dictionary on the desk.
example_sentences.furigana: 机[つくえ]の上[うえ]に辞[じ]書[しょ]を置[お]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 傘をどこに置きましたか。
example_sentences.english: Where did you put the umbrella?
example_sentences.furigana: 傘[かさ]をどこに置[お]きましたか。

example_sentences.japanese: 財布をかばんの中に置きました。
example_sentences.english: I put my wallet inside the bag.
example_sentences.furigana: 財[さい]布[ふ]をかばんの中[なか]に置[お]きました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, someone parks a go-kart beside the lone vending machine and wanders off for a drink. By the time they turn back, the kart has already rolled halfway down the slope on its own, nobody behind the wheel, nothing pushing it — it's simply moving.
items.reading_mnemonic: Watching the driverless kart trundle downhill, you swear its engine mutters <reading>a go-kart</reading>, which is about as close as English gets to <reading>うごく</reading> — the sound of something moving all by itself.

example_sentences.japanese: 電車が動きました。
example_sentences.english: The train started moving.
example_sentences.furigana: 電[でん]車[しゃ]が動[うご]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: あの時計は動きません。
example_sentences.english: That clock doesn't move.
example_sentences.furigana: あの時計[とけい]は動[うご]きません。

example_sentences.japanese: 猫が椅子の下で動きました。
example_sentences.english: The cat moved under the chair.
example_sentences.furigana: 猫[ねこ]が椅[い]子[す]の下[した]で動[うご]きました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, a rowboat sits beached and refuses to budge. Sue plants both feet in the mud, braces against the hull, and shoves until it finally slides free into the current. The boat never moves itself — Sue is the one who moves it, which is exactly what it means to move something.
items.reading_mnemonic: As the hull finally scrapes free, someone on the bank yells <reading>a go-car, Sue!</reading> — cheering her on, and about as close as English gets to <reading>うごかす</reading>, moving something that wouldn't move on its own.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は椅子を動かしました。
example_sentences.english: I moved the chair.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は椅[い]子[す]を動[うご]かしました。

example_sentences.japanese: 猫が箱を動かしました。
example_sentences.english: The cat moved the box.
example_sentences.furigana: 猫[ねこ]が箱[はこ]を動[うご]かしました。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は机を少し動かした。
example_sentences.english: He moved the desk a little.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は机[つくえ]を少[すこ]し動[うご]かした。

items.mnemonic_text: Bring it to a halt: tomeru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's onigiri cart breaks loose and rolls for the door. You don't chase it — you do what the mountain trail already taught your foot: plant it flat and hard, right in the cart's path. The wheels ram your ankle and jam dead, frozen mid-roll. That's your foot learning to <kanji>stop</kanji> something other than itself.
items.reading_mnemonic: 止（と）＋める gives you the reading <reading>とめる</reading> straight from the と you already know for 止 plus the plain める ending — nothing new to memorize here.

example_sentences.japanese: 父は家の前で車を止めました。
example_sentences.english: My father stopped the car in front of the house.
example_sentences.furigana: 父[ちち]は家[いえ]の前[まえ]で車[くるま]を止[と]めました。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は音楽を止めた。
example_sentences.english: He stopped the music.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は音[おん]楽[がく]を止[と]めた。

example_sentences.japanese: 母は時計を止めました。
example_sentences.english: My mother stopped the clock.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]は時計[とけい]を止[と]めました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You leave the house and immediately start replaying the stove, the door, the iron — did you actually turn them off? By the time you reach the corner you've invented three new disasters that haven't happened yet. That spiral of manufactured dread, dragging you back home just to check, is what it feels like to worry.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat named Shin balances a warm <reading>shin pie</reading> on his knee and paces the mossy steps, certain it will slide off. His fretting whisper is the sound: <reading>しんぱいする</reading> — worry itself, baked into a pie he can't stop watching.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は明日の試験を心配する。
example_sentences.english: I worry about tomorrow's exam.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は明日[あした]の試[し]験[けん]を心[しん]配[ぱい]する。

example_sentences.japanese: 母は毎日僕の仕事を心配する。
example_sentences.english: My mother worries about my job every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]は毎[まい]日[にち]僕[ぼく]の仕[し]事[ごと]を心[しん]配[ぱい]する。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は旅行の天気を心配する。
example_sentences.english: He worries about the weather for the trip.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は旅[りょ]行[こう]の天[てん]気[き]を心[しん]配[ぱい]する。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You're washing dishes at the riverbank when a heron that's been standing motionless for an hour suddenly explodes upward in a panic of wings and shrieks, sending dishes clattering into the water. That full-body jolt — the one where your whole body reacts before your brain has caught up — is being surprised.
items.reading_mnemonic: びっくりする is written exactly as it sounds — <reading>びっくりする</reading> — no kanji to decode, just the kana as your eyes see them.

example_sentences.japanese: 猫の声を聞くと、びっくりする。
example_sentences.english: You get surprised when you hear the cat's meow.
example_sentences.furigana: 猫[ねこ]の声[こえ]を聞[き]くと、びっくりする。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女の手紙を読んだら、びっくりすると思います。
example_sentences.english: I think I'll be surprised when I read her letter.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]の手[て]紙[がみ]を読[よ]んだら、びっくりすると思[おも]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 大きい犬を見ると、びっくりすることがあります。
example_sentences.english: Sometimes you get surprised when you see a big dog.
example_sentences.furigana: 大[おお]きい犬[いぬ]を見[み]ると、びっくりすることがあります。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the mountain trail's summit, a hiker collapses to one knee in front of the lone vending machine, holds up a coin like a ring, and asks it to supply him forever. The machine accepts, clunking out two canned coffees like vows exchanged. That absurd, binding transaction at the top of the mountain is what it means to marry.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kek, a scheming toad, runs his wedding tent as one long con, selling rings he calls forever deals. He names the racket <reading>けっこんする</reading>, and every couple lining up for <reading>Kek's con</reading> has no idea the scam is what actually binds them for life.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は来年結婚する。
example_sentences.english: I'm getting married next year.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は来[らい]年[ねん]結[けっ]婚[こん]する。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は医者と結婚すると思います。
example_sentences.english: I think she'll marry a doctor.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は医[い]者[しゃ]と結[けっ]婚[こん]すると思[おも]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 兄は来月結婚することにしました。
example_sentences.english: My older brother has decided to get married next month.
example_sentences.furigana: 兄[あに]は来[らい]月[げつ]結[けっ]婚[こん]することにしました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a monk barges through a crowd of cats mid-ceremony, gives the enormous bell one stiff bow, and backs straight out through the gate before the abbot can even turn around. That clipped, apologetic retreat — bow, mutter, gone — is exactly what to excuse oneself means: leaving politely before you've overstayed the room.
items.reading_mnemonic: The monk's name is Ray, and every time he flees a cat pile at the shrine he mutters it fast — <reading>しつれいする</reading> — which lands on your ear as <reading>she, too, RAY</reading>, like someone ducking out right behind him. That hurried, apologetic double-exit is the sound of the word.

example_sentences.japanese: 私はこれで失礼する。
example_sentences.english: I'll excuse myself now.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]はこれで失[しつ]礼[れい]する。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は晩ご飯の前に失礼すると言いました。
example_sentences.english: He said he'd excuse himself before dinner.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は晩[ばん]ご飯[はん]の前[まえ]に失[しつ]礼[れい]すると言[い]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は会社を失礼すると思います。
example_sentences.english: She thinks she'll excuse herself from work.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は会[かい]社[しゃ]を失[しつ]礼[れい]すると思[おも]います。

items.meaning_mnemonic: On Sei's sports field, a wren lands by the goalpost and shoos the same three pigeons off the grass, over and over, a hundred times before the whistle even blows. It never varies the routine, never skips a rep — that relentless repeating drill, doing the same motion until it's automatic, is what to practice means.
items.reading_mnemonic: The wren on the field never just shoos once — it shoos, resets, shoos again, and the coach starts calling the drill <reading>れんしゅうする</reading>, which sounds exactly like <reading>wren-shoo, over and over</reading>. That repeated wren-shoo routine is the sound of the word.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎日日本語を練習する。
example_sentences.english: I practice Japanese every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は毎[まい]日[にち]日本[にほん]語[ご]を練[れん]習[しゅう]する。

example_sentences.japanese: 図書館で漢字を練習するのが好きです。
example_sentences.english: I like practicing kanji at the library.
example_sentences.furigana: 図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]で漢[かん]字[じ]を練[れん]習[しゅう]するのが好[す]きです。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、友達と歌を練習する。
example_sentences.english: Tomorrow, I'll practice a song with a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、友[とも]達[だち]と歌[うた]を練[れん]習[しゅう]する。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a yak shoulders its way to the onigiri shelf before opening hours, plants a hoof on the exact spot it wants, and refuses to budge even when customers stack up behind it. Claiming a spot ahead of everyone else, locking it in before anyone can take it, is exactly what to reserve means.
items.reading_mnemonic: The yak at the shelf grunts a greeting every morning before claiming its spot — a flat <reading>yo</reading> followed by a stubborn <reading>YAK</reading> — and Koichi has started calling the whole ritual <reading>よやくする</reading>. That yo-YAK grunt, locking down the spot before anyone else can, is the sound of the word.

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、レストランを予約する。
example_sentences.english: Tomorrow, I'll reserve a restaurant.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、レストランを予[よ]約[やく]する。

example_sentences.japanese: 兄は飛行機を予約すると思います。
example_sentences.english: I think my older brother will book a flight.
example_sentences.furigana: 兄[あに]は飛[ひ]行[こう]機[き]を予[よ]約[やく]すると思[おも]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 部屋を二つ予約することができます。
example_sentences.english: I can reserve two rooms.
example_sentences.furigana: 部屋[へや]を二[ふた]つ予[よ]約[やく]することができます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a bee named June spends the whole climb before the cold sets in — stocking the hive, patching every gap, checking the vending machine at the top for one last snack. Getting everything lined up and ready before the real thing starts is exactly what to prepare means.
items.reading_mnemonic: June the bee never starts the climb without her checklist, and the other bees have started calling her ritual <reading>じゅんびする</reading> — said fast it lands as <reading>June-bee, sure</reading>, her name and her certainty rolled into one. That pre-climb checklist is the sound of the word.

example_sentences.japanese: 母は晩ご飯を準備する。
example_sentences.english: My mother is going to prepare dinner.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]は晩[ばん]ご飯[はん]を準[じゅん]備[び]する。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日試験があるので、今準備する。
example_sentences.english: I have an exam tomorrow, so I'm getting ready now.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]試[し]験[けん]があるので、今[いま]準[じゅん]備[び]する。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達は旅行のかばんを準備する。
example_sentences.english: My friend is preparing the travel bag.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]は旅[りょ]行[こう]のかばんを準[じゅん]備[び]する。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the till locks up mid-beep and nobody knows why. The new clerk grabs a marker, draws arrows all over a torn onigiri wrapper, and holds it up to the confused line of customers, mapping error code to fix one scribble at a time. That's the whole job here: to explain, arrow by arrow, until the confusion drains out of the room.
items.reading_mnemonic: Everyone at the konbini calls the diagram-happy clerk <reading>Setsumei</reading> behind her back, since that's basically what she does all shift. Picture her cornering yet another customer, marker in hand, doing full <reading>せつめいする</reading> mode over a jammed slushie machine.

example_sentences.japanese: 先生は問題を説明する。
example_sentences.english: The teacher explains the problem.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]は問[もん]題[だい]を説[せつ]明[めい]する。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は日本語で説明すると思います。
example_sentences.english: I think he'll explain it in Japanese.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は日本[にほん]語[ご]で説[せつ]明[めい]すると思[おも]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は友達に地図を説明することができました。
example_sentences.english: I was able to explain the map to my friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は友[とも]達[だち]に地[ち]図[ず]を説[せつ]明[めい]することができました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the new transfer student gets dragged in front of the class by the homeroom teacher, who cups both hands around her mouth like a game-show host unveiling a prize. Name, hometown, hobby — she rattles off all three before the poor kid can say a single word himself. That shove-and-announce routine is what it means to introduce someone.
items.reading_mnemonic: The homeroom teacher earned the nickname <reading>Shoukai</reading> from the class years ago, since introducing new people is basically her whole personality. Every transfer student gets the same routine: name, hometown, hobby, <reading>しょうかいする</reading> in full game-show voice before homeroom has even started.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は友達を紹介する。
example_sentences.english: I'll introduce my friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は友[とも]達[だち]を紹[しょう]介[かい]する。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は先生を紹介すると思います。
example_sentences.english: I think she'll introduce the teacher.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は先[せん]生[せい]を紹[しょう]介[かい]すると思[おも]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 会社で彼を紹介することになりました。
example_sentences.english: It's been decided that I'll introduce him at the company.
example_sentences.furigana: 会[かい]社[しゃ]で彼[かれ]を紹[しょう]介[かい]することになりました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: A vending-machine restocker's truck grinds up the mountain trail's switchbacks in first gear, engine screaming, cans rattling in the back, aiming for the one machine improbably parked at the summit. Nobody walks this delivery route — someone has to sit behind the wheel and wrestle it up every hairpin turn. That's the whole job: to drive, all the way to the top.
items.reading_mnemonic: The delivery driver grinding up the mountain trail goes by <reading>Unten</reading> to the vending-machine regulars, since that's all he ever seems to be doing. Ten hairpin turns in, he's still muttering <reading>うんてんする</reading> to himself like a chant, wheel in a death grip.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the cats gather every dusk under the little tent-roof shelter that is, as you already know, a roof made entirely of dinner. Tonight it's a full sit-down affair: bowls set in a row, tails tucked, nobody leaving until the tray's been properly cleared. That polite, four-legged sitting-down to <kanji>eat</kanji> is what the word describes — an actual meal, not just a snack.
items.reading_mnemonic: The shrine cats have one among them everyone calls <reading>Shokuji</reading>, because she's the only cat who sits down properly to eat instead of just snatching food. Even Grandma Kane comments on it — that cat, she says, actually does <reading>しょくじする</reading>, dining like a person instead of a stray.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi never really leaves his konbini. The fluorescent lights buzz all night, the onigiri shelf never empties, and he sleeps propped against the beeping till between customers. Every inch of that cramped bright box — from the door to the register — has become entirely his workplace, no separate word needed.
items.reading_mnemonic: Shigeko clocks out the instant the beep sounds, and every night without fail, <reading>she goes, to bar</reading> — same stool, same drink, before she's even said goodnight to the till. Everyone at the konbini agrees: <reading>しごとば</reading> is simply wherever she ends up, evening after evening.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's one true hobby is chasing the shrine cats with a broom, shouting them off the mossy steps every morning — then, the instant they scatter, she sits right down where they were and sighs happily, surrounded by the very cats she just chased. That ritual, pointless and adored, is what a hobby actually is.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every cat on Grandma Kane's mossy shrine steps knows the routine: she waves her broom and yells '<reading>shoo, me</reading> first!' at the fattest one, who never budges an inch. The neighbors just call it her <reading>しゅみ</reading> now — that daily standoff nobody ever wins.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, the vending machine at the summit isn't real — it never has cold drinks, it's always one more switchback past your last break, and it vanishes the moment you actually reach the top. Everyone who's hiked that trail knows the machine at the peak is only ever a dream.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the base of the mountain trail, a sign reads '<reading>you may</reading> rest here, traveler' — but climb further and the exact same sign keeps reappearing, word for word, at every switchback. Hikers swear the trail itself is a <reading>ゆめ</reading>, a dream that only pretends to have an end.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Under Koichi's konbini till sits that same roof-covered stash of gleaming <kanji>money</kanji>, kept buried safe the way it's always been. One slow night the clerk actually digs it up, counts every bill by hand, and slaps the stack flat on the counter — no card, no swipe, just physical bills you can hold. That dug-up, countable stack is cash.
items.reading_mnemonic: Ken forgets his card at the konbini every single week, so the clerk just sighs, '<reading>again, Ken</reading>?' and taps the register for cash instead. That resigned sigh is exactly the sound of <reading>げんきん</reading> — same till, same excuse, every time.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the summit vending machine, legs shaking from the climb, you watch the little display flicker between eight hundred yen and eight million before settling. It isn't broken, it's just deciding what altitude is worth. That flickering number, haggling with your exhaustion, is the price you paid to get here.
items.reading_mnemonic: Ned the horse trader neighs at dawn every morning before chalking a new number on his cart. Villagers set their clocks by his <reading>neigh-at-dawn</reading> ritual, since that's exactly how you say <reading>ねだん</reading>, the price he's picked for the day.

items.furigana: 領[りょう]収[しゅう]書[しょ]
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the register light dims like the sinking sun that once taught your hand to write. As it fades, the printer's little arm keeps that same sun-fed urge to <kanji>write</kanji>, scribbling out a curling strip of paper long after the customer's gone. That printed proof of the sale is the receipt.
items.reading_mnemonic: Leo Shoeshaw, the shrine's fussy clerk, won't hand back your coin offering until he's written a slip, barking his own name like a stamp: <reading>Leo! Shoe! Show!</reading> Grandma Kane says that clipped bark is exactly how you say <reading>りょうしゅうしょ</reading>, the receipt he presses into your palm.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a fisherman reels in his line expecting a fish and instead pulls up a dripping fistful of coins, more than he ever paid to be there. He shrugs, stuffs the extra into his pocket, and keeps casting. That unexpected excess handed back to you is change.
items.reading_mnemonic: Otsu, the riverbank fisherman, always over-tips the ferry boy, then waves off the leftover coins with a cheerful <reading>oh, too rich</reading>! Grandma Kane says his running joke is exactly how you remember <reading>おつり</reading>, the change he never wants back.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You cross the riverbank on a rickety ferry, soaked and shivering, and the only building on the far bank is a lantern-lit lodge with steaming baths and futons laid out. There's nowhere else to go, so you stay the night. That riverside shelter with a bath and a bed is an inn.
items.reading_mnemonic: Ryo, the ferryman, refuses to paddle back once the sun sets, mooring his boat with a satisfied <reading>leo-con</reading> and marching guests inside for the night. Grandma Kane says his nightly cry is exactly how you say <reading>りょかん</reading>, the inn he refuses to leave.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini run for onigiri turns into an all-nighter when the shelves multiply into fluorescent corridors, till after till after till, until he realizes he's wandered into a lobby lined with beds instead of shelves — he's checked into a hotel without meaning to.
items.reading_mnemonic: ホテル is a loanword written exactly as it sounds, straight from the English <reading>hotel</reading> — just recognize 「<reading>ホテル</reading>」 as the borrowed sound and move on.

items.furigana: 部屋[へや]番[ばん]号[ごう]
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the gym gets carved overnight into a maze of tiny rooms with no labels, so students keep wandering into supply closets looking for homeroom. The janitor storms through stapling a number to every single door until each one wears its room number like a name tag.
items.reading_mnemonic: A hall monitor at Sei's school bellows through a megaphone, <reading>hey, uh — bang, GO!</reading>, banging a gong before sprinting off, and the scrambling classroom just catches her cry fading down the corridor: 「<reading>へやばんごう</reading>」.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A courier at the riverbank keeps miscounting his stack of parcels, so he starts tying each one to a labeled post driven into the bank, one per house upstream, until every home along the water has its own numbered post marking exactly where its mail belongs — its address.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the riverbank, the courier hollers a <reading>zoo show</reading> parade of names through his megaphone before untying the last parcel — the post reads 「<reading>じゅうしょ</reading>」, the address stamped in waterproof ink, and off he paddles.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the summit of the mountain trail, the lone vending machine refuses every coin unless you first announce which slot you want, so hikers gasping from the climb start shouting out a number before they can get their can of coffee — the machine only understands you by your number.
items.reading_mnemonic: Partway up the mountain trail, hikers bang on the summit vending machine's glass, yelling <reading>bang, GO!</reading> at the slot they want, and the machine finally clatters out a can once it hears 「<reading>ばんごう</reading>」 shouted correctly.

items.furigana: 電[でん]話[わ]番[ばん]号[ごう]
items.meaning_mnemonic: The storm's <kanji>electricity</kanji> knocks the lights out at Koichi's konbini, and in the sudden dark the till clerk won't stop the <kanji>talk</kanji>, tongue wagging as he shouts a string of digits into the dead payphone. Nobody asked, but now you have his phone number.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, she bangs the enormous bell nine times, grabs the old phone, and chants <reading>でんわばんごう</reading> like a mantra while thumping a spare <reading>Denver bongo</reading> drum on every digit, refusing to hang up until the whole number lands.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You have exactly one afternoon and four separate errands — a form, a package, a shrine offering, a lost cat — and a goose at the riverbank follows you between every stop, honking as if supervising your business for the day. Four errands, one honking overseer: that's the whole word, errand, business, sorted.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a butler skids up to the vending machine and announces himself before every single errand: '<reading>ようじ</reading>, sir!' It comes out like <reading>yo, Jeeves</reading> shouted through cupped hands, over and over, one errand at a time.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Sei's school reschedules the exam for the exact hour the sports field floods and the vending machine jams — three disasters stacking into one tidy circumstance. The teacher just shrugs and cancels class: how convenient the timing turned out to be. That's circumstances, and convenience, in one word.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a fisherman reels in a vending machine still stocked with cold drinks, and all he can say is <reading>つごう</reading> — it comes out sounding like <reading>too good</reading> to be true. That's つごう: the lucky circumstance, the convenience nobody arranged.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, a hiker turns back at the exact same rock every single time, and every time he has a brand new one lined up before anyone even asks — the sun, his knee, a text he needs to send. Stack enough of those up and you've got his reason, freshly invented, every single climb.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane finds another cat sprawled on the shrine steps and demands, '<reading>りゆう</reading>?' — which comes out sounding like <reading>really, you</reading>? — insisting the cat explain itself before it's allowed to nap there. That demand for an explanation is exactly what りゆう means: the reason.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>spirit</kanji> puffing off your rice bowl never behaves the same way twice — some mornings it billows thick and warm, curling lazily upward; other mornings it comes out thin and jagged, quick to vanish. Whatever shape that rising wisp takes right now is exactly what you're carrying inside: your feeling, your mood.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kiki the tree spirit slips from the shrine's mossy trunk to check on the sulking cats and croons her singsong <reading>“kee-mochi, kee-mochi”</reading> at each one, her own way of asking <reading>きもち</reading> — how are you feeling — until every tail flicks back up happy.

items.meaning_mnemonic: That flexed-arm stroke you already know as <kanji>power</kanji> doesn't stay still — picture it arm-wrestling every kid at Sei's school, elbow slammed onto the sports field bench, muscle bulging. It flattens every challenger the same way every time: raw <kanji>strength</kanji>, just proving itself in a bigger arena.
items.reading_mnemonic: 力 keeps the exact reading you already learned for it, so the word for power and strength is simply <reading>ちから</reading> — no new sound to memorize.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>spirit</kanji>-wisp that curls off warm rice drifts up the mountain trail and meets the same blade that once cut a pie into eight wedges. It slices the wisp into shifting <kanji>parts</kanji>, some warm, some sharp, and whichever part you're holding when you reach the vending machine at the summit — that's exactly your mood, your feeling.
items.reading_mnemonic: 気分 just stacks the readings you already know, 気（き）plus 分（ぶん）, giving you <reading>きぶん</reading> straight down the line — nothing new to learn.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A heron wades to the exact same flat rock on the riverbank every single evening, shoves aside any duck already perched there, and refuses to fish from anywhere else. It has, unmistakably, claimed its seat, and nothing short of a flood will move it.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a heron waddles in from the riverbank and hops onto the one stool by the onigiri shelf, hissing <reading>“seh-kee, seh-kee”</reading> at anyone who gets close. The till beeps in protest, but the bird has already claimed its <reading>せき</reading>, and it isn't moving for till hours.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane pins a paper map to the shrine gate and stabs one finger at a single dot, refusing to move it no matter how the wind flaps the paper. Everyone who asks directions gets sent to that exact dot — the place, and only that place.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the mountain trail's lone vending machine, a badger drags out a hand-painted sign and slaps it against the machine, yelling that the <reading>bash show</reading> starts right <reading>ばしょ</reading> — this exact spot, nowhere else, no matter how far the crowd already climbed.

items.meaning_mnemonic: That dangling tail on the shelf mark doesn't stop at the floor — it keeps boring straight <kanji>down, below</kanji> the konbini's tile until it opens into a second, windowless shop stocked entirely in the dark. Everything down there, beneath ordinary ground, is underground — the basement level Koichi never mentions to customers.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa perches above Koichi's konbini and breathes one puff of fire clean through a floor grate. Down in the scorched cellar it leaves behind a cheeky little scorch mark — <reading>ちか</reading>, the <reading>cheeky</reading> ash patch — proof he was there, one floor underground.

items.meaning_mnemonic: That same spear, driven clean through the mouth-shaped opening, doesn't stop at one skewer — it pins three coins to the shrine step in a perfect row, and no matter how Grandma Kane's cats bat at the ends, the spear always balances dead level at its <kanji>middle, inside</kanji> point. Whatever sits there, exactly equidistant from both edges, is the center — the true middle.
items.reading_mnemonic: Chuu marches to the exact middle of the shrine steps and refuses to budge, topknot bobbing, no matter how the cats circle him. When Grandma Kane asks where he's planted himself, he squeaks the answer proudly: <reading>まんなか</reading> — <reading>the man in the middle</reading> — dead center, not one step off.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The mountain trail swaps its steep dirt slope for a perfectly cut staircase overnight, one vending machine still stranded at the very top like nothing changed. Climbers now count each step aloud, relieved someone finally built proper stairs instead of a slope.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a boy named Kai races his friend Dan up the new staircase, shouting a countdown as they climb: <reading>かいだん</reading> — <reading>Kai, Dan</reading> — one name per step, over and over, until they reach the landing out of breath. Stairs, and the boys who race them.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A vending machine sits at the very top of the mountain trail, impossible to reach on foot. Some hiker gave up climbing years ago and bolted a box to the cliff face that just goes straight up, dinging at each impossible landing until the doors slide open right onto the summit. That box is the elevator.
items.reading_mnemonic: エレベーター is a katakana loanword straight from English, so saying <reading>elevator</reading> is saying <reading>エレベーター</reading> — the sound is the whole word, no decoding needed.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's mossy shrine steps got tired of climbers stopping to catch their breath, so one day the whole staircase started crawling upward on its own, each step sliding onto the next in an endless diagonal parade. The shrine cats ride it like a conveyor belt straight past the enormous bell. That self-walking staircase is the escalator.
items.reading_mnemonic: エスカレーター is a katakana loanword straight from English, so saying <reading>escalator</reading> is saying <reading>エスカレーター</reading> — the sound is the whole word.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini has one doorway low enough that you have to duck your head to step through — that's the ducking figure who <kanji>enters</kanji>. Beyond it the sliding doors gape like a giant <kanji>mouth</kanji>, wide open all night, swallowing customers whole. Duck, then get swallowed by the mouth: that gaping doorway is the entrance.
